#3417. The Best Amazon Prime Benefits You Probably Don't Know About

If you’re going to commit to an Amazon Prime membership, you might as well squeeze as much as you can out of the deal. And there's a good amount of juice to squeeze there. The price you pay for Amazon depends on many factors, but regardless of how much you're paying, it's worth it for most people (we've done the math).

If you're on the fence about signing up, consider that Amazon's Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale is underway, and the company is hosting some amazing tech deals. It's a great time to sell your soul—or take advantage of the 30-day free trial—and there's a lot more to your membership than just deals and free shipping.

The standard Prime membership costs $14.99 per month or $139 per year, but there are other tiers that some people might qualify for. For example, the Amazon Prime for Young Adults program allows young adults between the ages of 18 and 24 to get all of the Prime perks for half the cost—$7.49 per month or $69 annually.

I'll be the first to admit I didn't know all of the benefits that Amazon Prime offers to its members. There are a lot more perks than people think. Here are the most impressive ones (and check out the full list):

Fast free shipping on millions of items: Depending on where you live, shipping can take one or two days, and some even come on the same day for orders of $25 or more in most areas—and it’s always free (if being shipped by the Amazon store).

Select pre-ordered items can be delivered on their release date for free (for most areas).

The option to have items delivered inside your garage with a smart garage device (depending on where you live) for $1.99 per order, or for free if you combine it with Amazon Day delivery.

Earn rewards for future purchases when you select free no-rush shipping.

The option to have all your weekly orders delivered on a specific day, to reduce waste from boxes.

Amazon Prime Visa card: Cardholders get 5% back on Amazon, Whole Foods, Chase Travel, and other purchases. Prime members who use this card extensively can earn rewards that offset the cost of membership.

A Grubhub+ and Uber Eats membership, normally $9.99 per month, which gets you free delivery on eligible orders, lower service fees, exclusive deals, and other perks as long as you remain a Prime Member (it used to be only for a year). The Uber Eats membership gets you free delivery on eligible restaurants of $25 or more.

Sharing with family or friends: Amazon Family is the existing program for sharing Prime benefits, and it allows you to add separate profiles for one other adult who lives in the same household as the primary account holder, up to four teens, and up to four child accounts. This grants access to all the standard benefits, such as free delivery, Prime Video with ads, Prime Reading, third-party benefits like Grubhub, and access to audiobooks, e-books, certain games, and Amazon Music.

Amazon Health: Prime users get One Medical access for an additional $9 per month or $99 per year. Through your devices, you’ll have 24/7 access to on-demand virtual care, plus real-life access to primary care offices in a number of U.S. cities. It accepts most major health insurance plans, too.

Amazon Pharmacy: Access to free two-day delivery and other savings on medications.

Prime Video: Prime includes unlimited streaming of movies, TV shows, and Amazon Originals with ads, which normally costs $9 per month.

Amazon Music Prime: Access to Amazon's Spotify-esque music streaming service (not to be confused with Amazon's other music streaming subscriptions).

Amazon Luna: A cloud gaming platform that offers new free games every month, free downloadable PC games, content, a monthly Twitch channel subscription, and a free channel subscription on Twitch each month for Prime Members.

Amazon Photos: Unlimited photo storage plus 5 GBs for videos and other files (which extends to members of your Family Vault).

Prime Reading: Free access to a rotating selection of e-books and magazines for Kindle or Fire tablets and Kindle apps.

Amazon's First Reads: You get up to two free e-books every month from a curated list of books handpicked by editors.

#3416. This Year, Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade Is Doing Broadway a Little Differently

For theater lovers, this year’s Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade is going to look a bit different. Those accustomed to waking up early to get a glimpse of the five or so best performances from the current Broadway season will have to adjust their expectations. This year, there’s only one big Broadway number. But don’t fret, theater folk. For the milestone occasion of the parade’s 100th anniversary, the powers that be at NBC and Macy’s have put a new spin on their tried-and-true formula, gathering the Broadway community for one supersized performance, featuring more shows and performers than ever before.

The result is an epic 10-minute medley, introduced by Julianne Hough, who will star in Damn Yankees on Broadway this spring, featuring nine beloved Broadway shows: The Book of Mormon, Chicago, Disney’s Aladdin, Hamilton, The Lost Boys, Rent, Richard O’Brien’s The Rocky Horror Show, Schmigadoon!, and—what else?—Wicked.

The mastermind behind the mega-medley is none other than Tom Kitt, the Tony-, Emmy-, Grammy-, and Pulitzer Prize–winning composer behind Next to Normal, If/Then, and Almost Famous. Kitt is no stranger to writing a big production number, having cowritten the Tony Awards opening number “Bigger!,” performed by host Neil Patrick Harris with lyrics by Lin-Manuel Miranda in 2013, among other ambitious musical endeavors. Despite his previous experience, a 10-minute, nine-show medley presented a unique set of challenges the composer had yet to tackle.

A total of 133 people are performing in the medley—114 Broadway cast members, 17 dancers, a child actor, and Hough. On top of that, more than 125 other Broadway professionals—including stage managers, wardrobe supervisors, and hair and makeup teams—are on site to facilitate the production, bringing the total number of people involved to well over 250.

“Most important to me in doing something like this—to celebrate this community, this beautiful community that I’m so lucky to be a part of,” Kitt tells me. “Everyone who’s participating, you want them to feel happy and excited about what they’re doing.”

A little over a month ago, Kitt and creative producer Sarah O’Gleby got to work figuring out how to make a cohesive musical number out of nine very different shows. He wrote the first draft of the arrangement over the course of a few days. “It was way too long,” he says. That might be because Kitt had to figure out how to connect these disparate shows musically while also finding room for Easter eggs for theater fans: musical nods to shows that might not otherwise be featured in the medley, including Anything Goes, The Music Man, A Chorus Line, and Kitt’s personal favorite, Into the Woods, whose music kicks things off.

“Into the Woods was one of those shows that made me want to write for the theater,” he tells me. “The downbeat of the prologue is one of the most beautiful musical gestures; every time I hear it, I get goosebumps. So that was really special and important for me to get to plug into, and there are so many others.”

Surprisingly, it will be Kitt’s first time attending the parade in person. “The parade has meant so much to me,” he says. “I’ve watched it for years. I’ve taped it. I’m lucky enough to have shows that have been a part of it. I think that celebrating that relationship and celebrating the history of Broadway and being able to spotlight so many important shows and artists just feels very exciting and gratifying.”

“I’m a tiny little person, but I love to do really big things,” says O’Gleby. A former performer on the West End, O’Gleby moved to the States almost two decades ago to pursue a career as a Broadway performer, dancing in revivals of Brigadoon and How to Succeed in Business Without Really Trying. Now she choreographs Broadway productions like Shucked and, most recently, Pink’s widely celebrated Tony Awards opening number. Given her Broadway bona fides, she’s also intimately familiar with the magic of the parade. “I was lucky to perform on the parade as a Broadway girl and the associate choreographer and dance captain on shows that I was in,” she says. “It was so wonderfully American.”

The first of two rehearsals took place Friday afternoon at Pier59 Studios at Chelsea Piers. Around 4 p.m., as the sun began to set over the Hudson River, Broadway performers from different shows practiced the medley. O’Gleby, wearing silver leather pants and clutching a God mic, was charged with organizing the chaos and managing the more than 100 Broadway performers in the room. Standing offstage between a broomstick and a red Les Mis flag, I could still see traces of green makeup on the face of Wicked’s current Elphaba, Keri René Fuller. Most of the performers gathered had a show of their own to perform in just a few hours, but that didn’t stop them from giving it their all in rehearsal, onstage and off, cheering the other productions along as each got its moment in the spotlight.

Case in point: At the end of the rehearsal, the whole room erupted into cheers for the original cast members from Rent—including original Angel, Tony winner Wilson Jermaine Heredia, and original Joanne, Fredi Walker—who are gathering to perform “Seasons of Love” in the parade. (During the rehearsal, Aladdin’s current Genie, Sherri Shepherd, couldn’t help but mouth along to the words of the seminal song.) “It was that moment of why we’re a part of this community,” O’Gleby says, nearly choking up. “Everyone in the room—stage managers, costume, I mean everybody in the room—the way they were applauding these original cast members and what they gave to all of us as a community, really all over the world, it was incredible.”

At the second rehearsal, on Monday night outside on 34th Street beneath Macy’s giant turkey, the mood remained high even as the temperatures dropped. By 11 p.m., performers were bundled in winter jackets, sweatshirts, and leg warmers, with their character shoes still on. They hugged one another for warmth and jumped up and down, kicking their feet to stay loose between setups. Margaret Cho, who stars as the Narrator in The Rocky Horror Show, danced “The Time Warp” with her Chihuahua, Lucia, tucked into a pouch in her jacket, the dog’s head peeking out.

For O’Gleby, a smooth Monday-night rehearsal means setting each show up for success come Thursday morning and making sure all nine shows are “represented in the most powerful and clear storytelling way that we can,” she says. “This is a huge moment for these shows to sell lots of tickets so everyone gets to keep making their magic every night. And so it’s important to me that each team gets to communicate what they need and what they think would really make their show shine.”

The weather forecast looks less than ideal for Thursday. Per the New York Post, there’s a “significant chance” that the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade could be grounded because of an incoming nor’easter, potentially rendering all that preparation moot. Nevertheless, the powers that be remain optimistic that, rain or shine, the show will go on.

“The weather will be what it will be, but we will delight in that and deliver the best,” says O’Gleby.

#3415. The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping Explains One Haymitch Detail Nobody Ever Questioned

Spoilers for "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" ahead.

It's obvious why prequels are appealing. After all, they allow you to see more of the characters you love in situations that are (hopefully) less miserable than the ones you previously saw them in. The problem with prequels is that they often offer origin stories and explanations for details that no one asked about. This is how we end up with stuff like, perhaps most infamously, the bizarre explanation for how Han Solo got his name in "Solo: A Star Wars Story."

In contrast, you have the "Hunger Games" film prequels, which actually flesh out the inhabitants and world of Panem in meaningful ways. Take "The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes," which is good enough to get you rooting for the "Hunger Games" franchise's big bad, Coriolanus Snow, as a young man despite knowing how monstrous he eventually becomes. It also reveals how the Games themselves came to be after nearly being canceled once upon a time. Notably, these explanations feel natural and crucial to the movie's story, as opposed to coming across as forced connections to the previous "Hunger Games" films.

The trend continues with "Sunrise on the Reaping," a fantastic movie that makes Haymitch Abernathy not only a hugely important character to the overall "Hunger Games" saga but one of its saddest, too. (If anything, this film shows he should be drinking more as an older man in the prior movies.) It even turns Plutarch Heavensbee into this franchise's version of Luthen Rael from "Andor," depicting him as a revolutionary stuck behind enemy lines and burning for a sunrise he'll never see.

And on top of all of that, it gives us the last backstory we expected — one for the gap in Haymitch's teeth when he's older.

Joseph Zada does a very good job in "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" as Haymitch, making the character his own to embody this particular period in the character's life. At the same time, he does capture a lot of Woody Harrelson's mannerisms as Haymitch from the original "Hunger Games" quadrilogy, including his voice. That being said, there is no denying that Zada does not look that much like Harrelson — especially with his curls and noticeable lack of a gap between his two front teeth, which is Harrelson's most distinguishable facial feature.

However, rather than relying on viewers' suspension of disbelief, "Sunrise on the Reaping" actually closes the gap (pun intended) between the two actors. In the film, Haymitch is beaten within an inch of his life right before winning the titular Games, at which point he sets off an explosion as a final act of defiance. As a result, he's knocked unconscious, only to wake up later with his wounds having been stitched shut. Even so, he looks different now, with the impact of the explosion having broken his nose and smashed his teeth

This is the "Hunger Games" equivalent of Hercule Poirot's mustache getting a gritty origin story tied to the horrors of WWI in Kenneth Branagh's "Death on the Nile" film adaptation, only here, it somehow works. It's because Haymitch examining his teeth is a blink-and-you-miss it detail, as opposed to one that the movie draws heavy attention to. Thus, there's no grand score announcing this as something important (like when River Phoenix's young Indy gets his scar and hat in "Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade"). Instead, it's simply showing the natural aftermath of a brutal fight.

Is Hollywood embracing Gwyneth Paltrow's return to acting?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Gwyneth Paltrow returned to the big screen for her role in the Academy Award-nominated film Marty Supreme, starring Timothée Chalamet. Ultimately, Paltrow ended up receiving considerable praise for her performance as Kay Stone. And the A24 sports dramedy about a ping-pong prodigy earned major praise and multiple awards-season nods. However, before all of that, Paltrow wondered if Hollywood would want her back.

Beyond the role itself, what ultimately got Paltrow to sign on for Marty Supreme was the fact that both the son she shares with Coldplay frontman Chris Martin and her husband Brad Falchuk’s son left for college, freeing her up for the first time since Avengers: Endgame. She recently recalled that time in her life while appearing on Today:

I think what happened was when our boys went to college two years ago, at the same time, it was like, right as they were going, I was offered Marty Supreme. And I thought, ‘Wow, what a great…’ It really opened up this idea that I could maybe do it, and since the kids were no longer at home, I was really free to go [film it].

After first appearing in the Marvel Cinematic Universe via Iron Man in 2008, Paltrow was a regular presence throughout the films. However, she eventually took a step back and devoted much of her time to running her wellness company, Goop, raising her kids and enjoying a quieter life away from film sets.

But just because Paltrow wanted to return to the big screen, it didn’t mean that anyone else would necessarily embrace her decision. During the recent interview, the Pepper Potts actress was asked if she had thought about whether anyone would even want to see her taking on roles in Hollywood again, and her answer was very candid. She said:

Yes, I did. I really did. I thought, ‘I don’t know if there will be a place for me anymore.’ But I’m really glad that there seems to be.

Marty Supreme turned out to be a really smart choice for the former Glee star to jump back into the acting game with. Paltrow also revealed that the process of acting and making a movie is pretty much the same since the last time she did it. The thing that has changed is the approach to marketing and press junkets.

It’s no longer just about finding out whether Hollywood wants you back when you take a break, or even about how your performance is received. You also have to find a way to generate buzz to capture the attention of audiences, with social media playing into it all. The Seven star explained:

I think the doing of it is pretty much the same. I think all the marketing around it — that’s all changed a lot. There’s all the social media component to marketing something. Press junkets are not what they used to be. That format has totally changed, but I think it’s largely the same.

When it came to generating buzz for the Timothée Chalamet starrer, the PR blitz included a massive orange blimp touring across the U.S., fans camping out for the viral Marty jackets, and even the Las Vegas Sphere being turned into a giant ping pong.

I can’t imagine Paltrow having to do anything like that when she was campaigning during the awards season for Shakespeare in Love, before ultimately taking home Best Actress for her performance. If that film were coming out today, someone in marketing would likely have to think about what the promotional popcorn bucket should be.

With Marty Supreme behind her, the Sliding Doors star is back in Hollywood and has a few projects in various stages of development. While waiting to see what Gwyneth Paltrow has in store for the 2027 movie schedule, Avengers: Doomsday will be in theaters on December 18th, finally providing answers to any and all rumors about whether it will include Pepper Potts.

#3413. These 14 New Features Are Coming to iOS 27.3

Apple has been beta testing iOS 27.3 since Nov. 3. While this update isn't as large as iOS 27 proper, it's surprisingly feature-filled for a 0.3 update. This is only a beta, so anything could (and likely will) change before Apple officially launches the update. But, as it stands, iOS 27.3 tests 10 new features—including one feature the company trialed in the previous beta.

Technically, anyone with a compatible iPhone can try out iOS 27.3 right now—assuming you enroll your Apple Account in the developer program. But a word of warning: Betas can be temperamental, and could be risky. As such, I'd recommend avoiding the beta until Apple releases the public beta, which comes after a bit more testing to iron out larger issues. Either way, make sure to make a full backup of your iPhone to a Mac or PC first, as issues with the beta could result in permanent data loss.

The iPhone Duo is Apple's first foldable smartphone, but also the company's first phone since the iPhone SE 3 to ship with Touch ID. While it works well enough for unlocking your iPhone, it's still an adjustment for those of us used to Face ID. With iOS 27.3, Apple is now testing face unlock for the Duo—not Face ID, mind you. The Duo's front camera doesn't have the tech required to power Face ID or its secure protocols. Instead, this feature simply unlocks your iPhone Duo with a face scan. In addition, your Duo will still require Touch ID for Apple Pay and passwords, or after 45 minutes of inactivity. You can read more about this new feature here.

iOS 27.3 also comes with a new setting that lets you lock your iPhone Duo by closing it—as you would expect from, say, a laptop—or, dare I say, a flip phone? Currently, closing the Duo seamlessly transitions what's on the big screen to the smaller display, and you have to press the side button to lock the phone.

With watchOS 27, Apple released "Audio Intelligence," a new set of features for Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. Audio Intelligence uses the watches' new S11 chip, along with on-device AI and cloud-based AI, to run new features, like Sound Recognition and Shazam (music recognition).

With iOS 27.3, however, the company is now officially testing the other two Audio Intelligence features it originally announced with watchOS 27. First, there's Live Rewind: By double-clicking the watch crown, you can pull up a transcript of the last 15 seconds of a conversation. Siri Recap, on the other hand, displays summaries of conversations you had that day, in case you need a refresher on any chats you might have otherwise forgotten about,

The company generated some controversy when it first announced these two Audio Intelligence features, since, on the surface, it sounds like these new Apple Watches are essentially spying on people all day long. According to Apple, however, that isn't really the case. The company says Audio Intelligence is private, and never records or stores any audio. No speakers are ever identified, and text results (both transcripts and summaries) are deleted automatically after a set period of time unless the user saves them to the Siri app. You can read more about how Audio Intelligence works here.

Despite their claims, I'm sure there will still be strong feelings surrounding these Audio Intelligence features. We'll have to see whether Apple can prove Live Rewind and Siri Recap aren't all that creepy throughout the iOS 27.3 beta process.

iOS 27.3 also introduces app actions for Siri AI. Apple is testing new abilities for Siri AI, including organizing files, planning events, or adding photos to albums. You could ask Siri to organize your Downloads folder, or delete files that haven't been opened in more than a year. You could ask Siri to find a coffee shop you went to last week, or to save an article to your Reading List in Safari. You could ask Siri to check your calendar and set up a time for an event based on when you're free. You can even ask the assistant to schedule, edit, or unsend messages.

For example, you could ask Siri AI to help you plan a trip with your friends. You could ask the AI to put together a themed playlist in Apple Music, schedule a message to a group about an upcoming trip, organize the websites you've been visiting in Safari into a tab group, and, after the trip, ask Siri to move your best photos to your favorites album. These new actions work in the following apps: Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather. Developers can also add Siri AI app actions support to their own apps.

Apple started testing its new Health app with the iOS 27.2 beta, but pulled the redesign before the official release. Now, with iOS 27.3, the new app is back. The new Health app has a health dashboard for the first time, as well as new features like Health Age and movement assessments. It seems to be pulling from some popular competitor services, hopefully, for the better. For more on the new Health app, check out Lifehacker health editor Beth Skwarecki's explainer.

Continuing on the Health track, iOS 27.3 also introduces "Gym Strength." This is a new Fitness+ feature that offers a personalized four-week strength-training plan. You can customize these plans to meet your goals, experience level, and schedule, and they adapt as you progress. You'll get recommendations based on your experience with exercises, reps, and sets, including video demos for exercises. You can access Gym Strength on both iPhone and iPad, and Apple Watches are optional—though you can log your progress with the wearable if you have it.

Apple is also testing a new Siri AI feature in Safari, that gives the bot access to entire webpages, including the parts of the site that aren't on-screen. Say you want to know all the gluten-free options on a menu on a restaurant's website, but only a portion of the site is actually in view. You could ask Siri to read you the gluten-free options, and it would pull from the whole page, even though you can only see part of it.

Vertical tabs have been a favorite among browser aficionados, as they give you more screen real estate in your browser while keeping your tabs off the side. Apple hasn't made the jump—until now. This feature works with iPads running iPadOS 27.3 as well as Macs running macOS 27.3.

Another new Safari feature in testing is "Adaptive Dark Mode." This feature forces websites into a dark theme, if they don't have a native theme of their own. There are third-party apps that can do this, but this is the first time Apple has offered this feature built into Safari.

Apple is also testing new StandBy experiences with iOS 27.3, which were previously only available on the iPhone Duo. When you turn your iPhone sideways while plugged in, you'll find new Analog and Digital Clock faces with new customization options. There's also a new Photos face, with the option to pull images from Shared Albums.

"Reachability" pulls your iPhone's display down towards the bottom of the screen, so you can access items towards the top of the display with one hand. It's a useful feature for those of us with big iPhones, and now, there's no iPhone bigger than the Duo. With iOS 27.3, Apple is testing Reachability for its first foldable phone. It's a bit like the inverse of how Reachability currently works: You can swipe on the left or right side of your Duo's display to shift the other side of the screen towards your current position. If you're holding your Duo in your left hand, a swipe of the left side will pull the right side over to the left, and vice versa.

Apple is also rolling out new languages for Siri AI in iOS 27.3. Now, Apple's smart assistant supports Traditional Chinese, Vietnamese, Turkish, and Norwegian.

If you have an Apple Intelligence-compatible iPad running iPadOS 27.3, you now have access to Siri Mode in Camera. As with iOS, you can open the Camera app on iPadOS to access Siri Mode, and ask Siri about your surroundings.

If you watch videos in Apple Podcasts, you can find them in more sources than the Podcasts app. With the new updates, you'll find these videos on Apple TV 4K, select smart TVs, your iPhone, iPad, Mac, and even in CarPlay. (Please don't watch video podcasts while driving.)

There's nothing quite like hearing "Your call is important to us" for the 15th time while trying to track down a missing holiday package. And apparently, I'm not alone in my frustration.

A new survey from voice AI company PolyAI found that 69.4% of respondents would be willing to speak with an AI voice assistant instead of waiting for a human customer service representative if they were guaranteed zero wait time.

The survey of 1,087 U.S. consumers, conducted in November 2026, suggests that despite reservations about AI replacing human workers, many Americans are open to the technology when it solves an everyday problem.

With Black Friday deals already underway and Cyber Monday just days away, AI could offer some relief from one of the biggest headaches of holiday shopping.

According to the survey shared with Tom's Guide, nearly 68% of respondents say automated phone menus frequently or almost always fail to resolve their problems no matter how much customers try to get around them. Just one in four consumers reports having their issue resolved on the first call.

Poor customer service is also affecting where people shop. Some 64.4% of respondents have abandoned a holiday purchase or canceled an order because of a bad customer service experience.

Perhaps the most entertaining findings from the survey are what people would rather do than navigate an automated phone menu:

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

While Gen Z is often associated with AI adoption, millennials were the most receptive to AI-powered customer service in this survey. More than 75% said they would use a voice AI assistant if it meant eliminating wait times.

Perhaps more surprising is that 62% of baby boomers and older respondents said they would do the same.

However, consumers aren't necessarily ready to give up human customer service entirely. Nearly 68% of respondents said they would feel comfortable using voice AI if they could be transferred to a human representative when necessary.

Shoppers surveyed also wanted AI to do more than answer basic questions. They were interested in assistants that could tell them whether something was in stock, solve a problem without asking for the same information twice or text them a receipt or boarding pass before they hung up.

Of course, there's a big difference between an AI assistant that sounds human and one that can actually get things done. Much of that comes down to how well a company has integrated AI into its existing customer service systems.

We've all been stuck on a customer service call, pressing buttons and repeating ourselves just to get through to someone who can help. Conversational AI promises to make that experience a little less painful.

Instead of sitting through a lengthy phone menu, you could simply explain that your package was delivered to the wrong house or that you need to change your flight, much like you would with a human agent. What do you think about AI customer service? Share your thoughts in the comments.

#3411. The Rings Of Power Season 3 Finale's Most Revealing Moment Perfectly Sets Up Season 4

Warning: This article contains major spoilers for the Season 3 finale of "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power."

Well, that was anticlimactic ... or was it? For much of "The Rings of Power" Season 3, we've been bracing ourselves for the onset of open war. Sauron's (Charlie Vickers) forces, bolstered by the hordes of followers loyal to the Dark Wizard (Ciarán Hinds) in Rhûn, have had their eyes on conquering Middle-earth. Even before the Dark Lord forged his One Ring, victory seemed all but certain. And, in the finale, the arrival of the Númenórean army in support of the Elves finally appeared to give us the epic battle we've been building towards all along. Instead, Sauron opts for the most shocking choice imaginable: He takes off his One Ring, kneels before King Pharazôn (Trystan Gravelle), and surrenders himself to his enemies without a fight.

Unless this is your first encounter with Sauron the Deceiver, of course, it's plain to see that he has plans within plans. While the details of this particular one are left entirely off-screen (we only see him look meaningfully at the approaching army and presumably inform Tyroe Muhafidin's Nazgnagôl Theo of his intentions), there's one revealing moment that tells us all we need to know. Inspired by Elrond's wisdom (Robert Aramayo) and his insistence that death is not a curse but a gift, the Men of the West begin chanting in the language of Quenya. Sauron translates for his puzzled ally: "They're asking for death." And while Theo wants to grant their request through battle, Sauron calmly implies that he has a different scheme in mind.

With just a single exchange, "The Rings of Power" perfectly tees up what's to come in Season 4.

Did you catch the subtext dripping from Sauron's words? If not, be aware that the rest of this article will contain spoilers for what's to come in Season 4 of "The Rings of Power." For the book readers, we know it all has to do with this year's season-long interest in mortal Men. Remember that conversation between Elrond and his twin brother Elros in Episode 5, when Elros revealed that he'd chosen mortality as a human over an unfathomably long life as an Elf? Elrond couldn't understand this pivotal decision then, but he's since come to understand why the godlike Valar intended this as a "gift" rather than a "doom." Between the tragedy of surprising main character Eärien (Ema Horvath) in choosing a quick death over a life of torture, the bittersweet hopes of lovers Míriel (Cynthia Addai-Robinson) and Elendil (Lloyd Owen) reuniting in the afterlife, and Elrond grappling with his own grief over his brother, we've seen numerous instances proving that death need not be the worst outcome.

So, perhaps it was only a matter of time before Sauron reached a similar conclusion. Having witnessed the Númenórean soldiers publicly embrace the concept of death, as the Faithful have always done, the Dark Lord smirks to himself and promises to give them what they ask ... just not in the way they think. Indeed, as we know from the canon, Sauron's abrupt surrender is exactly what goes down in J.R.R. Tolkien's original writings. In the face of overwhelming numbers, the Dark Lord allows himself to be captured and brought back to the island kingdom of Númenór, where he immediately begins causing mischief that ends in disaster.

Yeah, you probably knew where this was headed. Ever since Season 1, "The Rings of Power" has been teasing the inevitable fall of Númenór. Like Atlantis, Rome, or any number of haughty civilizations before it (both real and mythological), this empire of Men has been doomed to be humbled from the moment Galadriel (Morfydd Clark) first washed up on their shores with Sauron (then disguised as Halbrand). Even before Season 3 ramped up the conflict between the two enemy factions fighting for control of the island, the cracks in the foundation had been very apparent. And, in a bold choice, showrunners J.D. Payne and Patrick McKay haven't shied away from that, even giving Míriel visions of a "great wave" consuming them all back in Season 1.

Well, we're now right on track for this worst case scenario. With Sauron on his way and with every intention of putting the arrogant Pharazôn (Trystan Gravelle) in his place, expect yet another storyline where the Dark Lord manipulates one of our main protagonists — first with Galadriel, then the Elven smith Celebrimbor (Charles Edwards), and, most recently ,Celeborn (Jamie Campbell Bower). How, you ask? Well, it has to do with Númenór's proximity to the Undying Lands to the west. Once these Men begin looking towards the Valar with envy at their immortality, encouraged by Sauron himself, it takes very little effort to imagine Pharazôn leading his forces against these godlike beings ... and paying the ultimate price for it.

Yeah, fans are going to want to stick around for everything to come in Season 4. All eight episodes of "The Rings of Power" Season 3 are now streaming on Prime Video.

#3410. Focker In-Law Sets A New Standard For Legacy Sequels

It's a little surprising to realize, but legacy sequels like "Focker In-Law" aren't the outliers they used to be. In fairness, legacy sequels are not a brand new phenomenon. For example, Martin Scorsese's "The Color of Money" was a sequel to "The Hustler" released 25 years after its predecessor's debut in 1961.

Yet, the "legacy sequel" is a more specific concept than merely a belated sequel. Whether intended as a soft reboot or a larger continuity pivot, a legacy sequel typically involves a perspective shift to a new (and often younger) protagonist, relegating the former leads to supporting roles. This trend arguably began with J.J. Abrams' "Star Trek" in 2009, and it was solidified by "Tron: Legacy" the following year. In fact, it's entirely possible that the latter film gave the legacy sequel its terminology.

Many more legacy sequels have cropped up since then, with most of them following this template. For a period, they were generally limited to science fiction films, including 2015's "Star Wars: Episode VII — The Force Awakens" and "Blade Runner 2049" from two years later. Since then, though, the legacy sequel has moved beyond the sci-fi genre to encapsulate action ("Top Gun: Maverick"), horror ("28 Years Later"), and even comedy ("Coming 2 America").

That brings us back to "Focker In-Law," the fourth film in the "Meet the Parents" franchise. Most legacy sequels attempt to recapture (if not re-stage) the movie that started it all, and "Focker In-Law" does indeed revisit the basic premise of "Meet the Parents." But rather than having longtime star Ben Stiller pass the torch to new cast member Ariana Grande, the film keeps his Greg Focker as the protagonist. It's proof positive that legacy sequels don't always need to replace older characters and can let them grow gracefully with audiences instead.

In "Focker In-Law," the now fully-middle-aged Greg Focker has two grown children of his own, and his son Henry (Skyler Gisondo) has met the love of his life, Olivia Jones (Ariana Grande). With Gisondo and Grande being buzzy young stars, it would've been understandable if writer/director John Hamburg decided to make the film from their perspective. This would essentially be "Meet the Parents" again, only this time, Olivia and Henry would be in the position Greg was years ago when he had to impress his fiancé's father, Jack (Robert De Niro). But changing Greg from the protagonist to the antagonist could've made for a lot of easy gags and forced sentiment, and it would've been very unoriginal.

However, Hamburg instead chooses to keep the focus on Greg's neurosis and knack for making huge messes out of non-issues, which has been the comedic driving force for the rest of the franchise. As such, the premise of the film is less about Olivia fitting in (she effortlessly does so with everyone but Greg) and more about Greg coming to terms with his age, his son's adulthood, his overprotectiveness, and his self-centered nature.

In this way, "Focker In-Law" is almost a coming of age story about a middle-aged adult. It's not totally rare, but it does feel notable in a medium that primarily tries to appeal to young viewers. Hence, by instead flipping the script and placating older audience members, the film's focus on Greg feels like an extension of the franchise's themes rather than a recapitulation. After all, growing up and learning doesn't stop when one hits middle age and oftentimes meeting the parents can be just as nail-bitingly uncomfortable if you're now the parent yourself.

#3409. GTA 6 Fans Are Hissing Mad About Dolores the Snake

After more than a decade of waiting, Grand Theft Auto 6 is finally here. Perhaps most surprising of all, it's actually living up to the world's sky-high expectations, and players everywhere are sharing their delight and awe at the game's immaculate attention to detail on social media. But there's one group of players who aren't so thrilled about the level of realism in GTA 6: snake owners.

Over on Reddit, a post from the r/mildlyinfuriating subreddit about GTA 6 has garnered more than 92,000 likes in just a few days. The user was eager to share the game with a friend from southern Florida. However, rather than being dazzled by GTA 6's intricate attention to detail, the friend was horrified by Dolores the snake's habitat in Jason and Lucia's Key Lento bungalow.

The redditor wrote that their friend "went on this big long 10 minute rant about how the people that designed this game are idiots and terrible people and how they’re gonna cause people to go out and buy snakes and mistreat them and abandon them. Apparently she’s pissed about the lack of a heat lamp and a water dish. And the fact that the tank doesn’t open the right way and the fact that he doesn’t use tongs to feed the thing."

Ultimately, the dismayed snake fan concluded, “They [Rockstar] spent 13 years on this thing and did no fucking research.” If you've actually spent any time at all with GTA 6, you'll realize this is a pretty wild exaggeration. Clearly, this team did all kinds of research, whether its on the behaviors of the American alligator, vintage T-shirts, or telenovelas.

"I find it rather immersive that a Florida scumbag would have a cool snake poorly kept," observed one commenter.

In keeping with the spirit of the subreddit, other GTA 6 players shared their own mildly infuriating experiences with the game, mostly surrounding the home repair sequence in the opening hours. "If you think that is bad, you should try showing a roofer how Jason fixes the roof," wrote one user. "Im not even a roofer and I was complaining about most the home repairs, bro but some floor protection before you paint, what about the light switch 😭," said another.

While GTA 6 might be a remarkably accurate girlfriend simulator, it is sadly not the best example of responsible pet ownership. Given the exhaustive level of detail in other aspects of the game, it is a little surprising that these small details about Dolores's enclosure weren't considered. Then again, this is also a game that forces you to use a left-to-right slider instead of a numerical keypad at the ATM, so the immersion here isn't 100% consistent.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

The latest model I’ve been using, the Homerunpet Self Cleaning Cat Litter Box Kit, is the most expensive, and largest one I’ve yet brought into my house. I — or more specifically my cats — have been using it for about two months, and they seem to have taken to it well. However, before you spend upwards of $600 on this thing, there’s a few things you should know first.

This self-cleaning litter box is designed for cats up to 25 pounds, works with a variety of litter, a 12L waste bin with odor control, and has an app that lets you monitor your cats' weight.

This litterbox is huge. The box it came in was larger than ones I got with microwaves. Measuring 23.62 x 28.07 x 27.44 inches, you’re definitely going to need a lot of space for it, so I would not recommend it if you’re planning to put it in a smallish bathroom.

The HomeRun Pet litterbox looks kind of like a cement mixer. The main part of the box is a large drum with a hole in its side; this is where your cat enters and does its business. When they’re done, and after a minute or two, the litterbox rotates this section to empty the waste into a small storage bin on the side, and then refreshes the clean litter from a reservoir.

To the right of this main drum is a reservoir into which you pour fresh litter. The machine will draw from this reservoir to replenish the main tray.

No more scooping! When the machine empties itself, waste is funneled into a small bin on the right side, which you line with an included plastic bag. When the bag is full — you'll get an alert on your phone — you simply pull the bin out and remove the bag. Replacement bags cost $35 for a pack of 60. With two cats, we’ve had to replace the bag once every two weeks or so.

There’s actually two trays; a second one, which sits directly below the drum, can be used if you want to completely empty the litter box. And, every piece of the litter box that could possibly get dirty can be removed and washed.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

This being a “smart” cat litter box, you get all sorts of updates via the HomeRun app — when it needs to be emptied, when you need to add new litter, how long your cats take, and how many times they go per day.

One interesting feature of the HomeRun Pet is that it has a built-in scale, so you can keep tabs on your cats’ weight. I initially had to wait until each of mine used the box to figure out which was which, but after that, it would tell me which cat had gone, and when. Of course, if your cats are very close in weight, it might have trouble telling the difference. If that’s the case, you can adjust the weight error value, so it can better distinguish between multiple pets.

The app also lets you customize all sorts of things, like the type of litter you’re using, cleaning schedule, and even “kitten protection,” to prevent the device from activating automatically.

In order to use the HomeRun, your cat has to step up about a foot to get inside the opening; knowing how a cat of mine had trouble walking in his later years, I highly doubt he’d have been able to make it up. Something like the PetSafe Smart Self-Cleaning Litterbox would make more sense (and it’s a lot cheaper and takes up a lot less space).

The Homerunpet Self Cleaning Cat Litter Box Kit is not a small investment; even with Black Friday sales, you’re still going to spend $659 at Amazon on this thing. And, it takes up a lot of space. However, it does make cleaning up after your cat incredibly convenient - just slide open a tray, remove a bag, and you’re all set. Is that worth the price of a nice TV? That’s for you to decide.

#3405. New 'GTA 6' Leak Is Great News For PC Gamers, But There's A Catch

A new leak gives PC players a sense of what to expect from GTA 6 with souped-up settings

Much has been said about the differences between Grand Theft Auto 6 on PlayStation 5 and Xbox, but how will Rockstar Games' open-world game fare on PC? An official port has yet to be announced, but a recent leak of the Xbox build of the game has kicked off a race to recompile the game and make it unofficially available on more platforms. As that work continues, yet another leak offers PC players some perspective on what might be possible in GTA 6 when the game isn't held down by console constraints.

On Wednesday, known GTA leaker Tex2 shared a Pastebin that lists GTA 6's apparent console settings shipped by Rockstar. These are tunable options that exist to help the game shine on platforms with varying capacities, like the less-powerful Xbox Series S. The text dump has since been pulled by Pastebin, but Polygon viewed the document before the platform made it unavailable.

Some aspects of the game, like Global Illumination Quality, Ray Traced Directional Shadows, and Texture Quality are already set to high on PlayStation 5. The same aspects are sometimes lower or altogether absent on Xbox, though reports suggest the platforms have more parity than Sony's marketing would like you to believe.

There are even a couple of settings that Rockstar has already set to Ultra, such as Vehicle Max Texture Quality and Bounding Volume Hierarchy. A surprising number of settings — 18 to be exact — are set to medium or low on PS5 and Xbox Series X​​​​​​​. That number jumps to 38 settings on Xbox Series X that are set to low or medium.​​​​​​​

The conservative presets are of significance for PC gamers. Settings such as Tree, Terrain, Impostor, and Grass Shadows are set to medium and affect draw distance and pop-in.​​​​​​​ Lighting and Ambient Lighting, which influence​​​​​​​ how the game renders background lights such as streetlights and neon signs, are also set to medium across platforms.

Volumetric Lighting​​​​​​​, another setting currently on medium, determines how light is depicted in conditions such as fog and crepuscular rays​​​​​​​. On consoles, aspects like 'god rays' can appear grainy or blocky — especially​​​​​​​ while the camera is in motion.

Even elements that might sound small on paper, like Weapon Textures, could meaningfully change the experience. There's a lot of shooting in this game, even if you play non-lethally; players will stare down the barrel of a gun for much of the game.

Players experiencing GTA 6 on PS5 Pro have slightly more presets set to high than the base platform​​​​​​​, but by and large, a potential PC port​​​​​​​ of the game will likely look much better than its console counterparts, depending on hardware configuration. GTA 6 is no graphics slouch, either — so it's almost hard to fathom how this incredible-looking game is still nowhere near its full potential​​​​​​​.

GTA 6 could theoretically look phenomenal on PC if Rockstar ever releases it on that platform or if the AI vibe coders figure out a port. Here is the other shoe dropping: in order to push GTA 6 to the limit, PC gamers are going to need top-of-the-line hardware​​​​​​​.

Graphics cards like the RTX 5080 or 5090, which could potentially get the game running on high or ultra across the board, cost anywhere from $2,000 to $6,449​​​​​​​. PC gamers will probably want 32 GB of RAM to accommodate​​​​​​​ these graphics cards, and those components are more expensive right now as well. Getting the most impressive version of GTA 6 running could cost many thousands of dollars​​​​​​​, especially if the player is starting a rig from scratch or needs extras like monitors, keyboards, or mice.

Compared to a PC build, the PS5 Pro's higher price tag​​​​​​​ might feel a little less eye-watering​​​​​​​ — if you're able to find one at all. For now, though, all of this is speculative — GTA 6 is not available for PC.

#3404. New Avengers: Doomsday Footage Puts RDJ's Doctor Doom Accent In The Spotlight

The geography of Earth in the Marvel Cinematic Universe is mostly similar to our own world, but it does have a few fictional countries thrown in, including Wakanda, Sokovia, and now Latveria. The home nation of Victor von Doom/Doctor Doom (Robert Downey Jr.), Latveria is sandwiched between Romania, Hungary, and Serbia in Marvel's comics, but it's generally just sort of vaguely Eastern European. That means that the role of Doctor Doom in "Avengers: Doomsday" called for a vaguely Eastern European accent.

Based on what we've heard from the film's trailers so far, especially this new international teaser for "Avengers: Doomsday," Downey certainly seems to have delivered on the "vague" part. In this latest promo, Doom issues a warning that "You shall all kneel before Doom," while also conveniently acting as a bit of a hype man by name-checking some of the big superhero teams that will appear in the movie. (The Thunderbolts are missing from the list, though, possibly because Doom was confused by their branding).

New international teaser for 'AVENGERS: DOOMSDAY'.

In theaters December 18. pic.twitter.com/wTudC8pKc9

— Avengers Updates (@AvengersUpdated) November 24, 2026

Downey's Doom accent has been widely compared to the voice of ancient vampire Nandor the Relentless (Kayvan Novak) in the TV show "What We Do in the Shadows." (Nandor is also from a fictional country, Al Qolnidar.) However, in this particular teaser it's more reminiscent of eccentric German filmmaker Werner Herzog. Even Downey himself has said that he struggled to settle on an accent.

"Part of me didn't want to go Eastern European," Robert Downey Jr. explained, regarding Doctor Doom's accent, in an interview with Empire. "I had written this manifesto speech that [Doom] makes, and I laid down this voice note of him addressing his people, and I started to find it there."

Downey already appeared in 10 Marvel Cinematic Universe movies as Tony Stark, aka Iron Man, so Doom presented a fresh challenge for him: "I don't want to say Tony's like rolling off a log, but I know that swing pattern." Comparatively, the process of figuring out Doom, from superficialities like his accent to his deeper motivations, was "painstaking." The fact that the character spends most of his time — possibly the entire movie, if you believe Downey's co-star Chris Evans — wearing a full face mask presented another challenge. "Honestly, a lot of it was just the eyes," Downey told Empire, adding, "I ain't gonna lie to you. A lot of this we were just trying to figure it out ... It was a bit of an exploration."

The question of whether or not Doom will take his mask off is a major one, as Downey's face is pretty recognizable within the world of the MCU. For now, though, much about Doom is still shrouded in mystery. Fans will have to wait until "Avengers: Doomsday" releases on December 18, 2026, to see (and hear) more from this classic Marvel villain.

#3402. Marvel Reveals What Happened On Patrick Stewart's Final Day Filming Avengers: Doomsday

"Avengers: Doomsday" may feel like the grandaddy of all Marvel Cinematic Universe films, but even this gargantuan production can't hold a candle to the absolute icon at its heart. The legendary Patrick Stewart left us in October of 2026, and his loss will continue to be keenly felt among family, friends, and fans for years to come. The fact that he agreed to return to the Marvel franchise and reprise his role as Charles Xavier already lent tremendous weight to the story. But now, knowing that his final day on the set of "Doomsday" was also his last on any film, moviegoers will end up bringing mountains of emotional baggage with them on opening weekend.

In a new profile with Entertainment Weekly, the cast and crew of "Doomsday" opened up about their memories of working with Stewart, the immense legacy he leaves behind, and the unforgettable experience they had watching him on his very last day filming. To Kevin Feige, the Marvel head who was present as a lowly associate producer during Stewart's very first appearance as the mutant leader in 2000's "X-Men," the words Stewart spoke after wrapping filming on "Doomsday" feel even more poignant in retrospect:

"He stood up and he gave a speech to the crew. We didn't know necessarily it would be his last day on a set, but he was sort of indicating to us that he thought it was."

Co-director Anthony Russo noted that, "It was clear that he was struggling with his health, and he worked so hard to deliver a performance and a presence — for us as directors, for his other actors, for the crew." Stewart passed away from Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia, so it must've taken a Herculean effort for him to show up and perform each day.

Despite Patrick Stewart's irreplaceable loss, it does feel like a gift that we'll be able to enjoy one last performance of his in the weeks ahead. In fact, according to "Avengers: Doomsday" co-director Joe Russo, Charles Xavier's journey in the film will feel like a poignant echo of Stewart's celebrated life:

"In a lot of ways, Xavier's the conscience in the movie. He has a lovely scene with Ian McKellen, who's his best friend, in the film. It's a very emotional scene about forgiveness and I think very resonant in the wake of his passing."

After watching both Xavier and McKellen as Magneto butt heads, debate each other, and play peaceful games of chess across several "X-Men" movies, it'll undoubtedly be a treat to watch them do so one more time (all the more so given Stewart and McKellen's real-life friendship). For his part, Kevin Feige acknowledged that he and the Russo brothers have been busy putting the final touches on "Doomsday" — including a tribute in memory of Stewart, likely in the end credits of the film. As he put it:

"We're long done filming that movie, and he did an amazing job for us. We're looking now at how we can put something together that honors and respects our friend."

Considering similar memorials for dearly-departed figures like Leonard Nimoy, Carrie Fisher, Chadwick Boseman, and many more in recent years, don't expect a single dry eye in the house once the lights come on. "Avengers: Doomsday" will arrive in theaters on December 18, 2026.

#3401. The Further Mis-Adventures Of Cliff Booth Features A Delightful Quentin Tarantino Easter Egg

Spoilers for "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" follow.

Forget the MCU. Real ones know that Quentin Tarantino has been building his own cinematic universe for years. For instance: while this is never officially stated by anyone on screen, Michael Madsen's character from "Reservoir Dogs" is supposed to be the brother of John Travolta's character from "Pulp Fiction" (there was even a plan for a crossover movie, but it never happened). Beyond character connections, Tarantino also likes to drop his own fictional products into his films, and "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" keeps this trend going.

Tarantino didn't direct "Cliff Booth" — he handed those duties over to David Fincher. But Tarantino still wrote the script, and Fincher keeps the Easter eggs intact. The biggest example: Big Kahuna Burger. Early in the film, we see Brad Pitt's Cliff Booth pick up some food at Big Kahuna Burger to bring home to his dad, Gus (Peter Weller). Tarantino fans will, of course, recognize that burger joint: it was prominently mentioned in "Pulp Fiction," and we see Samuel L. Jackson's character Jules take a big bite of a burger while intimidating some crooks who are about to meet a violent end.

But wait, there's more! Another Tarantino product that shows up in "The Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" are the famous Red Apple Cigarettes. Red Apples have been mentioned in virtually every Tarantino film, and they were even a part of "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood," the film that "Cliff Booth" serves as a sequel to.

In "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood," Leonardo DiCaprio's Rick Dalton filmed a commercial for Red Apple Cigarettes (believe it or not, kids, there used to be commercials for cigarettes on TV). "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" keeps the tradition alive while also giving us a nice little callback. During one scene, we see Cliff watching a new Red Apple commercial on TV. And who is starring in that commercial? None other than Sharon Tate, played by Margot Robbie in a cameo.

"Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" ended by literally changing history, and allowing Sharon Tate and her friends to completely avoid their tragic murders at the hands of the Manson family. "Cliff Booth" confirms that since Sharon is still alive in 1977, when the film is set, she's still out there acting, too.

#3400. GTA 6 Players Are Running Into a Game-Breaking Bug

Grand Theft Auto 6’s Leonida is full of dangers: murderous wildlife, over-eager cops, unhinged backwoods drug dealers, terrible drivers, and much more. However, all these threats pale in comparison to a particularly deadly foe. GTA 6 has a game-breaking soft lock bug that makes it impossible to progress.

The X user @SirGrotti posted a clip of the glitch, showing how they can no longer switch from Lucia to Jason, with the option permanently grayed out. The glitch can occur in Chapter 3 after the Missing Persons mission, and it’s game-breaking because the next story segment requires Jason. Comments on the post suggest several solutions, including leaving their house and then switching characters, saving and reloading, asking to meet up with Jason, sleeping, and more, but apparently, none of these worked for SirGrotti.

Unfortunately, SirGrotti isn't alone. The website GTA6Bugs tracks user-reported cases of crashes, softlocks, and other problems. Of the dozens of bugs logged on the site, the Chapter 3 softlock has the most views. While there are a few fixes that worked for some players, not everyone has been so lucky.

The first fix is to load a manual save from before you drove to the warehouse in Port Gellhorn for the final Missing Persons meeting. Then switch to Jason and play through the Dealer’s Choice mission until you can switch to Lucia freely. Make a manual save in a new slot and finish Missing Persons.

Beyond this fix, other potential workarounds include playing another Lucia or duo mission if one is available, calling Dunk from Lucia’s phone, and robbing a store as a pair before starting Raul’s job as Lucia. GTA 6’s 01.002.002 update didn’t seem to fix this problem, but considering this seems to be one of the most reported game-breaking issues, ideally Rockstar will address it soon. Beyond these softlocks, another common issue for GTA 6 players is a mysterious PS5 crash, which both Rockstar and Sony customer support have blamed on the other party.

Things can always be much worse, though: some GTA 6 players have uploaded videos of the game’s demanding graphics seemingly frying their PS5s. One clip from shivjam shows the console dying in real time, while another has a streamer's PlayStation billowing smoke. Console and controller technician Modyfikator89 described GTA 6 as "the toughest real-world PS5 stress test" he had ever seen. With the ongoing chip crisis driving game console prices higher than ever, it's a particularly bad time to be left high and dry.

#3399. ‘Paper Tiger’: James Gray Convinced Adam Driver He Was Playing the Hero, Then Crafted His Mythic End

Editor’s Note: The following story contains spoilers for “Paper Tiger.”

One night, after his second child was born, James Gray found himself up late watching C-SPAN coverage of the Global Economic Forum in Davos, and saw something he held onto for years.

“This corporate CEO said, ‘95% of people don’t know there’s a game, and they lose,'” said Gray on IndieWire’s Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast. “Of the remaining 5%, 4% know there’s a game and don’t know how to play it, and 1% knows there’s a game and wins. And he said it with evident pride. I thought it revolting.”

The CEO’s words hit home for Gray, showing a “cruel economic system that people can’t control,” where luck, timing, and “having skills that are popular at the right time” decide who wins. Related Stories ‘All of a Sudden’ Review: Ryusuke Hamaguchi’s Long and Thoughtful Plea for a More Hopeful Future ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ Made Nearly $4 Billion Doing What Movies Can’t

“I would love a system where everyone got rewarded, not one that picks winners and losers,” said Gray. “The idea of losers breaks my heart. The film was about my heartbreak over the world’s losers.”

The script for “Paper Tiger” centers on three lead characters, each representing a different side of Gray’s cautionary tale about the dangers of chasing the American Dream. Of his three main characters, Gary (Adam Driver) is best positioned to be one of the “winners.”

“[Gary] is the one person who knows the game, knows how to play it, and just [can’t] live with himself if he makes certain choices that might allow him to, quote-unquote, ‘win,’” said Gray of Driver’s character. “We don’t see that much in movies. We see people who are ‘bad guys’ who make the wrong choice, or ‘good guys’ who make the right choice and then wind up winning for it.”

Gary, the ex-cop turned savvy businessman, presents himself as comfortable crossing that ethical line, but as the story slowly reveals, a strong moral code lies beneath Gary’s slick, tailored suit and wheeler-and-dealer image. It’s a distinction Gray said Driver didn’t fully grasp at first.

“I would go up to [Adam’s] apartment, and we would talk about it, and I remember he was struggling and struggling and struggling, ‘Oh, what am I doing?’” said Gray. “One day in rehearsals, I said, ‘He has only the best intentions all the time.  We have to love him. He always means well. He’s not a sleazeball.’ And Adam went, ‘Oh, I got it.’”

Part of Driver’s problem was that Gary’s latest scheme places his brother Irwin (Miles Teller) and his family in the crosshairs of ruthless Russian mobsters, but Gray warned it was important, for both Driver and the audience, to understand that Gary’s actions weren’t particularly reckless at the time.

“We have the wisdom of 2026 about where organized crime would go in New York, but in 1986, the Russian organization was a totally unknown quantity,” said Gray. “He would not, as a retired police officer, have any knowledge of that.”

In 1986, the Italian mob’s stranglehold on the Gowanus Canal — where Gary is trying to help Irwin score a lucrative contract as an environmental consultant — had been decimated by RICO prosecutions. There was an assumption of a new day dawning, as different immigrant groups began moving into the vacuum left behind by the aggressive prosecution of the Genovese crime family. No one imagined, according to Gray, that one mob would ultimately be replaced by a far more violent and ruthless mob altogether.

“The sadness to me was that the story of immigration in New York at that time was, ‘Oh, these are dissidents, these are engineers, they’re scientists, they’re doctors.’ The expectation wasn’t they were going to set up gasoline, oil, and racketeering. None of that was on the plate,” said Gray, before connecting his point back to Driver. “Adam had the key now that everything was not done for nefarious reasons, that he was trying to bring his brother along. As soon as he could approach it that way, it really opened things up for him.”

Much like the rest of the world, the ruthlessness of the Russian mob would catch Gary by surprise, but it would be how Gary responded to the threat that got Gray’s storytelling juices flowing.

“I was anxious to show a character who you might think would be the one who does the wrong thing, but in fact, does something beautiful in death, which is he sacrifices himself,” said Gray.

This last part is important to Gray, who discussed how his three young adult children constantly complain that “there’s nothing on TV,” despite having more channels and streaming services than ever before. “They always say that to me,” explained Gray, “and what they’re really saying is there’s very little with a streak of grandeur or nobility in it, because there’s a kind of smallness to the storytelling when you don’t have that quality.”

The question then became how to give Driver’s Gary that nobility in death, and build to a third act that gave Gray’s smaller film a sense of grandeur. As with most of his films, Gray drew on his life experiences growing up in Queens, along with great films from the past.

In Howard Beach, Queens, down by JFK Airport, a long stretch of marshes surrounded by tall reeds (phragmites grass) stands in sharp contrast to the urban landscape on the horizon.

“ My brother and I got lost in these very tall weeds,” said Gray. “I was very young. And it’s a recurring nightmare of mine, getting lost in there. And you have no sense of direction. Immediately, it’s extremely disorienting.”

Gray had tried to use the location in his 2007 film “We Own the Night,” but he wasn’t satisfied with the results. In “Paper Tiger,” he cracked how to stage and shoot in the tall grasses, drawing direct inspiration from Masaki Kobayashi’s 1967 “Samurai Rebellion,” resulting in Gary’s last stand being one of the most memorable sequences in recent American movie memory.

A key was how Gray drew meaning from the setting: “I was trying to give Adam Driver‘s character a nobility, but the other part of it is how do you give his character a mythic dimension? And through death, a lot of the times, you can imply transcendence, and I was trying to say that his character was essentially going back to the primordial ooze, that he was returning to something that had nothing to do with the urban landscape.”

On the podcast, Gray talked about how the final scene is stripped of period signifiers, with no glimpse of the urban landscape beyond the weeds, allowing the sequence to “devolve or evolve so that [Gary] would be at peace as he died.” The moment was further brought to life through an effective use of sound, rather than a more traditional score for such an operatic ending. “I just decided this is about him transcending, and so you hear — the track is very weird — birds and insects. There’s the intrusion of aircraft, but it’s also the calm of the wind and the undulation of the phragmites grass. And I just thought that was a way to separate his character and say that he’s reached a kind of mythic status.”

One lesson Gray took from his previous (and in Gray’s mind less successful) attempt to film in the Howard Beach marsh was that he would need more time for the hot and hellish shoot, in which the filmmakers experienced disorientation not unlike Gray did as a kid.

“There’s one shot which is up high where you see these guys converging on Adam’s character. And I remember how difficult the shot was because the minute you put the actor in there and the camera went up here, we couldn’t find the actors in the weeds,” said Gray. “It’s very upsetting and disorienting even to just shoot in that setting, to say nothing of the ticks. But that’s a whole other story.”

“Paper Tiger” expands nationwide on November 25.

#3398. David Fincher's Rejected Star Wars Movie Pitch Would Have Centered On Two Beloved Franchise Characters

David Fincher, the director of "Seven," "Fight Club," and many other classic films, very nearly had a major influence on "Star Wars" before Disney took control of the franchise. So, what would he have done with one of the most popular sci-fi properties on the planet? He would have focused on a pair of beloved characters, specifically the best droids in the "Star Wars" property.

On a recent episode of the "Happy Sad Confused" podcast, Fincher revealed that he had a conversation with former Lucasfilm President Kathleen Kennedy about taking th studio public before Disney bought Lucasfilm in 2012. But what would Fincher have done with "Star Wars" had that panned out? Perhaps not what you'd expect.

His interest lay with C-3PO and R2-D2, primarily. Not Luke Skywalker. Not Princess Leia. A protocol droid and his astromech companion. And while Fincher admitted he didn't have a full pitch, he did have a rough idea. Here's what he had to say:

"I said, 'The thing that has always interested me about — certainly from the first movie — was the relationship between [C-]3PO and R2[-D2]. That they were essentially slaves who would bear witness to the folly of man. I always thought that, them being captured by Jawas, and then sold off and being on the periphery and witnessing the Skywalker Saga, was such a crucial element to it. [...] There was a kind of moral judgment. It was fairly obvious even from 3PO [...] he had a kind of understanding as to what the Empire meant, how evil they were."

"He was kind of trying to decide whether or not he wanted to invest in having a relationship with Luke Skywalker when he's getting his oil bath [in 'A New Hope'], and they're talking," Fincher added.

"Even from ['The Empire Strikes Back'], when 3PO is turned back on, and he recounts for you what he sees with the stormtroopers already being in [...] Bespin," David FIncher continued. "Whenever they used the robots for that, I was always really excited. I always thought that was kind of interesting, that you have to go through the recorder, like the court reporter, to find out what it is that happened."

Notably, C-3PO actor Anthony Daniels is the only actor to appear in all nine main "Star Wars" movies, while Kenny Baker portrayed R2-D2 in the original trilogy. These are characters who certainly have earned time in the spotlight, but using them as the crux of a new era for the franchise? That's a strange idea.

Be that as it may, Fincher and Kathleen Kennedy were interested in seeing if they could make something happen. Fincher, however, revealed that Disney's purchase of Lucasfilm (a deal that encompassed $4 billion in cash and stocks) nixed those plans. As the filmmaker recalled:

"I said to [Kennedy], I kind of pitched her this idea, I said, 'Let's take this thing to Wall Street and let the market decide.' And I think it was a month later or something, she said, 'Bad news. Apparently there's a $7 billion offer on the table,' and I said, 'We're not going to beat that.'"

George Lucas later opened up about selling Lucafilm to Disney, describing it as "very, very painful." Of course, it proved to be enormously beneficial for Disney, financially speaking. Fincher, meanwhile, has gone on to continue enjoying a very fruitful career outside the confines of a galaxy far, far away.

#3397. 'Wifi Motion Sensing' Can Track Everything You Do Through Your Router

A simple wifi feature could let ISPs track your location and movement patterns within your home. "Wifi motion sensing" turns your ISP’s router into a motion detector, letting providers know exactly how many people are in the house, where they are situated, individual movement patterns, and, in some cases, even body shapes that could approximate a person’s identity.

Wifi routers rely on radio signals to connect wirelessly to your devices and appliances. Those same radio signals are also absorbed and reflected by the human body as they travel in all directions from the router. With the right software, ISPs can track how those wifi signals travel around your room, which can be studied to detect presence and sense motion patterns.

As long as your ISP’s router model supports this feature natively, it doesn’t require any additional hardware to be installed in your home. For example, Xfinity’s version of the feature pairs your router with five other connected appliances in your room to create oval-shaped sensing zones that can track your presence and movement within those spaces.

It isn’t a new feature, either—companies like Cognitive Systems and Origin Wireless that supply networking hardware to ISPs have been offering wifi motion sensing for years now, while early research prototypes from the MIT date back at least as far as 2015. In 2025, IEEE updated its Wi-Fi 802.11 standard to include motion sensing and lay out the architectural guidelines for it, which makes it likely that even more routers will now ship with the feature.

In its current consumer form, wifi motion sensing can help you control smart home apparatus like lights or thermostats, get pet safety notifications on your phone, set up a fall alert system for elderly users, and trigger appliances remotely based on human presence. But enabling it carries risks.

Most providers, including Cognitive Systems, claim that the technology isn’t sensitive to identity and can’t be used to track specific individuals. But even if true, that’s more likely to be a product decision rather than a technical limitation. Karlsruhe Institute researchers have shown that even ordinary wifi signals can identify individuals with a 99.5% accuracy.

Also worth noting: ISPs’ legal wording suggests that they may disclose the collected and stored motion data at any time to law enforcement, government agencies, regulators, and courts in response to subpoenas or during an emergency. ISPs may also retain your motion data in the cloud long-term in case they are required to facilitate a subpoena in the future.

As far as major ISPs are concerned, Xfinity (Comcast) is the only broadband provider that currently offers this feature across its commercial routers on the XB7, XB8, XB9, XB10, MXB1, and XER10 gateways. It’s opted out by default, but in case you or a family member already switched it on, you can disable it again by navigating to Home > WiFi Motion on the Xfinity app, click on the gear icon on the live view page, and tap Remove WiFi Motion.

Verizon Fios customers also had access to a Home Awareness feature on their routers that could be toggled on or off using the MyFios app, but that’s since been discontinued. In an official disclosure published shortly after the discontinuation, Verizon notified customers that it has deleted all associated movement logs from this service and no longer retains any motion data from users.

But there are other regional ISPs that offer it, too. For example, Breezeline (Atlantic Broadband) offers a feature called Motion within its Plume-powered application that alerts customers when movement is detected in their homes, among its other features. MidCo, a telecom company in the Upper Midwest, has a feature called Sense which can be toggled on or off using the MidCo Wi-Fi app. Plume, ADT-owned Origin Wireless, and Airties—all of whom supply technology to ISPs—have also been marketing motion sensing to customers for the last few years.

If you’re unsure if your wifi router or ISP has motion sensing features or opts you in by default, look for a feature called “Sense,” “Motion,” or equivalent in your broadband’s mobile app. Exact steps differ greatly from one ISP to another, so it’s best not to assume that they will all opt you out by default, or that they collect the same types of data. With the 802.11bf update to IEEE standards in 2025, this technology will be accessible to even more router manufacturers, so expect adoption to grow among internet providers as well.
