#3396. Lauren Ambrose on Playing the Mother of a Missing Teen in ‘The Unbelievers’ and Why ‘Six Feet Under’ Is a Hit with Gen Z

Lauren Ambrose sounds almost embarrassed to admit that she was puzzled the first time she read the script for Nick Payne’s “The Unbelievers.” “I was like, ‘Oh my God, what is this? I don’t understand this at all,'” Ambrose told IndieWire, scrunching up her face in a mask of bewilderment. “What’s he getting at?”

The drama, which is wrapping up its limited run at the Manhattan Theatre Club this month, is elliptical, moving backward and forward in time as it follows Miriam’s search for her missing son, Oscar. That description sounds like a thousand thrillers, but “The Unbelievers” resists easy classification — it’s a narratively daring story, overflowing with ideas about grief and faith and family. Related Stories ‘Paper Tiger’: James Gray Convinced Adam Driver He Was Playing the Hero, Then Crafted His Mythic End ‘All of a Sudden’ Review: Ryusuke Hamaguchi’s Long and Thoughtful Plea for a More Hopeful Future

It was only after doing a workshop for the play that Ambrose discovered that what she initially found so alienating about “The Unbelievers” was actually its greatest strength. “There’s a lot to talk about, and a lot to parse, and a lot to think about, and it’s highly interpretable and analyzable, and I think that’s actually a marker of good art is that it can be interpreted in many ways,” Ambrose said over Zoom, hours before she was set to take the stage again.

The role of Miriam is almost Everest-like in its difficulty. As the years pass without any sign of Oscar — not knowing if he’s been kidnapped or murdered or ran away — Miriam becomes more obsessed, more unmoored by the lack of resolution. That strains her relationship with her two daughters and Oliver’s father, who are processing their grief in different ways and worry that Miriam is growing fanatical in her insistence that he may still be out there.

“It’s fun in a perverse way to go on this crazy journey every night,” Ambrose said. “There are all these wild turns. It’s tiring vocally. My body hurts, my neck is messed up. But it’s amazing to get to play a part like this. You just have to throw yourself off a cliff.”

Ambrose made a name for herself in films like “Can’t Hardly Wait” and on “Six Feet Under,” where she played Claire Fisher, a rebellious dreamer growing up in her family-run funeral home. The show debuted in 2001 on HBO, where it aired alongside “The Sopranos” and “Sex and the City” at the peak of the cable channel’s cultural supremacy. Decades later, “Six Feet Under” has been rediscovered on streaming by Gen Z, giving it an unexpected surge in popularity.

“It was a golden age,” Ambrose said. “We were making these hour-long films each week. And HBO was so open and supportive of creative people. The attitude was, if you want to try something, try it. There weren’t algorithms determining everything. That freedom is palpable with the series, so I think that’s why it’s resonating and why it’s being embraced by this new generation.”

Ambrose remains in demand on the big and small screen, recently appearing on another water-cooler hit, Showtime’s “Yellowjackets.” But she’s made a point of returning to the stage throughout her career, appearing on Broadway in “Exit the King” and “Awake and Sing!,” as well as earning a Tony Award nomination playing Eliza Doolittle in a revival of “My Fair Lady.”

“I love the stage — I love it so much,” Ambrose said. “I love a rehearsal room. It’s my favorite place in the world. It’s where you’re figuring it out and making connections. But a play is always a living thing. We’ve opened ‘The Unbelievers,’ but I haven’t stopped my work of trying to scavenge around and figure out this mysterious character.”

#3394. 10 'Find Hub' Hacks Every Android User Should Know

Khamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.

He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.

Google's Find Hub app isn't just for tracking your lost smartphone. Over the past year, Google has consistently added features to manage your belongings, share your location with loved ones, and locate lost devices. Find Hub can now notify you when you've left your device or your tracker behind. Plus, you can use Gemini to remember where you left items, even without a tracker attached. Behind the scenes, there are even more hidden settings and features to help track your devices and make it easier to retrieve them in case they are stolen or misplaced. If you use Find Hub, you need to know about these 10 hacks.

This month, Google finally added Left Behind notifications to Android trackers—but you have to enable the feature manually. AirTags users should be familiar with this feature already. When you leave your tracker or device behind, and exit the location range, you’ll receive a notification that you left without your item. You need to enable this feature on a per-device basis. Go to Find Hub and select a device. Tap the settings gear icon next to the device's name, and enable Notify when left behind. While you’re here, go to Add location to add familiar locations where you don’t want to get a notification (like your home or workspace). Otherwise, Find Hub may spam you with left behind alerts.

There’s a hidden feature in the Find Hub app that helps you keep track of things without actually using a Bluetooth tracker. You can simply ask Gemini to remember where you put things, and it will show up in the Find Hub app. To use it, pull up Gemini and say something like, “Remember in Find Hub that the passport is in the downstairs wardrobe,” or “I’ve kept the spare car keys behind the garage door.”

You can then ask Gemini, “Where did I keep my passport?” and it will tell you. If you change the location of an item, just ask Gemini to update it for you. When you go to the Remembered tab, you’ll see the location of all remembered items. You can also add items manually here using the Add button.

Some Android smartphones can remain findable for several hours after they've been switched off or their batteries have run out. If you’re using a supported device (like the latest Pixel series smartphone), you can use a hardware feature to track the location using Google’s mesh network, relying on nearby devices (similar to how Android tags work).

To make sure this feature is enabled, go to Find Hub, and tap Find your offline devices. Here, make sure that either With network in busy places only or With network everywhere is selected.

If you’re using a tracker in your car, luggage, or on your keys, you might want to share location access with your spouse or family members. Find Hub has a feature called "Share Ownership" that lets you share the tracker details with up to 10 people. Only the location of your tracker is shared, not your personal device.

To set it up, go to Find Hub, and choose the tracker or accessory that you want to share. Tap the Share Ownership button and follow the on-screen instructions to share the invite link via a messaging app or using Quick Share. Once the recipient taps Accept, you’ll get a notification. Go to the device settings in Find Hub and tap the Confirm button to enable location sharing.

You can quickly share your live location with your friends or loved ones using Google Messages. Open a conversation, tap the Attachment icon, and choose Real-time location. Set the duration and tap Send.

If you don’t like using the Messages app, you can do so directly from Find Hub. Go to the People tab at the bottom of the screen, and tap the Plus icon. Choose the duration and select a contact to share the location with, then tap the Get Link button to copy the link. You can then share it via any messaging app of your choice.

You might have a Find Hub tracker in your luggage to help keep tabs on your bags. But you don't have to be the only one privy to its location. If your airline loses that luggage, you can temporarily share its location with your airline to help you retrieve it. This is an official feature, too: Google partnered with multiple airlines to make this data sharing easier. From the Find Hub, choose your tracker. Tap the Share Item Location button, and then tap Share Item Location again. Copy the generated web link and share it with your airline using the app or support page. The link will automatically expire in seven days, so you don't have to worry about your airline continuing to monitor your luggage's location long after your flight.

Find Hub uses a mesh network of supported Android devices to securely locate your lost device or tag. But by default, it waits until multiple Android devices detect the location of the lost device. This works well if you've lost the device in crowded areas, but it can increase your wait time if you lose it somewhere remote. Luckily, there is a hidden setting that triggers location sharing even if a single device reports its location. Go to Settings > Google > All services > Find Hub > Find your offline devices and select With network everywhere instead of With network in busy places only.

If you’ve lost your smartphone, you don’t need to rush to a computer or a website to track it. Borrow someone’s Android smartphone and head into their Find Hub. Tap Sign in as guest and sign in with your Google account associated with your device, then find and select your device in the account. If requested, enter the PIN that you’ve previously set up. You can now track the device’s location, get directions to the device, or play a sound to help track the device if it’s nearby. If the device is truly lost, you can use the Mark as Lost feature to remotely lock your device.

Map-based tracking is helpful in getting to the general vicinity of your lost device. But your smartphone or tracker is hidden; finding it may require precision tracking. Many newer trackers like the Pixel Tag come with an ultra-wideband chip that helps you find the exact location of the tracker, given you are nearby. This also works on Pixel smartphones (Pixel 8 Pro series and above) and Samsung Galaxy devices (S21 and above, Plus and Ultra models only).

When using this feature, make sure you have Bluetooth enabled on your smartphone, then open Find Hub. Choose your tracker, and tap Find Nearby. Follow the on-screen instructions to locate the nearby device. You can also tap Play Sound to make the location process easier.

If you think your Android smartphone is lost or stolen, don’t rush to erase all data. While a remote factory reset is great for protecting your data, it also removes the device from your account. It’s best to try to get the device back. Two-factor authentication (or a passkey) on your Google account, along with a biometric lock on your smartphone, will protect the data itself.

Go to the Find Hub website, or use Find Hub on someone else’s phone in guest mode. Choose your device, and instead of Factory Reset, choose Mark as Lost. Here, you’ll see an option to enter a message. Type an alternative contact number, and a message to help recover the device.

#3392. Blade Runner 2099 Revives A Major Element From Philip K. Dick's Original Novel

Any fan of "Blade Runner" knows that the source material for the film, Philip K. Dick's novel "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?," didn't exactly make it to the big screen fully intact. As influential and unique as it is, Dick's work proved too unwieldy for filmmakers to adapt wholesale. Instead, Hollywood took Dick's themes and concepts and heavily rewrote his stories for the screen. That trend began with "Blade Runner," as original screenwriter Hampton Fancher took the neo-noir concept from Dick's trippy, weird 1968 novel of a human hunting down illegal androids and pretty much discarded the rest. The relationship between "Androids" and "Blade Runner" can be succinctly summed up by the fact that Fancher and director Ridley Scott didn't use Dick's title for the film, eventually going so far as to borrow the title from a completely different novel by William S. Burroughs.

To be fair, "Blade Runner" retains a surprising amount of Dick's novel, with whole swathes of dialogue making it all the way from the author's page to the screen. Yet numerous other plot elements and characters were either altered or omitted altogether. One element in "Androids" which is very important to Dick's worldbuilding is the concept of Mercerism, a religion in which devotees share a looping, pre-programmed experience via a virtual reality machine called an empathy box.

This idea didn't make it to "Blade Runner" in any shape or form, however it does appear (and largely intact, too) in this month's "Blade Runner 2099" sequel series. The use of Mercerism in the Prime Video show is a great example of showrunner Silka Luisa and her writers knowing Dick and "Blade Runner" well. In fact, the inclusion of a missing element of Dick's novel in a "Blade Runner" sequel is a bit of a franchise tradition.

In "Blade Runner 2099," it initially seems that Silka Luisa and company have included Mercerism as a little Easter egg, as a couple of animated billboards in Los Angeles advertise it. Yet this isn't a winking reference to Philip K. Dick's novel, but is instead foreshadowing. In Episode 6, entitled "Kill the Killers," Cora (Hunter Schafer) and Olwen (Michelle Yeoh) travel to a hideaway where Cora and her brother grew up. It turns out this hideaway is a defunct Mercer Monastery, a place where those who worship the man could come to and use an empathy box or interact with automated priest-like programs (shades of George Lucas' "THX 1138" there).

Mercerism, as detailed in Dick's "Androids," is a religion based around the idea of increasing empathy, since the future of the novel has become so dystopian and isolating that people need to be reminded to have empathy for others (sound familiar?). This is done through the empathy box, which allows users to experience a moment from the life of Wilbur Mercer, apparently some kind of martyr. In the box, Mercer endlessly climbs up a hill while being pelted with rocks, and the "empathy" the user experiences is holding onto sensors which deliver increasingly harsher shocks, sometimes resulting in death.

The idea was first introduced by Dick in a short story in 1964 entitled "The Little Black Box," and then re-used in "Androids." The ironic twist in "Androids" is that Mercerism is revealed to be a total sham, with the video loop having been shot on a soundstage with an actor. Though this isn't addressed in "2099," the obvious decline in Mercerites and decay of the monastery implies that the religion isn't as popular as it once was.

Even though Mercerism didn't make it into a previous iteration of "Blade Runner," the themes behind it are so integral to the story of "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?" and its world that its inclusion feels natural. "Blade Runner 2099" smoothly weaves it into its storyline, using it as an allegory for its doomed principal characters as well as its apocalyptic vision of Earth in general. It's used in the show in much the same way Dick uses it in "Androids," as a satiric commentary on how what was initially intended as an aspirational endeavor has devolved into something more pathetic than never believing in it in the first place.

Ironically, Mercerism is not the first element in "Androids" that was left out of "Blade Runner" but made a return appearance in a sequel story to Ridley Scott's film. In "Androids," the character of John R. Isidore (or J.R. Isidore) was reconceived and rewritten as J.F. Sebastian for "Blade Runner," and he was killed during the events of the film. However, when Dick's friend K.W. Jeter wrote the 1995 novel "Blade Runner 2: The Edge of Human," Jeter brought J.R. Isidore back into the story. It's not entirely clear if Jeter intends his Isidore to be the literal same character, or if he's "borrowing" the character in the same manner as Dick borrowed Mercerism from his short story for "Androids." Either way, it established a neat little tradition for the franchise, in which anything or anyone could come back, and perhaps come back different. For a series infamous for characters not ever fully knowing their true identity and heritage, the tradition feels rather poignant.

"Blade Runner 2099" is now streaming on Prime Video.

#3391. ‘The Mosquito Bowl’ Review: ‘Friday Night Lights’ Meets ‘Five Came Back’ in Peter Berg’s Formulaic Netflix Movie About a World War II Football Game

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on October 27, 2026 during the 2026 AFI Film Festival. The film is available to stream on Netflix today.]

There have been any number of movies about the hell of fighting in World War II, the most visceral of which have been made in the years since “Saving Private Ryan” provided a very enduring template for how modern filmmakers could render that carnage with both the spectacle of a blockbuster and the horror of a memory. Peter Berg’s brutal and concussive “The Mosquito Bowl” is definitely one of them! No one could ever say that it’s not.

What differentiates this unsparing epic from the scores of other stories about the Greatest Generation, however, is that some of its characters are good at football. Indeed, these All-American college boys are so good at football that, on Christmas Eve 1944, the soldiers are ordered to play a morale-boosting game of two-hand touch on the beach where their units are preparing for the Battle of Okinawa. Related Stories Lauren Ambrose on Playing the Mother of a Missing Teen in ‘The Unbelievers’ and Why ‘Six Feet Under’ Is a Hit with Gen Z ‘Paper Tiger’: James Gray Convinced Adam Driver He Was Playing the Hero, Then Crafted His Mythic End

And for the span of the eight-minute montage during which “The Mosquito Bowl” actually makes good on its title, it’s easy to picture how the famous scrimmage — fought between a roster of impossibly beautiful athletes in their primes — might have been used to backstop a story that accentuated the senseless waste of sending thousands of young men to their deaths. Alas, for the rest of this 126-minute film, that waste is better expressed through Berg’s failure to make anything more of their lives, as the “Spenser Confidential” auteur’s latest Netflix project does almost nothing else to distinguish itself from a genre so well-worn that it’s seemingly run out of ways to blow up a human body.

Why “almost”? I was hoping you wouldn’t ask. For starters, there’s the decision to cast thin-skinned ESPN commentator Pat McAfee as an R. Lee Ermey-inspired drill sergeant. “The Mosquito Bowl” also stands out for how confusingly it conflates the thrill and teamwork of combat sport with the violence and camaraderie of armed conflict; war is presented as both a natural extension of what these boys have been trained to do on the gridiron (to the point that the soldiers briefly diagram their plan of attack as if it were a football play), and also the catastrophe that robbed them of a more innocent purpose. (Berg loves the troops as much as he hates the fact that generals and presidents so wantonly sacrifice their lives.) Someone declares that “The Marine Corps is the greatest offensive line in history,” and yet the film’s characters don’t seem to have any special advantages on the field of battle, as it would be glib to suggest that even the country’s best college running back might be able to slip free of a mortar blast. It’s one thing to argue that football is war, and another, much more asinine thing to argue that war is football.

Perhaps that’s why the Mosquito Bowl itself only took up a single page of the Buzz Bissinger book on which Berg’s film is based, and why that source material used the game as a lens through which a light could be shined on the semi-forgotten men who found their way into the lineup that day. It’s been suggested that Bissinger played up the sports angle in order to capitalize on the success of his “Friday Night Lights,” and given that Berg adapted that book into a film as well, it stands to reason that his “Mosquito Bowl” should do the same.

The problem is that, in stark contrast to Bissinger, Berg and co-writer Mark L. Smith only seem to care about their characters as a means to an end. The project’s anti-war ethos is solely conveyed by reducing collegiate legends into cannon fodder, as the movie is considerably less interested in what bonds these boys together than it is in the shells that blast them apart.

Perhaps that explains why I’ve been able to write almost 650 words without bothering to mention any of their names. To the extent that it matters to a film so blandly de-saturated that everyone in it looks half-dead from the start, Nicholas Galitzine stars as Brown University legend John McLaughry — the only character we know for certain will survive the assault on Japan. (The movie opens with a sustained flash-forward of John staring longingly at an empty football field as “Friday Night Lights” veterans Explosions in the Sky layer their post-rock shimmer over the soundtrack). He’s got sad eyes, a square jaw, and a brunette girlfriend, which is more than you can say for Bob Baumann (Bill Skarsgård), who has a devil-may-care attitude that disappears real quick once his unit makes land on Tawara. The only real source of contextual friction is owed to the rivalry between Purdue fullback Tony Butkovich (a glinty and magnetic Ray Nicholson) and the straight-laced mama’s boy he beat in a big game before the attack on Pearl Harbor (Tom Francis as the stoic and decent Dave Schreiner).

Individually, Butkovich is the only one of these characters who has the chutzpah to carry the movie on his back. Incidentally, he’s the only one of these men who was heading to the pros before the war got in the way. Still, it’s engaging to see them all blitz through life on their home turf, and “The Mosquito Bowl” benefits from Berg’s handheld and ruggedly naturalistic approach to how the players comport themselves off the field (read: they say “fuck” a lot and generally aspire to feel more like real people than they do patronizing impressions of what men were like in the ’40s).

But then the war comes to Hawaii, a match-cut turns a flock of birds into some fighter jets, and these beloved football stars all find themselves rendered nearly anonymous by the sea of shaved heads that are waiting for them at book. Little is made of their civilian celebrity, and even less of their individual decisions to enlist. “This is my rifle — there are many others like it, but this one is mine.”

Berg takes militaristic uniformity as all the excuse he needs to avoid deviating from expectation, and nearly everything that happens between basic training and the big game on the beach near Okinawa feels like it could have happened in several dozen other World War II movies, and almost certainly did. Defiant warriors curdle into terrified kids, bullets whizz through ocean waves, snipers pick off predictable characters at unsuspecting — or very suspecting — moments, and even the most hardened of marines find themselves staring blankly into the middle distance as their friends are decimated on all sides. Berg has always had a flair for the frenetic, and while there’s a perversely fetishistic veneer to the attention he devotes to entrails and enemy screams, it serves the film’s purposes that war has seldom seemed less survivable than it does here. (The film has no interest in humanizing the Japanese, but tries to compensate for that by presenting a few of the Americans as unrepentant monsters).

Still, for all of its supposed verisimilitude, “The Mosquito Bowl” seems less indebted to the reality of war than it does to Hollywood’s idea of it, and its abject refusal to flesh out its characters — a dereliction of duty, if ever there was one — makes it feel more contrived rather than less. I’m happy for Berg that he found a way to combine all of his favorite things into a single project (football, the military, and massive fireballs are all well-accounted for, even if Mark Wahlberg’s absence makes the whole movie feel like it’s forgotten something important), but “The Mosquito Bowl” accomplishes very little beyond violently illustrating that war is worse than football. It does that with such fervor that it loses all sight of what those things might really have in common.

Netflix will release “The Mosquito Bowl” in theaters on Friday, October 30. It will be available to stream on Netflix starting Wednesday, November 25.

#3390. How to whistle to distract enemies in GTA 6

Knowing how to whistle in Grand Theft Auto 6 might sound like the least useful skill that Jason and Lucia would need to achieve their goals. As you progress through the game, you unlock different tools to help you deal with enemies and invade locations. However, none of the fancy technology you may have will work as well as a simple whistle in certain situations.

If you want to be prepared for all kinds of mission, then you should learn how to whistle in GTA 6.

Whistling in GTA 6 is quite simple, although it is only available in specific situations. To whistle, hold L2/LT to target an NPC and bring up three options appear in the bottom-right corner of the screen. Among them, you will find the "whistle" option, which you perform by pressing Triangle on PS5 and X on Xbox.

The whistle action is only available when targeting hostile NPCs, such as guards and gang members. I tried hiding behind a wall while targeting a regular NPC on the street, but the option didn't appear. Hiding or crouching is not a prerequisite to using the whistle command, but you should try to stay out of sight, because if the target has already spotted you, the whistle won't work.

When you whistle at an NPC, they will move to your location. Using this method to distract them is a great option when you want to remain stealthy and avoid attracting too much attention. However, whistling does not always work on more than one target at the same time. On some occasions, all the NPCs near my target looked for the sound, while on others, only one became curious about the sound. Keep this in mind, because it might affect your plan on how to handle a group of enemies.

#3389. Avatar Fans Just Got Some Good News About The Franchise's Future At Disney

"Avatar" fans can thank Eywa, because more sequels are indeed coming. As reported by Collider, Disney's upcoming film release slate includes "Avatar 4" (dated for December 21, 2029) and "Avatar 5" (dated for December 19, 2031). These dates aren't necessarily etched in stone; during the 2010s, the release date for "Avatar: The Way of Water" got pushed back so much that many convinced themselves the movie was never coming out. You simply can't rush the quality that director James Cameron demands of the "Avatar" films. But it's a sign Disney wants the movies out sooner than later.

Was the future of a billion dollar franchise like "Avatar" ever in doubt? Keep in mind, the third movie, 2025's "Avatar: Fire and Ash," was the lowest grossing movie in the series. It still grossed just under $1.5 billion, but that's a notably diminished return next to "The Way of Water," which pulled $2.3 billion internationally. "Fire and Ash" was also, like its predecessors, one of the most expensive movies ever made.

There's also the fact that director James Cameron, who has spent decades immersed in the world of Pandora, wants to direct other projects. Cameron is currently working on "Ghosts of Hiroshima," based on the non-fiction book by author Charles Pellegrino, and he's likewise attached to an adaptation of Joe Abercrombie's dark fantasy book "The Devils."

Cameron, who is 72 years old, is in the stage of his life where he has to balance the films he wants to make against the time he has left, and he knows it. As he told the Empire Film podcast back in May 2026, he wants to make the fourth and fifth "Avatar" films in less time, and for less money, than it took to make "The Way of Water" and "Fire and Ash."

James Cameron told People in 2023 that "Avatar 4" will feature a six-year time jump. Parts of the film were even shot concurrently with "Fire and Ash" to capture the series' younger actors, like Jack Champion (Spider) and Trinity Bliss (Tuktirey), while they still pass as kids.

The "Avatar" films have strong environmentalist themes; humanity wants to colonize Pandora because, by the 22nd century, Earth is polluted, overpopulated, and seemingly dying. We've only seen small glimpses of that in the previous films. Producer Jon Landau told Syfy back in 2023 that "Avatar 4" will change that:

"There's over-population and a depletion of our natural resources that make life harder. But we don't want to paint a bleak picture for where our world is going. The films are also about the idea of that we can change course."

What about lingering threads on Pandora? "Fire and Ash" ended with the recombinant Colonel Miles Quaritch (Stephen Lang) seemingly plummeting to his death. But one of the most essential rules of fiction is if you don't see a dead body, and sometimes even if you do, don't treat mortal peril as confirmed death.

Quaritch already beat death once, and it feels like he still hasn't quite completed his story yet. Even if Lang/Quaritch does sit "Avatar 4" out, "Fire and Ash" ended with his accomplice Varang (Oona Chaplin) still at large. Varang was easily the breakout character of "Fire and Ash," and I'd be shocked if we don't see her return to attack the Sully family again in movie number four.

"Avatar 4" is currently scheduled for theatrical release on December 21, 2029.

#3388. The Wallet-Sized Xteink X4 Pro Is Lifehacker's E-Reader Gift of the Year, and It's on Sale for Black Friday

I've read more than 30 books in the past year, all of them on an e-reader with a screen roughly the size of a credit card. If you think that sounds untenable, I say: Don't knock it 'til you've tried it. Once you're immersed in a book, you'll find the size doesn't matter, and the convenience of being able to slip it into any pocket and forget it's there means you need never be without it.

Right now, the Xteink X4 Pro, the best tiny e-reader I've tried so far—and Lifehacker's pick for the 2026 E-Reader Gift of the Year—is on its best sale yet for Black Friday: When ordered directly from Xteink, you'll save 15% off the usual $99 price, bringing it down to $84. This is the cheapest e-reader with a light and a touchscreen that you can buy right now, and it's well worth the money.

The X4 Pro is the newest and best e-reader from Xteink, the Chinese tech startup that turned the e-reading world upside down last year with the launch of the original X4 pocket e-reader. While the X4 Pro is the same size as the basic X4 Classic, it adds two big upgrades—a temperature-adjustable front light and a touchscreen—plus a faster processor and more memory. As a result, it costs a bit more, but you can pick one at a $15 discount right now. (Even at full retail, the X4 Pro is $50 cheaper than the entry-level Kindle after its recent price increase—and even considering the Kindle's current Black Friday discount).

Meanwhile, if you're a reader who prioritizes the crispest text over conveniences like a front light, the 4.3-inch Xteink X4 Classic and the smaller 3.7-inch Xteink X3 are about $30 less during Amazon's own Black Friday sale.

As much as I love them, these minuscule e-readers aren't for everyone. Some may indeed find the screen too small (though if you've ever read a book on a phone, the experience is similar). Then there's the fact that they can't load your existing libraries of Kindle books; you'll need to source copies of e-books lacking Digital Rights Management (DRM) software. But if you can jump those hurdles, you might just discover it's the weirdest, most lovable piece of tech you've used in years.

#3387. ‘The Holy Boy’ Review: A Teenage Boy Heals People with His Touch in an Eerie Italian Horror Movie About the Price of Avoiding Your Pain

In March 2009, a train crash kills 46 people near a picturesque village nestled deep within the Italian Alps. In the present day, an alcoholic gym teacher named Sergio (Michele Riondino) — nursing some recent grief of his own — is relocated to Remis, only to find that the surviving townspeople have never been happier, despite the shared tragedy that would seem to overshadow their lives.

It’s uncanny. It’s disturbing. It’s what Sergio wants for himself more than anything in the world. And he’s told that all he has to do to make the pain go away is to hug “The Holy Boy” mentioned in the English title of Paolo Strippoli’s third feature, a slick and effectively spine-tickling horror movie about the harm sown into people convinced they can avoid their own hurt. (It’s also one hell of a calling card for the young Italian director, whose recent festival hit “The Spiral” will receive an Oscar-qualifying release later this year, and an English-language remake sometime after that). Related Stories ‘The Mosquito Bowl’ Review: ‘Friday Night Lights’ Meets ‘Five Came Back’ in Peter Berg’s Formulaic Netflix Movie About a World War II Football Game Lauren Ambrose on Playing the Mother of a Missing Teen in ‘The Unbelievers’ and Why ‘Six Feet Under’ Is a Hit with Gen Z

For a time, Sergio becomes one of those people. When he first arrives in Remis, sobbing in his car as it chugs up the curvy mountain roads, it feels like a cruel joke that the surly ex-Judo champion has been relocated to a place known as “The Valley of Smiles.” He’s a belligerent asshole to the kids in his P.E. class, acts violently toward the beautiful waitress (Romana Maggiora Vergano as Michela) at the local bar, and generally brings a “Bad Santa” energy to a town with more of a “Pleasantville” vibe.

But from the start, it’s clear Remis hides a secret darkness — a darkness so deep that none of the residents can see clearly that they live in a horror film. It isn’t normal for a weasel-eyed man to stand in the bushes and glare at the village high school all day. It isn’t normal for everyone to meet in a barn on the outskirts of town in the middle of the night and participate in a vaguely Catholic ritual that sees them all line up for a chance to lay their hands on a sullen 15-year-old kid (Giulio Feltri as Matteo). It isn’t normal for them to feel like they might go insane, or worse, if they go too long without his touch. Give people a panacea for their pain, and they’ll do anything to keep it, logic be damned.

Of course, logic is hardly the only thing that’s damned in “The Holy Boy,” whose concussive soundtrack, broadly demonic symbology (e.g., dropped coins transforming into bloody egg yolks), and genre-inflected visual motifs (lots of upside-down camerawork and clever uses of soft focus) help consecrate this high-altitude “Twilight Zone” story’s rather literal approach to elevated horror. But Strippoli’s script, co-written by Jacopo Del Giudice and Milo Tissone, isn’t content to settle for mere social allegory, even if the movie tacks harder in that direction with every new detail we learn about Matteo’s effect on the people who touch him. On the contrary, the film’s excellent second act — during which Sergio is fully seduced by the town’s healing power and even settles into a sexual relationship with Michaela — leverages its premise in service of a tenderly ominous character study.

Closeted, sanctified, and at the mercy of a purpose that he never chose for himself, Matteo struggles to see his gift as a miracle; if anything, he worries that it’s more like a curse in disguise. It was, perhaps, easier for him to live with (and be used for) when he was a child, but the self-determination of teenage desire has complicated his relationship to the power he embodies. It’s not just that nobody understands Matteo, or cares to — he also struggles to understand himself. If the local bully is so mean to him at school every day, why does Matteo touch himself when he thinks about him at night? The answer may be obvious, but it doesn’t bring peace to the boy’s tormented heart, which pumps with a pain no one else in town allows themselves to feel. Not even Sergio, whose curiosity toward Matteo proves humanizing — and the basis for a real friendship — even as he grows addicted to the child’s power himself.

It’s here, between the smiling eeriness of its first act and the somewhat “Akira”-coded psychic collapse of its third, that “The Holy Boy” settles into its skin-crawling purpose. The film is at its most confident and secure as a “Thelma”-like coming-of-age story that weaponizes teenage growing pains against the world at large, as Matteo’s limitless potential is poisoned by the unmet needs of the wanting and selfish people around him. In his own way, and despite his best efforts, Sergio is such a person himself, even if he’s still close enough to his own heartache to see Matteo more clearly than most.

But Strippoli is only interested in Sergio as a way to push back against Matteo’s power (and therefore escalate things to the wild places they go before arriving at the film’s satisfying final beat). A richer pas de deux that probes deeper into the grown man’s loss — and his rather complicated history of fathering teenage boys — is gradually sacrificed at the altar of social commentary.

Religion and fascism are Strippoli’s most obvious targets, but “The Holy Boy” is wary of anything that people rely on to absolve them of their pain, and of how the things we turn to for comfort are liable to control us the moment we convince ourselves to believe in miracles. Touched by evil from the moment it starts, Strippoli’s film never invites the kind of faith from its audience that it abuses from its characters en masse, but I didn’t have any trouble believing the moral of its twisted sermon: Keep your pain alive, as it might be the only thing protecting you from something so much worse.

“The Holy Boy” will be available to stream on Shudder starting Friday, November 27.

#3386. If You Loved 'The Diplomat,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

The Diplomat is a show that loves mess (complimentary). Kate Wyler (Keri Russel) is a mess in many ways, and almost every major character is at emotional, moral, or intellectual loose ends. This would all be in good fun if these characters weren’t also some of the most powerful people in the world—presidents, prime ministers, and the high-level politicians and diplomats that serve them.

If you’ve been following the Wylers’ emotional journey up the power ladder as Kate navigates her role as the U.S. ambassador to the United Kingdom during what could be described as tumultuous times (and you’ve watched all our series streamalikes), allow me to suggest the one perfect movie that delivers similar vibes: 2009's In the Loop.

Released in 2009, In the Loop doesn’t have the modern edge of The Diplomat, but it perfectly captures a similar sense that international diplomacy is being conducted by people with an affinity for chaos. It’s actually a spinoff from a British TV series from the same co-writer/director, Armando Iannucci: The Thick of It. Many of the characters and situations are based on some of the people actually running the U.K., but you don’t need to be familiar with the show or the real history to enjoy the heck out of this movie. That goes double for Peter Capaldi’s absolutely ferocious performance as Malcolm Tucker, a man so creative with his profanity that many of his F-bombs will live rent-free in your head for years to come.

When a not-so-bright minister in the U.K. government (played by Tom Hollander) makes some dimwitted remarks that threaten to blow up Britain's carefully crafted diplomatic messaging around potential military adventures in the Middle East, Tucker (the prime minister's director of communications) has to tamp down the growing chaos that results. This eventually requires a contingent of British diplomats and officials to head to Washington, where they are quickly overwhelmed by the superpower vibes they encounter.

It’s a more profane, faster-paced, and outright comedic story than The Diplomat, but it’s also easy to imagine most of the characters showing up on that show. The film also shares that same sense of controlled chaos that drives The Diplomat—the idea that a handful of tired, dedicated people are continuously racing around to prevent World War III even as dumber and more powerful people keep creating new crises. If Kate Wyler’s constant state of exhausted anxiety is your jam, you’ll love this movie. Stream In the Loop on The Roku Channel, Kanopy, or Plex, or rent it on Prime Video.

Want more cynical diplomats, secret plans, and international skulduggery with a side of personal emotional crises? Here are a few more movies fans of The Diplomat will love.

If you want a sense of what actual back-channel diplomacy is like, watch Ben Affleck’s Best Picture winner Argo, from 2012. Based on the remarkable true story of how six U.S. diplomats were rescued from Tehran during the Iran Hostage Crisis under cover of a fake sci-fi movie production, the film has the snappy energy and fast pace of The Diplomat combined with real-world danger. You can easily imagine Kate and Hal (Rufus Sewell) being part of the secret, off-the-books conversations that brought what’s known as the Canadian Caper into reality. Stream Argo on Paramount Plus or rent it on Prime Video.

If your favorite parts of The Diplomat are the schemes various players (mostly Kate and Hal) get up to in their efforts to shape world diplomacy and history to their liking, Wag the Dog is a good bet. When a sex scandal threatens to swing the Presidential election away from the incumbent, a spin doctor (Robert De Niro) wades in to save the day by convincing a top Hollywood producer (Dustin Hoffman) to “produce” a fake war in Albania to distract the American public. It’s equal parts funny, compelling, and depressingly instructive, and fans of the show will love the back-channel hijinks. Rent Wag the Dog on Prime Video.

One of the great things about The Diplomat is watching Kate Wyler, a smart and capable woman who generally knows more than anyone else in the room. If that’s the dynamic that grabs you, The Contender is the overlooked gem for you. When the vice president dies unexpectedly, the President (Jeff Bridges) nominates Senator Laine Hanson (Joan Allen) to take the post. A conservative senator (Gary Oldman) opposes her nomination and launches a smear campaign to derail her confirmation. There are dirty tricks and secret deals, and in the middle of it all, Allen’s terrific performance as a woman who refuses to back down in the face of sexist, unfair attacks. Stream The Contender on The Roku Channel, Kanopy, Hoopla, or Tubi, or rent it on Apple TV.

Nicole Kidman plays an interpreter at the United Nations, a woman who has a unique heritage and linguistic knowledge. When she overhears an assassination plot in an obscure dialect, she becomes embroiled in a dangerous game of espionage and high-stakes diplomacy as she races to prevent disaster (and keep herself alive). The Interpreter is a more serious and much more tense story, but it delves into the background work that makes the global system function, which puts it right in the sweet spot for fans of The Diplomat. Stream The Interpreter on Netflix, or rent it on Prime Video.

This might not seem like a match at first glance—a comedic treatment of the power struggle that followed the death of Soviet Premier Josef Stalin in 1953—but it absolutely is. Making a farce out of the political wrangling among the members of the Central Committee, the film has the same spirit as The Diplomat, showing that the people in charge are a bunch of schemers, tricksters, dummies, and sociopaths. Watching them run around making deals and angling for advantage offers the same energy as the show. Plus, it’s just plain hilarious. Stream The Death of Stalin on Kanopy, or rent it on Prime Video.

#3385. Avengers: Secret Wars Setting Confirmed By Marvel, Spoiling Doomsday

It looks like we're heading to the Marvel Cinematic Universe's version of Battleworld in "Avengers: Secret Wars." The final "Avengers: Doomsday" trailer promises a major showdown between Robert Downey Jr.'s Victor von Doom and a conglomerate of heroes from various timelines. As it stands, "Doomsday" has a real shot at the biggest box office opening weekend ever, which would bode very well for the second part of Joe and Anthony Russo's upcoming duology, "Avengers: Secret Wars." That sequel is due out on December 17, 2027, and if "Doomsday" does what "Infinity War" did back in 2018, it should have a grand old time at the box office. That is, if Marvel Studios head Kevin Feige doesn't spoil things before then.

We've known for some time that one of Marvel Comics' greatest modern writers, Jonathan Hickman, is a secret MCU consultant, and that "Avengers: Doomsday" is loosely adapting his "Avengers: Time Runs Out" storyline from 2014. That arc serves as a prelude to Hickman's 2015 "Secret Wars" storyline, and together these two runs see the Marvel universe collapse due to "incursions," after which Victor von Doom uses fragments of the shattered multiverse to create a new planet named Battleworld. In an interview with Entertainment Weekly, Feige basically confirmed that this is the setting for the MCU's version of "Secret Wars," basically spoiling "Doomsday" by strongly hinting how that film ends and where the next one begins.

The Marvel Studios president told the outlet, "'Secret Wars' is different than any other movie we've ever made. Look at the comics. The characters and the settings and the worlds within this singular planet where our movie 'Secret Wars' takes place is the imagination gone wild, which is what's exciting about it." So there you have it. Most fans expected to see Battleworld in "Secret Wars," but now it's as close to official as you can get.

The first "Secret Wars" comic book arc arrived in 1984, with writer Jim Shooter and artists Mike Zeck and Bob Layton delivering a story in which the cosmic entity known as The Beyonder forced various Marvel characters to fight to the death on the planet Battleworld. It seems Marvel Studios will draw from this original run for some aspects of "Avengers: Doomsday" and "Avengers: Secret Wars." But for the most part, Jonathan Hickman's 2015 run serves as the basis for the two movies.

This second "Secret Wars" arc, illustrated by artist Esad Ribić with cover designs by Alex Ross, and the run that preceded it, "Time Runs Out," are the essential inspiration for "Doomsday" and its sequel. Feige told Entertainment Weekly that "Doomsday" is basically the MCU's version of "Time Runs Out," while the filmmakers described "Secret Wars" as "a little bit of both" that storyline and Hickman's "Secret Wars."

Asked to comment further, Feige said, "If you wanted spoilers for 'The Odyssey,' you could go read the book. If you want spoilers for 'Doomsday' and 'Secret Wars,' you can go look at the comics," adding, "It is very much the same thing that we're doing." Clearly, then, Hickman's work is integral to the two upcoming MCU releases, with Feige going on to say that "Secret Wars" is "very much" the "culmination of an incursion, multiversal-collapse event." With that in mind, you can bet the "Doomsday" sequel will play out pretty much entirely on the MCU's version of Battleworld, with the surviving heroes from "Doomsday" taking the fight to its god emperor, Doom, in an attempt to overthrow his regime and restore the multiverse. Whether "Secret Wars" will include Marvel's infamous Spider-Man bathroom scene, however, remains unconfirmed.

None of Kevin Feige's latest revelations should come as a big shock to Marvel fans who've known Marvel Studios has been drawing from Jonathan Hickman's "Secret Wars" run. But this is the closest Feige has come to officially confirming Battleworld as the setting for "Avengers: Secret Wars." The Marvel Studios head didn't use the name "Battleworld," but his comments about a "singular planet" were in response to a question about it.

Otherwise, Feige characterized "Avengers: Doomsday" as "a culmination of what's come before," and "Secret Wars" as "a launching pad for [Marvel Studios'] films in 2028 — the 20th anniversary of the MCU." Clearly, then, whatever happens at the end of "Secret Wars" will set the stage for new characters, timelines, and storylines that will reshape the way the MCU looks going forward.

We know that Marvel Studios is preparing its Jake Schrier-directed X-Men movie, which is set to debut in the wake of "Secret Wars." First, though, Marvel is reworking its cinematic universe with "Doomsday" and "Secret Wars." According to co-director Joe Russo, this simply had to be done with two movies due to it being "such a major storyline." He continued: "Doom as a character needs a lot of space, especially when Robert Downey is playing him. So the scale of the story, the emotional scale of the story is so large that it really needed to be a two-parter."

Whether the second part of that two-parter will actually debut on December 17, 2027, however, remains unclear. Production on "Secret Wars" has been moved to 2027, suggesting a delay might be imminent. For now, we'll have to wait and see how things play out. But regardless of when the movie actually arrives, prepare yourselves for a big screen visit to Battleworld.

This will be the first-ever Marvel Rivals set, though plenty of Marvel sets already exist, and to mark the occasion, it will turn the beloved Jeff the Land Shark into a brick-built figure.

Jeff the Land Shark debuted in Kelly Thompson's West Coast Avengers in 2018 and has since become a mascot for Marvel across comics and games since.This includes Marvel Rivals, where he is playable as a Strategist hero. The Jeff the Land Shark lego set will be released on Jan. 1, 2027 and will cost $49.99​​​​​​​. You can pre-order it now at the official Lego store.

In a press release (via GameSpot), Lego Marvel design lead Jesper C. Nielsen said that, "Jeff brings together everything players love about a breakout gaming character: an unforgettable silhouette, a personality you understand instantly, and the ability to turn any match into a story.”​​​​​​" He continued that the Lego team "wanted​​​​​​​ this Lego model to capture both sides of him, from the lovable companion fans want beside their screen to the unpredictable strategist they meet in battle."

The Jeff the Land Shark set will be a modest 495 pieces in total and is rated for ages 12 and up. The store page states that once fully built, Jeff's head, legs, tail, and fins are all movable, allowing Jeff to be posed in multiple stances​​​​​​​. You can also detach his tongue and close his mouth. The fin can be detached as well, so you can move it around on the ground as if it were about to pop up on an enemy​​​​​​​.

NetEase Games will celebrate the second anniversary of Marvel Rivals by bringing its year-long Path to Doomsday event to a close​​​​​​​. At the end of the year​​​​​​​ Marvel fans can catch Avengers: Doomsday in theaters on Dec. 18. However, you won't be able to see it on IMAX screens, since Dune: Part 3 has those locked down.​​​​​​​

I like 'Blade Runner 2099.' I wish I loved it

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The TV gods are clearly smiling on me. Last year my favorite sci-fi series of all time, “Alien,” was adapted for TV in Hulu’s “Alien: Earth,” and now my second-favorite sci-fi series gets its own small-screen show in the form of Prime Video’s “Blade Runner 2099.”

The good news is that “Blade Runner’s” first TV show doesn’t besmirch the franchise’s good name. However, “2099” doesn’t quite manage to live up to the peerless legacy of the 1982 classic and the criminally overlooked 2017 sequel, “Blade Runner 2049.” In fact, frustration was the feeling I felt most keenly while watching the show’s first four episodes (of eight total).

Not because “Blade Runner 2099” is bad; I want to make it clear upfront this is a solid show, but because, to borrow a phrase from another iconic sci-fi universe, “We were on the verge of greatness. We were this close.” This Prime Video original gets so much right that the key areas where it comes up short stick out even more and leave me frustrated with what could have been.

Set 50 years after Ryan Gosling’s Officer K went on the hunt for Harrison Ford’s Rick Deckard, “Blade Runner 2099” leaps forward to a point in the timeline where humanity and replicants have reserved roles. The androids are on top, with humans now treated as second-class citizens, and replicant Blade Runners soon squash any fleeting thoughts of rebellion.

While it’s not the most inspired route to take — a role reversal is hardly an original narrative trope — it does set the stakes appropriately, assuming you as a viewer are rooting for the human race to prevail. Though the moral greyness of the “Blade Runner” series is here, and many replicant characters point out that they’re only doing to humanity what was done to them.

Our leads are Olwen (Michelle Yeoh), a Replicant Blade Runner just days from retirement (aka impending death), and Cora (Hunter Schafer), a human resistant to the new world order, pretending to be a Replicant to secure a future for herself and her younger brother. The two soon partner up, forming less of a playful “buddy cop” dynamic and more of an icy, uneasy alliance.

There is intrigue in watching Cora try to remain undetected and in Olwen’s personal plight, as she grapples with her own morality, but despite committed work from Yeoh and Schafer, the overarching narrative threads only threaten to become truly interesting, at least at the midway point. It’s a MacGuffin hunt where the MacGuffin feels barely worth all the trouble.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Even when the narrative sputters and gets lost in meandering side quests, at least “Blade Runner 2099” consistently looks phenomenal. The grimy cyberpunk aesthetic of its sci-fi world has been successfully retained in the move from the big screen to at-home streaming. Visually, it hits all the right notes, and the foreboding score adds to the dark noir atmosphere.

But take my advice, and watch with subtitles; the dialogue audio often fades into the larger soundscape. “Blade Runner 2099” might be the first time in years I’ve had to rewind scenes multiple times just to try and decipher what the characters are actually saying to each other.

When it comes to production craft, “Blade Runner” is a triumph; it looks absolutely excellent, and sounds great too (well, apart from the dialogue levels). On the surface, it’s every bit the continuation of the “Blade Runner” universe, and as a longtime fan, that was enough to get me invested.

Where “2099” struggles is delivering enough narrative momentum to satisfy. Frustratingly early on, large chunks of the episode are a real slog, but to the show’s credit, it’s kept me coming back with well-timed narrative wrinkles. Just when my attention begins to wane, it delivers a precious, spectacular moment when it all comes together, and the clear potential is evident.

It’s these highs that will keep me watching, and as I move into the back half of the season, I hope the show’s sharpens up and fully realizes its potential. But if I were being truthful, I could see the slow pacing of the early episodes turning more than a few viewers away. “Blade Runner 2099” is in no rush. It asks viewers to be content exploring this fractured world at a crawl.

So, “Blade Runner 2099” isn’t perfect, but the franchise has always ruminated on the flaws of humanity passed down to our own android creations. Maybe the show’s unevenness could be considered poetic. Or maybe I’m just making excuses for a show I want to love more than I do.

#3382. How Blade Runner 2099 Took Inspiration From Denis Villeneuve's Legacy Sequel [Exclusive]

It's impossible enough to have to live in the shadow of an unabashed classic of cinema, so just imagine dealing with two of them. There aren't many who would have a bad word to say about Ridley Scott's original "Blade Runner (well, except for those unfortunate critics who dismissed it upon release), but Denis Villeneuve's highly-acclaimed sequel "Blade Runner 2049" ain't too shabby, either. Now, Prime Video's "Blade Runner 2099" series has the added responsibility of picking up the story where its beloved predecessors left off ... along with all the pressure that comes with that.

For showrunner Silka Luisa, this could've required one of two different approaches: stay suffocatingly faithful to the look and feel and tone of the two films or purposefully set off in the opposite direction. Well, in this case, how about a secret third option instead? During a recent press junket for "Blade Runner 2099," I spoke with Luisa over Zoom about where this show fits in next to its movie kin and how it finds its own niche amid a much wider world:

"I knew we were definitely going to have an opportunity to lay our own track, because — it's right in the title, the fact that you're so many years past 2049, it gives you enough space to really carve out your own identity."

Impressively, Luisa looked to Villeneuve's 2017 movie to figure out the ideal way to do just that. "What was so fantastic about what Denis did with '2049' was, he didn't just rehash what Ridley had done," the showrunner told me. "He really created his own take on 'Blade Runner' that is very much his aesthetic. But it still felt like an evolution of Ridley's conversation." In effect, the key was to thread that very tricky needle for "2099."

When it comes to the recent trend of legacy sequels that have dominated the last decade or so of franchise filmmaking, it can certainly feel like we can count the worthwhile ones on just one or two hands. Fortunately, for Silka Luisa and her creative team on "Blade Runner 2099," Denis Villeneuve's "Blade Runner 2049" is basically the poster child for legacy sequels done right. Rather than simply retread all the same ground as before (looking at you, "Star Wars: Episode VII — The Force Awakens"), "Blade Runner 2049" moved the story forward and took some seriously big risks along the way.

According to Luisa, this gave her all the permission she needed to follow in its footsteps and take things in bold new directions with her show. "That freed us up in a lot of different ways, because it meant we weren't just beholden to repeating the same thing over and over again," she explains. One massive wrinkle in the Prime Video series is the fact "Blade Runner 2099" takes place after a Replicant uprising has shaken up the status quo, putting humans at the bottom of the food chain for once. It's a strange dynamic that our two main characters Olwen (the Replicant Blade Runner played by Michelle Yeoh) and Cora (the human posing as a Replicant played by Hunter Schafer) are forced to navigate throughout the season.

As fans tune in, they can rest assured in the knowledge that the series is taking its cues from one of the most ambitious and boundary-pushing legacy sequels of them all. You could do a lot worse than that. All eight episodes of "Blade Runner 2099" are now on Prime Video.

#3381. Quentin Tarantino Did More Than Just Write The Further Mis-Adventures Of Cliff Booth

Quentin Tarantino has returned to the world of "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" with "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" (why not read our review of the new movie here?). But this time, while Tarantino penned the script, he isn't in the director's chair. Instead, he's handed directing duties over to his pal David Fincher (who is ending his exclusive deal with Netflix with the film). Tarantino might not be behind the camera, but he still has a presence in the film, and it echoes something he did in "Hollywood" as well.

Early in "Cliff Booth," we're introduced to Charlie Peters, a hot-tempered TV star played by Scott Caan. To speed-run us through Charlie's successful career, we're given a little montage of his various roles, and that montage is narrated by none other than Tarantino, whose very recognizable voice provides some humorous details about Charlie's work.

Fans of "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" will recall that Tarantino also provided narration in that movie, too. He actually wasn't the only narrator, either, because during one scene, Kurt Russell, who plays a stuntman named Randy in that film, also provides a little narration. As for Tarantino, he also voiced some crucial narration during a pivotal scene in "The Hateful Eight."

In fact, the filmmaker has a history of popping up in his movies, either via a voice cameo or a physical appearance. He has a pretty significant role in "Reservoir Dogs," makes a memorable cameo in "Pulp Fiction," gets to use an abysmal Australian accent in "Django Unchained," has his voice heard during a movie playing in "Inglourious Basterds" (and also plays a corpse in the film), plays a bartender in "Death Proof," portrays one of the members of the Crazy 88 gang in "Kill Bill," and lends his voice to an answering machine in "Jackie Brown."

So while "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" may not technically be a Quentin Tarantino movie, it still feels like one, right down to the obligatory cameo.

#3380. ‘The Trip’ Returns for Fifth Installment, Next Sending Steve Coogan and Rob Brydon to Frigid Arctic Circle

What does “Michael Caine” sound like in the freezing cold? We’re about to find out with the just-announced release of “The Trip to the Northern Lights,” which is the reunion of Steve Coogan, Rob Brydon, and director Michael Winterbottom for what is the fifth installment of “The Trip” franchise of miniseries/movies.

Independent Film Company and Sapan Studio picked up the U.S. rights to the fifth “Trip” film (IFC has released all four of the other films into theaters in the U.S.) and will release it theatrically on April 9, 2027. It will have been nearly seven years since the release of the last feature, and it sees Brydon now at 60 and Coogan at 59, so we’re guessing their ages may have made their wit and appetites even more ornery since. Related Stories ‘The Holy Boy’ Review: A Teenage Boy Heals People with His Touch in an Eerie Italian Horror Movie About the Price of Avoiding Your Pain ‘The Mosquito Bowl’ Review: ‘Friday Night Lights’ Meets ‘Five Came Back’ in Peter Berg’s Formulaic Netflix Movie About a World War II Football Game

“The Trip” movies are known for their food and travel porn as much as they are for their litany of impressions between Coogan and Brydon playing versions of themselves, but this one turns that concept on its head slightly by sending Coogan and Brydon up north, this time throughout Scandinavia, including Sweden and some islands in Norway, all in search of some other fine food and wry conversation.

The first look at the movie above sees the duo in ridiculously huge parkas in the snow as guided by some sled huskies. Try doing your best Bane impression at 10 below zero.

“We are very happy to be back on the road with IFC. They have been brilliant partners ever since the first ‘Trip’ all those years ago. ‘The Trip to the Northern Lights‘ takes Steve and Rob from Malmo in southern Sweden through Norway’s spectacular fjords to the Lofoten Islands in Norway’s Arctic circle,” Winterbottom said. “I hope the audience enjoys the journey as much as we did.”

“The Trip” franchise began all the way back in 2011, and since then the films have spanned trips in England, Italy, Spain, and Greece. As has been the case with all of the installments, they’ve been miniseries airing on TV in England but then edited into films for the U.S. release. The first movie made $3.9 million worldwide across several re-releases, “The Trip to Italy” in 2014 made $6.1 million, 2017’s “The Trip to Spain” made $1.9 million, and “The Trip to Greece” in the COVID-addled summer 2020 still managed to make $259K worldwide.

All four of the “Trip” movies are currently available for streaming on Sun Now, which is the streamer owned by Independent Film Company parent AMC Global Media.

“The Independent Film Company is thrilled to continue our longstanding relationship with this world-class group of filmmakers on the latest installment of this beloved franchise. Few comedic partnerships have the enduring appeal of Steve Coogan and Rob Brydon, and under Michael Winterbottom’s inspired direction, each new trip remains the comedic gift that keeps on giving. This time around, we can’t wait for audiences to join us on the road to the Northern Lights,” said Ayo Kepher-Maat, Independent Film Company’s Vice President of Acquisitions and Production.

“Michael Winterbottom, Steve Coogan, and Rob Brydon have created a franchise filled with taste, wit and belly laughs. Independent Film Company has brought each one to audiences with characteristic care and capability. ‘The Trip to the Northern Lights’ advances the history with the delight of something completely fresh and tasty,” said Josh Sapan of Sapan Studio.

The film is produced by Melissa Parmenter and Josh Hyams for Revolution Films. The deal was negotiated by Ayo Kepher-Maat on behalf of Independent Film Company and Tristan Whalley MD of Goalpost Films on behalf of the filmmakers.

Executive producers are Winterbottom, Coogan, Brydon, Alex Moody, Josh Sapan, Tristan Whalley, Paul Wiegard. “The Trip to the Northern Lights” is a Revolution Films, Baby Cow, and Small Man Production in association with Sky Studios.

This series will help you pick the perfect presents, decor, and activities to make this Christmas the Best Christmas Ever.

These days, though, everyone from your tech-obsessed granny to your cutting-edge teen wants to be impressed. Luckily, there's a mind-blowing high-tech gadget out there for everyone.

I don't know anyone who wouldn't appreciate finding these display glasses in their Christmas stocking. It can be set to track you from behind, from the side, or it can circle you, and you can adjust what it is doing from the app or remote on the fly, so there's no limit to the kind of elaborate shots it can pull off. #3373. 10 Hacks Every 'GTA 6' Player Should Know

I've been playing Grand Theft Auto VI since launch, and I'm having a blast so far. The world feels even more detailed and immersive than previous GTA games, which means there's a lot to learn beyond the basic tutorials and prompts the game shares at the beginning. These are the 10 GTA 6 hacks I used to improve the game's quality of life. If you do the same, you'll spend more time immersed in the world, and less time fighting the game's default settings.

I'm not going to share any spoilers here, but you should know that the side quests in Chapter 1 are important. If you ignore all the optional quests or small asks by other characters, you won't be able to return to those later. These are small things like fixing up the house for Lucia, meditating with her, and buying her a necklace when she asks you to. All of these have an impact on your progress. Take your time in this chapter, and remember to save before starting the mission called "Recalibration." That mission leads to Tourist Trap, which is the point of no return for Chapter 1.

If you're used to playing racing games, you'll find the driving experience in GTA VI to be quite different. It's hard to keep an eye on minimap directions while you're also getting used to vehicles in the game, and I used voice navigation to ensure that I don't keep getting lost, particularly for time-sensitive missions. You can enable this by going to GTA VI settings > Audio > GPS Voice > Voice. If you're playing the game on PS5, your DualSense controller's speaker plays GPS voice prompts. This is great as those alerts can be hard to hear over all other in-game sounds from your TV's speaker.

Using GTA 6's default controls, making Jason and Lucia run is quite annoying. The game makes you hold L3 to run, which hurts my thumbs. If you alter movement speed in settings, you can make the characters run just by using the left stick. You can walk by easing off the left stick, or switch to a fast walk, jog, or run when you push the stick all the way. Tweak this by going to GTA VI settings > Gameplay > Movement Speed > Jog. This lets you move faster without draining your stamina. You can also change from Jog to Run if you want the fastest possible movement speed with the left stick. Having said that, my pro tip is to go to Control Scheme in settings, and switch to Classic. This lets you run by holding the X button, as opposed to L3 with default controls.

Haptic strength is one area where GTA 6 takes the immersion a bit too far, as it's dialed up to the maximum level by default. This makes the controller's vibration strength a bit too intense for my liking, and also has a negative impact on battery life. You can fix that by reducing haptic strength a little. It's under GTA VI settings > Controller > Vibration & Haptics Strength.

Many modern controllers develop "stick drift," an issue where small movements of the analog sticks register as large inputs. This causes a big problem in games that require precise inputs, such as GTA 6. To counter this potential problem, the game allows you to adjust the deadzone for each analog stick in your controller. That said, this setting can be used to your advantage, even if you don't have stick drift issues in your controller. I recommend dialing up the deadzone to 7 to improve the driving experience. I find most cars in GTA 6 to be a bit floaty to drive, and adjusting the deadzone fixes this issue to a large extent.

Committing a heist attracts heat in GTA 6, and there are many different ways to escape the attention of in-game cops. The usual tricks include stocking up on outfits to change into, parking your vehicle a block or two away, and being so stealthy that you leave no witnesses to your crimes. However, an underrated trick involves using the pickup truck you get at the start of the game. Get a bike in the game, and stash it in your pickup truck. Then, use the truck to drive to the crime scene, and hide the truck a short distance away. Unload the bike, and use it to get to the crime scene. Once the heist is complete, ditch the bike, and run to your truck. Witnesses won't have seen you using the truck, which allows you to escape the area quickly.

If you are using a car as a getaway vehicle, you can use two tricks to make a smooth escape. First, double-tap the Triangle button to exit your vehicle without switching off its engine. When you return to the vehicle in a hurry, you can escape a lot faster. If you have quick fingers, you can double-tap Triangle first, and just as your character is about to exit the vehicle, press L3 (or X, if you use classic controls). This leaves the car's door open, and saves you a little more time when you're fleeing.

I suffer from chronic migraines, and I am sensitive to bright lights. Fortunately, GTA 6 has a bunch of accessibility settings that help me play the game for longer. Even if you don't face the same issues, these settings will help reduce eye strain in longer play sessions. Go to GTA VI settings > Display > Flashbang, and switch to Dark. This stops flashbangs from showing a bright white light when they go off. On the same settings page, you can tweak Player Status Effects Intensity to reduce screen effects when your character is low on health or stamina. You can also enable Brightness Reduction to reduce the intensity of bright lights in the game, and try Focus Trail Colorblind Mode if you find it hard to distinguish between different colors.

I haven't been able to play first-person shooters for decades because the camera movement makes me nauseous and gives me a headache. Of late, I've noticed that it's getting harder to play third-person games too. My first two hours in GTA 6 had me quite worried because I was feeling quite sick, and I had to turn off my PS5. Luckily for me, I found a few tweaks to mitigate this problem. You can do that in GTA VI settings > UI > Persistent Center Dot. This permanently shows a white dot in the center of the screen, and it reduced my motion sickness enough to help me play the game. You can also go to GTA VI settings > Camera, reduce Camera Bob, and turn off Camera Shake, and Weapon Sway. I also recommend going to the Controller tab in settings, and tweaking all the options under Aim & Look Sensitivity until you find a comfortable level.

GTA 6 includes realistic ringing sounds that linger after explosions in the game. This may be fine for some people, but it can negatively affect some players' gaming sessions. Those who suffer from tinnitus or chronic migraines may not enjoy those ringing sounds, and, luckily, the game allows you to disable them. Open GTA 6's in-game settings, and enable the feature from Audio > Tinnitus Reduction.

#3372. Fortnite Cracks Down on Pirate Shop Token Cheaters and Teammates

With just over a week before Fortnite Treasure Hunters comes to an end, desperation has set in, as players begin to lose hope of finding the Pirate Shop Access token. This is the most coveted item in Fortnite history because it grants up to 28 days of free Item Shop cosmetics.

The long search for the token has driven players to cheat. Epic Games has managed to catch these cheaters red-handed and has publicly announced that it will be banning them from Fortnite.

The consequences aren't limited to the players who resorted to cheating software. Players who win the token by teaming up with a cheater will not be banned, but they will be stripped of the token as well as any Item Shop goodies they claimed while it was active — even if they were unaware that a person in their party cheated. Players who teamed up with the cheater via Squad Fills are the only exception. This measure aims to prevent players from creating a smurf account exclusively for cheating.

The Pirate Shop Access token may be a reward that's almost too good to be true, but it's also extremely rare. The odds of finding the token are low (0.000007273%). Some players have opened over 150,000 chests with no luck, so it can definitely be frustrating to continue on. Players' best bet is to keep searching and collect other treasure from chests along the way.

With Golden Week coming up on Nov. 28, players will at least have increased chances of finding the rare gilded skins. Additionally, the week-long event begins on Saturday, when the final Treasure Hours of the season will be active, cranking up token odds by 1.5x. Fortnite Treasure Hunters ends on Dec. 5, so players still have some time to open chests and get the token before it's vaulted for good.
