#3356. ‘Filipiñana’ Could Be the Philippines’ First-Ever Oscar-Shortlisted Feature — Even as the Film Was Dealt an Unexpected Tragedy

A posh, Philippine country club’s colonial secrets are exposed in Rafael Manuel’s evocatively creepy, grimly funny, and austerely constructed social satire, “Filipiñana,” set outside Manila.

Writer/director Rafael Manuel’s film, which won a World Cinema special jury award at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival, also stands a chance at being his country’s first representative on a Best International Feature Film Oscar shortlist. While the Philippines was among the eight countries that submitted during the category’s inaugural year in 1956 (with Lamberto V. Avellana’s “Child of Sorrow”) along with France, Italy, and others, it’s never been nominated or shortlisted. Related Stories IndieWire Honors Film Celebration to Fête John Turturro, the ‘Artificial’ Cast, Los Javis, and More Cult Hit ‘Hundreds of Beavers’ Returns to Theaters for Big Christmas Expansion

Executive-produced by Manuel’s former mentor Jia Zhangke, “Filipiñana” follows a tee girl who discovers something is off (and downright sinister) about the club’s administration, specifically president Dr. Palanca (Teroy Guzman). She’s played by Jorrybell Agoto, who, at just 32 years old, died earlier in November after a short battle with lymphoma.

IndieWire’s interview with filmmaker Rafael Manuel took place a week before the news, though he shared in a later statement, “The tragedy of this loss cannot be put into words. The world has just lost one of its brightest stars. We have just lost a great friend. But our thoughts and prayers go out especially to Jorybell’s family, who have just lost a loving ate [the Filipino word for older sister] and a devoted daughter.”

An elegaic air, too, hangs over the film in retrospect and even before Agoto’s passing, as “Filipiñana” dwells in ghosts of the Philippines’ imperial past and Spanish occupation.

“No one explains it to you beforehand,” director Manuel told IndieWire of touring with his first feature for nearly a year. (We spoke over Zoom while he smoked a cigarette in his Amsterdam apartment.) “What I’m starting to realize is the biggest difference between short and feature is that with short festival, it’s kind of the end goal. When you premiere at your festival, you’re so happy, and it’s done; it’s like people get to see it finally. But with a feature film, it’s just the beginning, and no one explained this to me.”

Manuel joins the ranks of Lav Diaz, Brillante Mendoza, the late Lino Brocka, and many others to represent the Philippines at the Academy Awards — a concept, he said, that was never really on his radar.

“When we were coming up with this film and the genesis of the film, you don’t really think about an Oscars race,” said Manuel. “You just think about making the best film you can. And especially coming from Southeast Asia, access to the American market, even getting a U.S. theatrical release, it’s not something that’s very common. Usually, your usual route is via the European arthouse market. So it’s been really surprising and in the best way possible, seeing how well received the film is in the States, in North America, and in the Anglo world in general.”

The process was a “very challenging one,” he said, as the Philippines is taking the Oscar push very seriously from a governmental perspective. “And to be the first film that’s seriously backed by the government means a lot to us,” he said, especially for a film that’s critical of government and social hierarchy.

And there are hat tips not only to Jacques Tati, but also to Wes Anderson and Michael Haneke, at least in reviews, in terms of the movie’s flattened remove from violence and its dryly observational approach where everything in the frame is meticulously arranged.

“I get why people are saying Michael Haneke and Wes Anderson,” he said. “I mean, Jacques Tati, obviously, he’s a really big influence for me, but for example, with Haneke, I feel like we tackle violence very differently from how Haneke tackles violence. And I think with Wes Anderson, I see it because of the colors, because of the symmetrical framing and all of that, but I think this is very much a satire of that. And so, yes, we use a lot of Western codes and Western aesthetics in the film, but because it’s a film that deals with Western influence in the Orient, it was a film that deals with colonization. So the form and the aesthetic of the film is very much part of the satire. It’s the form.”

He added, “It’s a polarizing film. I think it’s either you love it or you hate it, and I think that’s the same whether you’re in the West or in the Philippines.”

The distribution of world cinema in the Philippines also helps to explain the divided palate for “Filipiñana,” as audiences have very little exposure to arthouse cinema from the outside world.

“In the Philippines, distribution of world cinema, it’s almost nonexistent. In Metro Manila, we have basically one or two arthouse cinemas, independent cinemas. The rest of the cinemas are all in shopping malls, and all they play are local rom-coms or Marvel movies,” he said. But issues in the West of audience fatigue over shopworn, recycled I.P. and familiar material also apply in the Philippines.

“It’s been a hot topic lately in the Philippines and consumers and audiences complaining about formulaic Filipino filmmaking. They’re tired of the formulaic rom-coms. But then the thing is that in the Philippines, I would say 90 percent of people have never seen a Lav Diaz film, even maybe 99 percent of people haven’t seen a Lav Diaz film,” Manuel said of the slow cinema master behind last year’s submission, the Gael García Bernal-starring “Magellan,” which also dealt in the Philippines’ colonized history. (Diaz and Manuel share producers, including Bianca Balbuena and Bradley Liew, though they’ve never actually met.)

“Filipiñana” marks a break from tradition in terms of its Westernized style — and chatter has been flying on Letterboxd over the film since the Sundance premiere. (“I look through Letterboxd sometimes. Well, I used to, I stopped. And then the unhealthy thing with Letterboxd, for me especially, is that I’ll skip all the good comments and I’ll just read all the bad comments,” he said.)

“When you’re faced with something different with arthouse cinema, like Filipino arthouse cinema, when Filipino audiences are faced with Filipino arthouse cinema, and you get some violent reactions, then it begs the question, ‘When you’re complaining about being tired of formulaic Filipino filmmaking, what exactly do you mean, and what exactly is it that you want?’ Do you just want Hollywood films but with brown faces in them? Because I don’t think that’s the answer either.”

“Filipiñana” is now streaming on Kino Film Collection.

#3355. 12 Things to Do on Christmas If You Don’t Celebrate

This series will help you pick the perfect presents, decor, and activities to make this Christmas the Best Christmas Ever.

In a way, the Christmas season is more fun if you don’t celebrate it. You get to enjoy all the brightly colored lights your neighbors put up, but you don’t have to put up your own. You don’t have to do any duty-shopping. There's no pressure. But Christmas Day itself leaves you in a mostly shuttered world that feels like there’s nothing going on. Fortunately, there are options to make Dec. 25 a fun day off, regardless of your observances.

You can’t go wrong with some moo shu pork and a trip to the multiplex. Chinese restaurants and movie theaters traditionally stay open on Christmas Day for those who don't celebrate, and they’re often filled with fellow Christmas refugees. Check Google for the hours of your local Chinese restaurant and give them a call to make a reservation. If you’re more adventurous and you’re in a city large enough to have a Chinatown (or a whatever-town), just head straight there on Christmas and see what happens—that’s how the best days usually start.

If Chinese food isn’t your thing, look at restaurants serving any non-European cuisine—Greek places, Japanese places, and Mediterranean places are usually open, as are plenty of Italian restaurants and steakhouses. Just make sure you check first. Lots of chain restaurants are open on Christmas Day too, including Applebee's, McDonald’s, Benihana, and more. You can even get Christmas breakfast at your local IHOP. But not every location of every outlet follows the same hours.

As for movies, most chain multiplex theaters are open on Dec. 25, and theaters are usually pretty full. The movies attract both people who don't celebrate Christmas and people who do, but want to get away from their families for a couple hours, so make sure and reserve a seat beforehand. Consider hitting up an out-of-the-way spot or that theater with the table service and cushy recliners to make it feel like more of an occasion.

Most people going to the movies on Christmas Day aren’t there for Christmas movies, so interesting “secular” movies are often slated for release on the 25th. This year's Christmas is unusually packed with interesting new movies, including family flick Jumani: Open World, a Robert Eggers horror movie called Werwulf, and the crowd pleasing football story Mr. Irrelevant, so you have serious options.

Chinese restaurants and movie theaters aren’t the only establishments open on Christmas. Here are some other options:

Go skiing or snowboarding: Most mountains are open on Christmas, and the lift lines are blissfully empty. There's no better way of celebrating a winter-based holiday than on a wide-open mountain.

Visit a skating rink: Speaking of winter sports, ice skating rinks are generally open on Christmas too.

Pretend to be a tourist: Tourist attractions are often open on Christmas, especially in larger cities. This includes places like Madame Tussaud’s and Ripley’s Believe It or Not, as well as ziplines and Segway tours—so do that touristy thing you’ve never done before.

Get a room: If you’ve got some spare cash and have nothing better to do, get a room at a hotel. Hotels don’t usually close on Christmas, and they typically offer plenty of amenities, so take advantage of the pool at the Holiday Inn or the spa at the Four Seasons, depending on your lifestyle.

Hiking and biking: Hiking trails and parks are open on Christmas if you want to get outdoors. If you’re into biking, hit the trails or hit the streets: Traffic is minimal on Christmas, so it’s a great time to put in some serious roadwork.

Volunteer: Not having anything to do on Christmas isn’t the biggest life problem, especially compared to people who have nowhere to go and nothing to eat. So use Christmas to help people and actually deliver on that whole “good will towards men” thing. Check your local Craigslist for volunteering opportunities.

Use Christmas as a catch-up day: This is strictly for type-A people, but if everyone is out of town and no one is going to call you, why not spend the day catching up on neglected chores or personal projects? You can spend at least part of your day knocking a few things off your to-do list and the rest of the time relaxing. That way you’ll get a break and still feel accomplished.

Just sleep all day: Type-B personalities like me see a day free of obligations and other people as a golden opportunity to do as little as is humanly possible, a day to fully commit to sloth.

Spend time with friends and family at home: Not celebrating Christmas doesn’t mean you can’t spend the day with family and/or friends. Get together with your loved ones, play games, watch a movie, cook together, talk, or whatever else you all enjoy. You don’t have to go out to have fun, so don’t rule out staying in with people you care about.

Shopping: This is at the bottom of the list because it’s iffy. Drug stores and convenience stores like 711 are usually open on the 25th. Grocery chains like Kroger’s and Trader Joe’s usually aren’t. Your local shopping mall or retail district might be open, but probably won't be, so check ahead.

Because so many places are closed on Christmas Day, you should plan ahead (unless you like spontaneity and are OK with the possibility of disappointment) by:

Making a list of the places you want to go.

Calling nearby locations to confirm they’ll be open, as not every chain follows corporate holiday hour recommendations.

Making reservations at any restaurant(s) you plan to visit.

Putting together a basic timeline of the day, accounting for travel time, so you don’t lose any reservations, miss a movie, or arrive after the store closes.

The most important advice here is to do something intentional on Christmas, even if it's sleeping in, so the day doesn't feel depressing or empty. So hit the slopes, suck down some dim sum, or keep your couch from floating away, but be sure you make Christmas your own.

#3353. 9 Years Later, Matt Reeves’ Sci-Fi Masterpiece Returns to Streaming

In the last few years, Matt Reeves has become widely known and celebrated as a director thanks to his work on The Batman starring Robert Pattinson. Production on The Batman Part II is set to come to a close soon, and now that Pattinson has been cast as the next James Bond, there’s doubt that he will continue as Batman after the film has been released. The future of the franchise was already in doubt after a personal matter forced Reeves to step back from shooting the sequel during its final stages, but the studio brought in Steven Soderbergh to finish principal photography in Reeves’ stead. Like many filmmakers, Reeves has given a large chunk of his career to a singular property, but the demand for more out of his Batman project is so great that fans have shown they’re willing to wait extended periods for another film — the sequel isn’t coming to theaters until 2028.

In the late 2000s, Matt Reeves exploded onto the scene as a director thanks to his work in Cloverfield, the 2008 disaster epic that’s currently streaming for free on Pluto TV. However, in 2014, Reeves helmed what many would argue is still the best film of his career, Dawn of the Planet of the Apes, the sci-fi thriller starring Andy Serkis. He returned three years later to direct the final film in the trilogy, War for the Planet of the Apes, which grossed nearly $500 million at the box office against a $150 million budget. Nine years later, the film has found a streaming home on HBO Max, where it has recently surged into the top 10 over the last week.

The first Planet of the Apes movie in the reboot series, which stars James Franco, follows Caesar as he becomes conscious and aware, breaking out of captivity and moving on to live as a free ape in the wild. The sequel sets the stage for the giant war between humans and apes in the trilogy-capper, which holds scores of 94% from critics and 84% from audiences on Rotten Tomatoes. The film also features plenty of other stars you might recognize, such as Woody Harrelson and Steve Zahn.

Check out War for the Planet of the Apes on HBO Max and stay tuned to Collider for more updates and coverage of Matt Reeves' future projects, including The Batman Part II.

#3352. Watch ‘The Sheep Detectives’ VFX Supervisor Break Down the ‘Sheep-Isms’ That Made His Characters Stand Out

It’s not every day you see a movie where talking sheep get to be the stars. But Kyle Balda’s “The Sheep Detectives” does exactly that. The Amazon MGM film flips the whodunnit formula on its head with a barnyard murder mystery in which a group of sheep have to solve the murder of their beloved shepherd. Much of the film’s success can be attributed to the juxtaposition between a whimsical plot and the realism with which it’s executed. The sheep might talk and solve crimes, but they look like real animals you’d find on any farm.

During the VFX section of IndieWire’s recent Craft Roundtables, “The Sheep Detectives” Visual Effects Supervisor Graham Page broke down the meticulous research process that made the sheep look so lifelike. Related Stories ‘Filipiñana’ Could Be the Philippines’ First-Ever Oscar-Shortlisted Feature — Even as the Film Was Dealt an Unexpected Tragedy IndieWire Honors Film Celebration to Fête John Turturro, the ‘Artificial’ Cast, Los Javis, and More

“To make them look real, talking about practical and how important that is, I from Day One felt like you had to base these characters on real sheep,” Page said. “We filmed [real sheep] with multiple cameras and getting on boxes. We had a script, almost, like ‘These are the things the sheep need to do in the film.’ Even before an animator can touch it, another artist modeled the skeleton and the muscle and fat. And then you have a rigger and a facial artist, all of these artists.”

He went on to explain how that research process produced character-defining details that they would not have discovered any other way.

“We started to come up with what we would call ‘Sheep-isms’ that help kind of bring some of that natural movement,” he said. “There’s a little ear twitch. And a human can’t twitch their ear, but it felt so right. We were like ‘This is really nice,’ and it emphasized the character and the story and the emotion. But it was brought out of a sheep.”

More coverage from our Craft Roundtables can be found here.

#3350. Scarlett Johansson’s New Horror Reboot Officially Continues 53-Year Rating Streak

Scarlett Johansson's The Exorcist: Martyrs will be pulling no punches.

Johansson is teaming up with Mike Flanagan for the latest reboot of the classic horror franchise, starring as New York City homicide detective Julie Miller as she is pulled into a dark murder investigation with apparent ties to a former Satanic serial killer she helped stop. Also starring Chiwetel Ejiofor, Diane Lane, Jacobi Jupe and Sasha Lane, among many others, The Exorcist: Martyrs is currently on track for a March 12 release date.

Now, with just over two months until it hits theaters, the Motion Picture Association has officially given The Exorcist: Martyrs an R rating, continuing the horror franchise's 53-year streak of landing the mature rating. The site further explains that the new reboot's rating stems from its "bloody violent content, grisly images, language, and some sexual references."

In addition to the franchise's tradition, The Exorcist: Martyrs securing an R-rating also continues Flanagan's streak of more mature films in the director's chair. Across his eight released films, only two have landed a PG-13 rating from the MPA, those being Netflix's Before I Wake and Blumhouse's Ouija: Origin of Evil. His TV shows have similarly landed firmly in the TV-MA rating, generally stemming from explicit language and, in recent years, some bloodier set pieces.

Interestingly, while it keeps the series' 53-year streak alive, The Exorcist: Martyr's R-rating does immediately stand out from its predecessors with its promise of "grisly images." Though the horror franchise is well-known for its more visceral material, the only other movie to explicitly list its gruesome imagery as part of its R-rating was that of the infamous Exorcist: The Beginning prequel film. See the chart below for the full franchise list of ratings and given reasons from the MPA:

Strong violence and gore, disturbing images and rituals, and for language including some sexual dialogue.

Some violent content, disturbing images, language and sexual references.

Bloody violent content, grisly images, language, and some sexual references.

The first Exorcist: Martyrs trailer already showcased Flanagan leaning into more gruesome territory for his reboot of the classic horror series. The crime scenes Johansson's character inspects come complete with dead bodies mutilated in different ritualistic manners, while another sequence saw Julie inspecting a barrel later with an unknown entity emerging and coated in blood. As Flanagan himself teased to ScreenRant, he was not looking to pull any punches with his film, calling it "very, very bloody":

Mike Flanagan: Yeah, I think the only thing that comes close to the amount of blood is we did melt that orgy in The Fall of the House of Usher in acid. That was pretty bloody, but that was funny, I thought. [Chuckles] As dark as it was, this is vicious, and that isn't a muscle I get to flex very often. It's very disturbing, and that was part of the fun of it. This whole story just felt very unsafe from the beginning, and yeah, that isn't a gear I go toward frequently. I like hope and heart and humanism, and there are moments of that if you squint, but this is a dark story, and it is scary. So yeah, that was very exciting for me, too.

With Flanagan also having been largely inspired by the cult favorite Exorcist III for his take on the franchise, it will be interesting to see if The Exorcist: Martyrs finds itself leaning closer to the 1990 film's atmosphere than the visceral nature of its 2004 successor. Given early test screenings, per the director, have been glowing, as has the response to the trailer thus far, it does at least seem like this push into hard-R territory is going to give viewers an unforgettable experience.

Thirteen years after stopping a satanic serial killer, New York City detective Julie Miller confronts a new murderer who appears connected to her past. With help from a former prison chaplain and a rookie detective, she investigates a sinister connection between history's most notorious killers.

#3348. 10 Hidden Controls Every 'GTA 6' Player Should Know

You can have a ton of fun in GTA 6 even if you only follow the core gameplay loop of running around, stealing cars, and completing missions and side quests. However, if you take a minute to learn a few hidden controls, I think you'll enjoy the game even more. These are fairly simple controls that let you hide from the cops, trash talk other drivers, or flip the bird when you're feeling like annoying NPCs. These are 10 of the best hidden GTA 6 controls that'll help you unlock an entirely new side of the game.

If you just want to sit back and relax as your character drives around Leonida in GTA 6, you should try the auto-drive mode. It's a relaxing way to enjoy the streets without having to worry about following traffic rules. To enable it, you need to get in a vehicle and add a waypoint on the map. This serves as your character's destination, so if you want a longer drive, be sure to drop the waypoint far, far away. Next, hold the down arrow on the D-Pad, and press the Option button. This enables cinematic mode. Then, hold the Circle button to enable auto-drive.

Your character is going to commit a lot of crimes in GTA 6. When this happens, you attract heat, and soon enough, cops will begin chasing you. Switching cars is a great way to reduce the amount of attention you get from law enforcement, but you can still be identified by your face or clothing. Until you can reach a safe spot to swap outfits, maintain a low profile by ducking while driving. Hold the Circle button while driving to duck.

EA's Road Rash was among the first racing games I played as a child, and I remember how much fun it was to kick your rivals while speeding through the game's various courses. You can have a taste of that in GTA 6 too. Press the Square button while you're riding a bike, and your character will kick anyone who's near you. If you do this in a car, it opens the door, and hits people around the car. To annoy other drivers, press R3, and your character will direct some trash talk towards NPCs.

Hold Circle to lean back against walls, or to sit on the beach. To rest on a ledge, you can hold L3. This lets you take a moment to soak in beautiful views in the game, or lounge around as you listen to NPC conversations. Paying attention to those conversations can lead to some fun side quests, and sometimes give you a tip or two for quick money or other rewards.

If you really want to rile people up in GTA 6, you can flip the bird. This works only when your character is unarmed. Hold L2, focus on a person, then press R1. Actions have consequences in GTA 6, so be prepared to fight NPCs when you do this.

When you're being chased by cops, enemies, or angry NPCs, you can use a quick shortcut to look back without turning the camera around. Just hold R3 to look behind you.

While driving, press Circle to toggle headlights (and switch to high beams). This is particularly useful when you're offroading at night. You can also hold left arrow on the D-Pad, and move the right stick up to access other vehicle controls like hazard lights, opening or closing windows, etc., in case you want to add to the realism.

Stealing emergency vehicles in GTA 6 is risky, but the reward is totally worth it. Not only do you find stashes of weapons, gear, and money in some of these vehicles, but you also have access to sirens that help you clear traffic off your path. If you steal an ambulance or a cop car, hold L3, and move the left stick up to go through different siren tones. Press L3 and the left stick up to enable the siren.

GTA 6 is a third-person game, but it has a first-person mode that partially works. It is useful for looking at smaller objects around your character, such as posters, small signs, or to look for clues in and around a house. (Yes, I am talking about Mandy's creepy house and bad vibes.) Hold L2 + hit R3 to switch to first-person mode. Sadly, you can't move when you do this, but you can look around. Try it in Mandy's property to observe a few nasty surprises.

When you sprint towards a car, press the X button to slide across the hood. This is much faster and smoother than running around parked cars or jumping over them. It also looks cool, which is reason enough to try this feature.

#3346. AI May Be Scanning Your Private Signal Chats

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you use Signal, it's likely you care at least a little bit about keeping your communication private so only you and those you're chatting with can see your message threads. Signal's end-to-end encryption keeps prying eyes out, but if you use agentic AI on your device, your chats may not be as locked down as you think.

Signal has already blocked screenshot capabilities for Microsoft's Recall AI, which by default was able to take and store screen grabs of Signal messages on Windows 11. While Signal cannot guarantee that AI won't have access to your data, there are a few protections now available for those on iOS and Android as well.

The main workaround in Signal for now is to restrict screenshots and screen recordings inside the app, though this does not prevent AI agents from potentially grabbing content from other parts of your device. According to Signal's support documents, these protections will now be enabled by default on iOS 27 and Android with the latest versions of the Signal app.

#3345. Casting HBO's Baldur's Gate Series: All 10 BG3 Party Members

Streaming platforms are in full swing with live-action video game adaptations, and HBO’s upcoming Baldur’s Gate series is among the most exciting currently in development. Reportedly set after the events of Baldur’s Gate 3, the show looks set to bring one of the most iconic settings from Dungeons & Dragons to the small screen. The city of Baldur’s Gate offers enormous possibilities for a live-action D&D TV show, especially since it follows on from the events of the hugely popular video game series.

Details remain scarce, but for fans of Baldur’s Gate 3, a key question is who will play its beloved characters if they return. Many want original performers such as Neil Newbon and Jennifer English to reprise their roles, and the HBO show’s developer, The Last Of Us’s Craig Mazin, has expressed interest in involving the game’s cast (via Deadline). However, his enthusiasm doesn’t guarantee that they’ll definitely return, or that they’ll play the same characters. Fortunately, there are some more than suitable actors to fill the shoes of any familiar party members returning in HBO’s Baldur’s Gate series.

Astarion can make an appalling suggestion sound like the most entertaining idea in the room. He has a unique combination of elegance, malice, and impeccable comic timing, all of which is familiar territory for Tom Hiddleston, whose performance as Loki made the MCU’s trickster god’s wounded pride and theatrical mischief irresistible. He’s also got prior experience playing a vampire thanks to 2013’s Only Lovers Left Alive. Both roles capture something that’s essential to Astarion: the arrogance of immortality being used to mask a sense of desperation and need for a greater purpose than simply living forever.

Tom Hiddleston could deliver Astarion’s most withering remarks with ease while also making the sudden disappearance of that confidence feel just as unsettling in HBO’s Baldur’s Gate TV show as it was in BG3. Any actor playing Astarion requires an understanding of how a charming character can quickly become a terrifying one. Hiddleston has the skills to make Astarion hilarity land without him being reduced to comic relief. He could make BG3’s vampire rogue funny, unsettling, and emotionally complex, all of which would be essential when following in the footsteps of Neil Newbon’s performance in the game.

Ben Barnes has already shown how fun to watch a charming, articulate man with dangerous magical ambitions can be. His time as General Kirigan/The Darkling in Netflix’s Shadow and Bone is a great glimpse of how he might handle Gale’s susceptibility to power in a live-action Baldur’s Gate story, while The Chronicles of Narnia: Prince Caspian demonstrates the sincerity needed for the wizard’s more approachable side. Any actor playing Gale needs to balance both sides for the performance to land.

The greatest challenge if Gale makes an appearance in HBO’s Baldur’s Gate series is ensuring the Wizard of Waterdeep feels approachable despite his intellectual ego. His elaborate explanations and social awkwardness make him considerably warmer than a stereotypical mysterious fantasy sorcerer. Still, this should never mean he comes across as weak or incapable. Roles like Billy Russo in The Punisher prove that Ben Barnes has no issue portraying characters who are charming yet still dangerous, especially those driven by ambitions those around them would struggle to understand.

Karlach should look capable of throwing an enemy across a room without breaking a sweat, and WWE superstar Rhea Ripley would make that immediately believable. While not an experienced actor, her wrestling career supplies the strength, explosive movement, and physical confidence needed for a tiefling barbarian who has survived the Blood War. Just as important is her ability to command attention through posture and facial expressions. Ripley can make a grin feel like a challenge or an invitation, a promising quality for a character whose excitement about being alive is just as memorable as her capacity for destruction.

True, it would be an ambitious move into dramatic acting for Rhea Ripley, especially given how much pain sits beneath Karlach’s enthusiasm. Her infernal engine makes the simple possibility of touching someone devastatingly important, and those scenes demand tenderness as much as rage. Ripley’s suitability for the role lies in the combination of playfulness with being physically intimidating. If she can pull of the more nuanced side of Karlach’s character too, she’ll be more than ideal for HBO’s Baldur’s Gate TV show cast.

Anya Taylor-Joy’s work as the titular road warrior in Furiosa: A Mad Max Saga makes a solid argument for giving her a sword and very little patience in the live-action Baldur’s Gate series. Characters like Furiosa as well as Margot in The Menu are all the evidence needed that she can communicate determination through a fixed stare and a stubborn refusal to show weakness, which is essential for Lae’zel. The Githyanki fighter’s severity comes from a culture that treats strength as survival and obedience as virtue. Taylor-Joy’s filmography leaves little doubt that she could make that conditioning visible in every moment Lae’zel is on-screen.

Anya Taylor-Joy's performance as Beth Harmon in The Queen’s Gambit in particular reveals that she can bring a convincing blend of near-unshakable pride even in the face of profound isolation. Lae’zel’s confidence in her abilities is compelling in BG3 because it survives encounters that dismantle her understanding of the world, and Taylor-Joy would have no issue ensuring this stays intact in a live-action performance. Her penchant for precise delivery would also suit the accidental comedy of Lae’zel’s blunt observations, keeping the humor rooted in the warrior’s absolute conviction that everyone around her is being ridiculous when she finds herself at odds with the room.

When voiced by Jennifer English in BG3, Shadowheart could make even an admission of ignorance or failure feel like somebody else’s embarrassing mistake. The half-elf cleric needs an actress who can deliver that same sarcasm while also making it clear that keeping those around her at a distance takes effort. Her damaged memories and religious conditioning mean that certainty about her place in the world has to be actively maintained. Fallout, Yellowjackets, and Sweetpea star Ella Purnell could ensure the contradictions that define Shadowheart survive the transition to live-action in HBO’s Baldur’s Gate series.

Viewers should want to understand Shadowheart even when she’s doing something atrocious, a quality Ella Purnell’s performance as Rhiannon in Sweetpea hinges on. Her portrayal of Lucy MacLean in Prime Video’s Fallout series shows how effectively she can capture someone discovering that the beliefs shaping her life conceal horrifying truths, another essential Shadowheart trait. Finally, her work as Jackie Taylor in Yellowjackets reveals a capacity to capture wounded pride and defensive cruelty. Together, these roles suggest that there are few actresses out there more suited to playing Shadowheart in live-action.

Regé-Jean Page already has experience in projects based on D&D. Not only that, he’s already played a character who exists in the same world as the city of Baldur’s Gate, the Forgotten Realms. As Xenk Yendar in 2023’s Dungeons & Dragons: Honor Among Thieves, Page brought effortless authority and wonderfully straight-faced humor to a hero whose defining personality trait is an unwavering commitment to doing good. Wyll would benefit from that same lack of embarrassment about heroism. While his character is far from simple, Wyll’s most immediate trait is that he sincerely wants to protect people.

Playing Xenk is all the proof needed that Page could make his borderline-theatrical confidence appealing while ensuring his willingness to put himself in danger feels sincere rather than sanctimonious. However, Wyll’s story also offers considerably more internal conflict than Xenk Yendar’s. His pact with the dark entity Mizora directly contradicts his noble intentions. Thankfully, Regé-Jean Page’s Simon Basset in Bridgerton showcased an ability to play polished charm that acts as a mask for concealed vulnerability and self-doubt. That experience would suit Wyll’s complicated relationship with his father and the personal costs of his pact with Mizora.

Few actors have a knack for playing approachable yet believable leadership figures like Anson Mount. His Captain Christopher Pike in Star Trek: Strange New Worlds can command a crisis and then make his colleagues feel comfortable around a dinner table. This is an excellent foundation for playing Halsin in HBO’s Baldur’s Gate series. The archdruid’s imposing appearance comes with an unusually gentle temperament. His experience gives him authority, but he rarely needs to flex his superiority. Mount could bring that reassuring confidence to a BG3 character who feels equally believable offering guidance, expressing desire, or becoming terrifying when someone threatens the vulnerable.

Any actor playing Halsin also needs to create a sense that the Baldur’s Gate character has interests beyond whatever emergency currently occupies the party. His devotion to nature, openness about pleasure, and concern for people damaged by conflict make him earthy and approachable despite his age. Anson Mount’s relaxed warmth would help those qualities emerge naturally, while his more rugged work in Hell on Wheels prove he has the action credentials for the druid’s less peaceful moments. With Halsin, the attraction is partly that strength and safety belong together, and Mount could definitely deliver this.

Long before the adventure in Baldur’s Gate 3 begins, Jaheira had already accumulated enough victories and losses to distrust a promising adventure. The veteran half-elf druid and Harper leader needs a cast member in the live-action Baldur’s Gate series who can bring that world weariness to life without turning every exchange into a solemn lesson. Hollywood veteran Michelle Pfeiffer could inarguably bring that authority, and her skills with dry humor would be just as valuable.

Pfeiffer’s Catwoman in Batman Returns is a perfect demonstration of how she can combine sharp wit with emotional baggage without making one quality cancel out the other. Her work as Lamia in 2007’s Stardust also shows how entertaining she can be in a high-fantasy setting. Jaheira needs a more grounded performance than many other Baldur’s Gate characters, with her sharpness honed by years of experience. Pfeiffer could make a cutting observation feel affectionate or devastating depending on who deserves it, while giving the character’s rarer admissions of grief the emotional weight they need.

Put physical powerhouse Dave Bautista beside a tiny hamster and much of Minsc’s visual appeal is already accounted for. The more important qualification is his understanding of how to make an enormous warrior funny through complete sincerity. As Drax in the Guardians of the Galaxy movies, Bautista repeatedly made literal-minded pronouncements entertaining because the character believed them so completely. Minsc needs that same commitment. His conversations with Boo, his miniature giant space hamster companion, should sound perfectly reasonable to him, however bewildered everyone around him becomes.

The BG3 ranger’s uncomplicated commitment to fighting evil would also give Bautista something substantial beneath the comedy. Just like Drax, Minsc’s understanding of a situation may be eccentric, but his love for his friends and determination to protect them are never minor details. Bautista has shown how tenderness can sit within an intimidating physical performance, and he could make those loyalties the reason audiences invest in the character. His size would sell the action immediately; his ability to express hurt or delight with disarming openness could ensure that Minsc remains lovable between the battles, too.

A quiet threat can be considerably more unnerving than a shouted one, and Rebecca Ferguson’s filmography proves she understands that distinction. Her Lady Jessica in Dune and Dune: Part Two combines controlled authority with a willingness to manipulate events toward ruthless ends. Those qualities would translate beautifully to Minthara, a drow paladin whose noble upbringing and brutal education inform nearly every judgment she makes. Ferguson could convey that instinctive expectation of obedience through her voice and stillness, making Minthara formidable before she ever reaches for a weapon.

However, alongside being terrifying, Minthara is also unexpectedly funny. Her devastating observations aren’t meant to be entertaining, but they often account for some of the funniest dialogue in Baldur’s Gate 3. Ferguson’s restrained delivery would suit these moments perfectly. The biggest challenge in the live-action Baldur’s Gate series would be showing the vulnerability beneath. Fortunately, thanks to roles like Juliette in Silo and Anna in The Girl on the Train, there’s every reason to believe that Rebecca Ferguson could do the subtleties of Minthara just as much justice, allowing moments of intimacy to complicate her character without erasing her more immediate, and troubling, qualities.

#3344. Nathan Fillion’s ‘The Rookie’ Officially Returns With a Major Schedule Change

Since its 2018 premiere, ABC's hit procedural The Rookie has performed well for the network. The series, led by Nathan Fillion, was an immediate hit, thanks to its premise of new beginnings and personal reinvention, no matter the challenges along the way. The story started as an exploration of John Nolan, the oldest rookie in the LAPD, but has evolved into one about a sharp police officer keeping the city safe alongside his coworkers in Los Angeles' Mid-Wilshire Police Department. Eight seasons have aired so far, with a ninth set for January 2027. It will also be accompanied by a brand-new spin-off.

This is not the first time ABC has tried to expand The Rookie, with the first attempt coming in 2022 when The Rookie: Feds premiered. Headlined by Niecy Nash-Betts as Simone Clark, the FBI-set spin-off followed a similar premise: Simone leaves her career in guidance and counseling to become the FBI's oldest rookie. The Rookie: Feds ran for one season and was canceled for several reasons, including the 2023 Hollywood strikes. Some of the show's stars have continued to appear in later seasons of The Rookie.

Next year finds the mothership on the move as ABC creates The Rookie Wednesdays. Beginning January 6, 2027, The Rookie will air from 9 pm ET, followed by the new spin-off The Rookie North at 10 pm. It will be an interesting night for ratings, since NBC's juggernaut One Chicago also airs that night from 8 to 11 pm ET. CBS won't be much of a competition, since it doesn't have scripted shows that night.

The Rookie started as a show about a man starting over at forty-five and turned into a proper ensemble drama somewhere around season three. Here is which of them you are, and the case for yours being the best of the four.

You started late and you are not embarrassed about it. Nolan walks into the academy at forty-five surrounded by people half his age, and the show is honest that this is both his biggest disadvantage and the only reason he is any good at the job.

You are better at this than people expect and you intend to keep proving it. Chen goes from rookie to the best undercover officer in the division, which works because she is genuinely good at becoming somebody else and genuinely bad at pretending she does not care.

You are hard on people because you have decided that is what caring looks like. Bradford is introduced as the worst training officer in the building and slowly revealed as the one who takes the job most seriously, which are the same fact seen from two angles.

You said what you wanted and then you went and got it. Lopez wanted detective from the first episode, said so out loud, and got there by being better at the work than the people who were quieter about wanting it.

ABC has already released teaser trailers for the upcoming seasons of both shows, and in The Rookie Season 9, Lucy Chen (Melissa O'Neil) and Tim Bradford (Eric Winter) are in trouble after being kidnapped during Tim's proposal. The department jumps into action to save them while they try to save themselves. Meanwhile, a new beginning takes place at 10 pm with The Rookie North. The series introduces Jay Ellis' Alex Holland, whose midlife crisis is activated by a violent home invasion. He joins the Pierce County Police Department. Rather than a slight refresh of The Rookie, the spin-off aims for a different feel by leaving the city for a slower, rural environment. The Rookie North also stars Janet Montgomery (New Amsterdam), Karen Fukuhara (The Boys), Chris Sullivan (This Is Us), Froy Gutierrez (Teen Wolf), Mya Lowe (My Life with the Walter Boys), and Malik Watson.

Tune in to The Rookie Wednesdays beginning Wednesday, January 6, 2027, and stay tuned to Collider for more updates.

#3343. Two Budget Smartwatches That Make Perfect Gifts

If you or someone on your shopping list wants a new smartwatch, you have plenty of options to choose from. The problem is, a lot of them can be quite pricey. Apple's cheapest smartwatch, the SE 3, starts at $249, and its other selections only skyrocket from there. On the flip side, the risk in picking a smartwatch that's too inexpensive is that the manufacturer likely made a series of sacrifices to get the price that low. At a certain point, the tradeoff just isn't worth it.

Luckily, you do have options. There are two smartwatches on the market that aren't just cheaper than the competition, they're not even in the same ballpark. And while you shouldn't expect the same capabilities as you would on flagship wearables, these devices are perfectly usable, both as fitness trackers and smartwatches—all while spending well below $100 a pop. CNET put both smartwatches through their paces to make these determinations, so you know whichever model you get, you won't be picking up a wearable paperweight.

Contrary to what you might expect, Amazfit has no ties to Amazon—other than that you can buy these watches from the latter. Amazfit is its own company, and produces a wide selection of smartwatch options. The Bip 6 happens to be the company's latest budget smartwatch, with an MSRP of just $79.99. In most cases, a price that low would be a red flag for a smartwatch, but not in the Bip 6's case.

The Amazfit Bip 6 holds its own against other flagship smartwatches. That's true on a surface level: This watch looks your average smartwatch, rather than a cheap imitation. In fact, at first glance, I'd bet most people would assume the Bip 6 is actually an Apple Watch. It has a rounded square design with a large 1.97-inch display with a resolution of 390 by 450 pixels (though there's no Always-On display). This isn't a cheap display, either: Amazfit put an AMOLED screen on the watch, which looks great indoors—though CNET Labs struggled to see the screen in direct sunlight.

Where the Bip 6 really shines, however, is with fitness tracking. This watch supports GPS, which makes tracking outdoor runs possible without a smartphone. CNET Labs found that it takes about 10 seconds to find a GPS signal, but once it connects, you're set. While running, the Bip 6 reliably tracks your heart rate. CNET Labs compared its sensor to the Polar chest strap HR monitor and found it on par, though, like other smartwatches, the Bip 6 is slower at detecting heart rate spikes. You'll get data like cadence and stride while tracking runs, and strength training and muscle groups while working out indoors. For example, CNET Labs found that it correctly identified arm muscle exercises while testing the watch during a pilates session.

You also get some health and wellness features, too. The Bip 6 can measure heart rate variations, body temperature changes, sleep stages, and even your breathing quality. Its One Tap Measuring mode supports a single reading for heart rate, SpO2 (blood oxygen saturation), stress, and breathing rate, and it supports cycle tracking—though CNET specifies it can't track skin temperature like other smartwatches and health trackers. There's an optional subscription that provides AI coaching tools and looks out for health conditions like sleep apnea and insomnia. While health and wellness tracking is solid, note that CNET Labs found Amazfit's app, Zepp, to be confusing, since it simply displays your data without much context or explanation.

For an $80 smartwatch, the Bip 6 has an excellent battery life. CNET Labs found that the watch could be pushed to its limits—multiple workouts using GPS, heart rate tracking, keeping the display on during workouts—and still run for eight days before needing a charge. In fact, reviewer Vanessa Hand Orellana speculates you could push the Bip 6 to Amazfit's two-week battery life claim by limiting some of the most intensive settings and features. The only downside here is that there is no fast charging, so it will take about two hours to get back to 100%. But if you're only charging the watch once every week or two, that isn't much of a burden. There's also no charger in the box, so you'll need to use a separate USB-C cable.

As a smartwatch, the Bip 6 can be a mixed bag. CNET found that the UI was clunky and sluggish, and the OS requires some user intervention before it's as usable as a standard Apple Watch or Galaxy Watch. While the watch has a voice assistant, Flow, CNET found it to be borderline unusable. However, CNET says Android users can reply to texts with a keyboard or dictation without needing the assistant. iPhone users can't do the same by default, but by downloading a third-party app, they can jerry-rig the watch to send and receive texts.

Based on CNET Labs' testing, the Amazfit Bip 6 is one of the best budget smartwatches you can buy. For $80, you get a reliable workout tracker that looks like most standard watches on the market. And while you're making some sacrifices at this price point, they're largely worth it for $80.

While the Amazfit is a good choice for both iPhone and Android users, the Galaxy Fit 3 might be the best choice for Samsung users. This isn't an option for iPhone users, and while it works with all Android devices, you get some Samsung-specific perks if you have a Galaxy phone.

The Galaxy Fit 3 is even cheaper than the Amazfit Bip 6: This watch is only $60, which makes it among the cheapest smartwatches you can buy. Now, this doesn't look like your average smartwatch. Samsung opted for a fitness tracker-like design, with a long 1.6-inch (40mm) AMOLED display. But for a fitness tracker/smartwatch hybrid, it's a solid look.

In CNET's testing, one of the Galaxy Fit 3's biggest strengths is its battery life—though it pales in comparison to the Bip 6. When pushed to its limits, the Fit 3 can run three days in between charges, though Samsung claims you can get it up to 13 days with the right settings. While the Amazfit has it beat, the Fit 3 might sound like a dream compared to other smartwatches, even from Samsung. Unlike the Bip 6, the Fit 3 supports fast charging. You can fill the watch up completely in just over an hour.

CNET did find that the "smart" elements of this wearable were a bit lacking, however. The Fit 3 doesn't support voice dictation or mobile payments like other watches do, and unless you have a Galaxy phone, you won't be able to access the camera remote or sync your alarms. And while the Amazfit Bip 6's "Flow" is hardly reliable, the Fit 3 doesn't have an assistant at all. You can see incoming calls and decline (but not answer) them, and you can send prewritten responses to text messages, but not initiate them. Still, CNET found that Samsung added the essentials: You have an alarm, calculator, weather app, camera remote, and, of course, the Samsung Health app. (What kind of health tracker would this be without it?)

CNET found that the Fit 3 is a reliable fitness tracker, particularly for $60. You can track over 100 different workouts, and the watch automatically logs exercises like runs, walks, rowing, and elliptical sessions—if you enable auto-tracking, that is. It also supports swimming with its IP68 water resistance rating. CNET Labs found that the heart rate tracking was "generally accurate" when compared to the Polar chest strap, though its slower with registering heart rate spikes. Interestingly, the heart rate tracker was a bit delayed in testing, but once CNET reviewed the data in the health app, the data had corrected to be largely accurate. You also get high and low heart rate alerts, though no ECG app. (The $249 Apple Watch SE 3 also omits this feature.)

In CNET's testing, the sleep tracker on the Fit 3 was useful, if not entirely accurate. The watch can detect your sleep stages and look out for snoring using your Galaxy phone's mic. Like other health trackers, you get a sleep score, but CNET found it a bit inaccurate, since it rated a six and a half hour sleep session "Excellent" (91/100).

Still, the Fit 3 is really the only other smartwatch option at this price point that people should seriously consider. Until another company drops a product around this MSRP, you have two solid choices in the Amazfit Bip 6 and Galaxy Fit 3.

The BirdBuddy has been one of the most popular smart bird feeders since it hit the market a few years ago, but even with Black Friday discounts, the BirdBuddy Home is still a pricey $199. However, the company recently came out with a cheaper alternative: the BirdBuddy Nook starts at $169, but can be found for as little as $99 for Black Friday.

I’ve been testing out the BirdBuddy Nook for the last few weeks in my yard, and I think it’s a fine budget option for those who want to get into smart bird watching.

The BirdBuddy Nook Solar has a 2K HDR camera with a 135° wide-angle view that can be rotated horizontally or vertically. It has a capacity of 3.8 cups (0.9 L) of birdseed.

The larger of BirdBuddy's feeders, the Home can be filled with up to 6 cups / 1.4 liters of birdseed. It can be pole- or wall-mounted, and comes with a metal attachment to hang it from a branch.

The BirdBuddy Nook regularly costs $169 and $189 for the BirdBuddy Solar. For Black Friday, the base model has been discounted to $99, and the Solar model to $129. If you can afford the solar model, go for it — it’ll save you from having to recharge the camera module. I’ve been using the Solar model, and not once have I had to plug it in.

You can also find the older BirdBuddy Pro Solar for sale at Amazon for $179, but that camera is locked to a vertical orientation.

So what’s the difference between BirdBuddy’s feeders, other than the price? Mostly it comes down to capacity. The BirdBuddy Home ($299; on sale for $199) can fit more seed than the Nook, so you won’t have to fill it as often, unless you have ravenous squirrels in your yard, like I do.

Of course, to get the most out of either feeder, you need to sign up for a BirdBuddy subscription, which starts at $7.99/month or $69.99/year. That lets you record video at the highest quality, enjoy automatic AI recognition, and the ability to connect it to Alexa+.

The other major difference is in how you fill the feeder. The entire roof of the Nook hinges upwards so that you can fill its innards; the Home has a smaller opening in its rear. I found it’s very easy to accidentally overfill the Nook, especially if it’s mounted on a pole.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Otherwise, the Nook has the same camera as the BirdBuddy Home, which, while not as good as the now-discontinued BirdBuddy Pro, delivers more than respectable 2K videos and photos. Like the Home, the Nook’s camera can be rotated so you can record either portrait or landscape videos. I’m still not a fan of how the camera has a bit of lens distortion, so that objects near the edges are elongated.

Birdbuddy claims that the Nook’s smaller shelf is better at deterring squirrels. I initially set it up with the perch extender, which may have been a mistake, as it gave the little furry creatures an easy spot to clean out the feeder. Don't get this attachment if you have problems with squirrels.

Given that the cameras on the BirdBuddy Home and BirdBuddy Nook are identical, I would definitely opt for the cheaper Nook; yes, you’ll have to refill it more often, but it’s $110 less expensive. During Black Friday, the price difference is just $70, but that’s still pretty significant.

As I mentioned earlier, get the model with the built-in solar panel. It’ll save you the hassle of having to schlep out to your yard in the middle of winter just to see the squirrels raiding your supply.

#3340. 7 'Peanuts' Episodes That Are 10/10 Animated Masterpieces, Ranked

Ben Brewster is a filmmaker, critic, screenwriter, and actor whose work sits at the intersection of film culture, craft analysis, and storytelling.

He is a movie list contributing writer at Collider and a contributing writer for High on Films, where he covers contemporary cinema, independent film, and festival releases with an eye toward narrative structure, performance, and visual language.

Ben is an active film festival participant, having worked with Newport Film, the Nantucket Film Festival and as a screener for the Austin, Boston & Woodstock film festivals.  He brings to that work a programming instinct shaped by years of close engagement with independent and documentary cinema. This comes with a deep investment in the kinds of films that rarely find their way into the mainstream conversation without someone willing to advocate for them.

His background spans documentary and narrative filmmaking, film marketing, and production, including work with award-winning directors. This as well as developing his own indie production company, Lilac Creative Studio, through which he develops and produces original work across fiction and nonfiction forms.  His debut documentary, Diamond in the Rust, is an examination of economic redevelopment and displacement in the Queens area of New York City. The film was recently accepted to the Unisphere Film Festival, the Defense of Democracy Film Festival, and the Urbanite Arts & Film Festival. This would mark his first festival recognition as a director.  In addition to his writing and programming work, Ben hosts Beneath the Bloom, a film podcast exploring the work behind the scenes in cinema, and the struggles one can face to make a movie become a reality. The show reflects the same sensibility that runs through all of his work. A conviction that film is not merely entertainment but one of the most powerful tools human beings have for understanding each other.

Across mediums, his work is driven by a deep belief in film as a communal, transformative art form.

Peanuts has outlasted almost every cartoon on television, and its holiday specials are its bread and butter. Thanksgiving is Thursday, and A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving is streaming only on Apple TV this year, with no traditional linear broadcast airing. However, a new special, Snoopy Presents: 12 Days of Snoopy, premiered on November 13th, featuring songs from Laufey and John Legend.

Together, the entire library makes the holiday season a perfect time to rank the specials that have built so many family traditions. A note on the choices. I picked specials that critics and viewers both live on and that tie to a date on the calendar. Streaming windows can be quick to change, so check Apple TV before you queue anything up. Spoilers, of course, are not a concern for specials this familiar in the public conversation.

Happy New Year, Charlie Brown! starts on the last day of school before Christmas break, when Charlie Brown's teacher assigns a book report on Leo Tolstoy's War and Peace. Charlie Brown ends up dreading his entire vacation, and attempts every shortcut imaginable around reading the novel. He asks a store whether it comes in a variety of different creative forms, including a computer game. Peppermint Patty keeps calling to invite him to her party, and Marcie, Sally, and Lucie get swept up in the drama of it all.

Charlie brings War and Peace to the party and tries to read it on the porch, but he falls asleep and misses the midnight countdown. The Little Red-Haired Girl shows up and ends up dancing with Linus. But by the end, Charlie finally finishes the book and turns in his report. The special is also a small musical, with songs by Ed Bogas and Desireé Goyette, including a dance lesson number. IMDb users rate the special 7.2, and Collider ranks it third among its best Peanuts specials.

Peppermint Patty spends nearly her entire allowance on eggs in It's the Easter Beagle, Charlie Brown! It is mainly due to the fact Marcie keeps ruining the eggs after she tries to show her how to dye them. She fries the first batch on a griddle, then cracks the next batch before boiling it. Meanwhile, Snoopy tries to find Woodstock a new home and botches that through several different birdhouse attempts. Linus swears the Easter Beagle will hand out eggs, yet Sally doubts him after the Great Pumpkin fiasco.

On Easter morning, Snoopy turns out to be the Easter Beagle. He distributes eggs, including one for Lucy, but runs out before reaching Charlie Brown. The special earned an Emmy nomination for Outstanding Children's Special, and CBS aired it every Easter from 1974 till 2000. Peppermint Patty's exasperated shouts became a running gag moment. IMDb users rate it at 7.5. Its plot is a little thin, but the visual gags, such as Snoopy's dance in a department store, foster memorable moments. Todd Barbee voiced Charlie Brown for the final time, and Linda Ercoli played Peppermint Patty.

The Peanuts are still doing Christmas like no one else can.

Charlie Brown incessantly checks his mailbox over and over in Be My Valentine, convinced that one is on the way. Like the Easter Beagle episode, this one aired on CBS for 25 years. At school, Charlie arrives with a briefcase to carry all the cards and love he expects to get. Snoopy builds an elaborate music box valentine and stages a puppet show about love. Linus, has a massive crush on his teacher, Miss Othmar. He buys her a huge box of chocolates before learning later on she has left with her boyfriend.

Sally mistakes the gift for her own and makes Linus a valentine in return. Unfortunately for Charlie yet again, he ends the day with a single candy heart that reads, "Forget it, kid." Linus chucks the chocolates he got off a bridge, where Snoopy and Woodstock are positioned to catch and eat them. After the special first aired, children across the country sent valentines to Charlie Brown. Violet's used valentine and Snoopy's surprise kiss give the special a bittersweet ending. A follow-up, A Charlie Brown Valentine, was released in 2002, and IMDb users rated the original 7.3.

Charlie Brown's All-Stars! was the first Peanuts special not constructed around a holiday. After Charlie Brown's baseball team quits on him after another loss, he finds himself at his lowest. The hardware store owner, Mr. Hennessy, offers to sponsor the team, put them in an organized league, and buy them real uniforms. The kids rush back, but Charlie Brown soon realizes that the league does not allow girls or dogs. He's then forced to choose between the new gear, and his loyalty to Lucy, Violet, Patty, Frieda, and Snoopy.

Charlie turns down the offer and keeps the secret until after the game. It, of course, leaves his team enraged after they lose. Schroeder finally scolds the girls for their selfishness, and they make Charlie Brown a uniform from Linus's blanket. Yahoo ranks the special fifth among the Peanuts episodes, and IMDb users rate it at 7.5. A Record Store Day release with music from the special is scheduled for November 27th, and the uniform storyline returned in a 1996 remake. The moral decision gives Charlie Brown one of his most admirable moments.

A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving premiered on CBS on November 20th, 1973. It begins when Peppermint Patty invites herself and her friends over to Charlie Brown's for dinner. Charlie is forced to improvise a meal. Snoopy, Woodstock, and Linus help him prepare a feast of toast, pan-fried popcorn, pretzel sticks, jelly beans, and sundaes. Patty rejects the meal for lacking traditional values and foods, until Marcie reminds her that she invited herself.

Rotten Tomatoes lists A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving at 67% from critics and 76% from audiences, a modest score for a special that families consistently rewatch every year. Linus tells the story of the first Thanksgiving along the way, while Snoopy and Woodstock's more traditional meal back at the doghouse adds a touch of sweetness. Peppermint Patty later asks Marcie to apologize for her, an echo of The Courtship of Miles Standish, and then apologizes directly.

In It's the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown, Linus keeps a lonely vigil in a pumpkin patch, certain that the Great Pumpkin will rise. Apple describes the special as Charlie Brown prepping for a party, Snoopy setting his sights on the Red Baron, and Linus awaiting a miracle. Sally joins Linus and misses the party, which leads to one of the funniest rants in the series. Snoopy's Flying Ace sequence turns a doghouse into a World War I airplane.

The special marked its 60th anniversary this year, which ends with Charlie Brown returning home from trick or treating with a bag of rocks. Rotten Tomatoes lists it at 90% from critics and 85% from audiences. Yahoo's ranking of the Peanuts specials put it first and calls it the best Halloween cartoon ever. After it aired, children across the nation sent candy to Charlie Brown and Vince Guaraldi's score includes The Great Pumpkin Waltz.

A Charlie Brown Christmas opens with Charlie feeling down and depressed about the commercialism of the holiday. Charles M. Schulz wrote it, Bill Melendez directed, and Lee Mendelsohn produced. It aired on CBS every year from 1965 till 2000, and then through ABC until 2019. Lucy asks Charlie to direct the gang's Christmas play, and he buys a small, scrawny tree that his friends end up mocking. The special used real child voice actors and left out a laugh track. These were choices that worried CBS mightily at the time, before it won an Emmy and a Peabody Award.

Snoopy decorates his doghouse for a contest, and Linus calmly recites the Christmas story from the Gospel of Luke. Vince Guaraldi's jazz score, including Linus and Lucy and Christmastime Is Here, became as famous as the special itself. Rotten Tomatoes lists it at 86% from critics and 93% from audiences. The 61st anniversary falls on December 9th.

#3339. Three Reasons Not to Use ‘Buy Now, Pay Later’ During Black Friday

Gone are the days of needing to wait until after Thanksgiving to shop some seriously substantial Black Friday sales. As you're adding item after item to your cart during the sale, you might be tempted by offers for an "affordable monthly payment system." Also known as "buy now, pay later" (BNPL), the pitch is a tempting one: Buy what you need now, and pay later, "on your own timeline." But as convenient as it sounds, you should think twice before using buy now, pay later options, whether during Black Friday, Cyber Monday, or at any other time.

While BNPL plans can allow you to pay for purchases in installments without interest, they come with a cost that can easily outweigh any big discounts. Let's take a look at the hidden costs of BNPL, and why you're better off paying upfront for all your Black Friday purchases.

To be clear, Amazon doesn't have its own buy now, pay later program, and the company is not uniquely misleading on this front. The process is straightforward: you choose your items, select Affirm (a third-party lender) at checkout, complete a quick application, and receive an instant decision on your loan terms. Individual transactions initiated through Affirm are limited to $25,000, with a daily maximum of $100,000 across multiple purchases—but of course, your Black Friday splurge will be nowhere near that big, right? (Right?!)

The main draw of these programs is the ability to "pay at your own pace." If you are required to pay a down payment, that is due at the time of the transaction. From there, your first monthly payment is usually due one month after your purchase is processed. Each following payment will be due one month later, on the same day of the month.

You can choose your own timeline, usually spanning 3, 6, 12, or 24 months, depending on the purchase amount and your creditworthiness. Unlike traditional credit cards, Affirm shows you the exact payment amount and total cost upfront, and claims no hidden fees or compound interest.

You need a separate Affirm account in addition to your Amazon Prime membership. The application process requires basic information, including your name, mobile phone number, date of birth, and the last four digits of your Social Security number. Affirm performs a soft credit check initially, which doesn't impact your credit score, though they may conduct a hard inquiry for some loans.

BNPL plans are helpful if you really need to finance something big, but whenever possible, it’s best to avoid taking on debt for everyday expenses.

The ease of this sort of financing can make expensive purchases feel more affordable than they actually are. When you can buy a $1,000 tablet for "just $67 per month," it's easy to lose sight of the total cost, as well as your overall financial picture. In turn, this makes it all too easy to overspend on items you might not have purchased otherwise. You're better off taking a breath, stepping away from your shopping cart, and setting alerts to be notified when a product hits a price you can stomach, at a time you can afford it.

Despite what you may have heard in the past, BNPL providers may report to credit bureaus, meaning your BNPL purchases can in fact affect your credit score. For instance, all Affirm payments (including on-time, late, and missed payments) are now reported to the credit bureau Experian. So if you miss payments or default on the installment plan, it will cause damage to your credit score—making it even harder to get approved for mortgages, auto loans, credit cards, and other financing down the road.

Still, not all BNPL providers report to credit bureaus or use the same type of credit check, so it’s important to understand the specific terms and practices of any service you’re considering.

When you use a credit card, you get valuable purchase protections like extended warranty coverage, price protection, and the ability to dispute fraudulent charges. BNPL plans generally don't come with these safeguards. This means you're on the hook if something goes wrong with your BNPL purchase and the retailer doesn't make things right. The smarter move is to only buy what you can afford during a sale, no matter how tempting those deals may seem.

Although installment plans are helpful if you really need to finance something major, it’s best to avoid taking on debt for everyday expenses. Better to wait for a good price for something you truly need and can afford to pay for right now.

If there's a big-ticket item on sale for Black Friday but it's still out of your budget, consider these two questions before you turn to BNPL through Affirm:

Is this really an essential purchase? BNPL should really only be used on completely necessary purchases that you can’t afford right now, but can afford in six weeks. On that note...

Will I be able to pay this off within six weeks? When a bigger payment gets broken down into smaller installments, you might find yourself overspending in the long run, because it "feels" like you can afford it. Stay on top of how much you’re actually spending—especially if you're considering multiple BNPL purchases—and how it will impact your overall budget going forward.

For more information about deals and discounts, keep an eye on all of Lifehacker's Black Friday coverage.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

The best thing you can do is compare the prices with other retailers that have Black Friday sales. If that seems like too much work, you can just follow our Black Friday coverage (we're already doing all the searching and vetting for you). Some other tips are making sure you're not being sold an older or cheaper version and always reading reviews.

#3338. DC Finally Reveals True Face And Backstory Of Batman's Huge New Villain

DC reveals the identity of Batman's new villain, a dark mirror to Bruce Wayne with even more wealth. Batman pulls off the impossible feat of maintaining his status as a Gotham billionaire socialite while operating nightly as the Dark Knight. By day, Bruce plays the charming if slightly reckless playboy philanthropist, hosting charity galas and staging harmless public distractions that convince Gotham’s media and criminal underworld he's far too pampered and scatterbrained to ever be Batman. Behind closed doors, his strict time management and trusted allies keep Wayne Enterprises running smoothly while Bruce puts on the Batsuit to fight crime.

Gotham City’s upper crust overflows with equally wealthy and influential elites who use their fortunes for less honorable purposes. Oswald Cobblepot runs a huge financial and criminal empire from the Iceberg Lounge, Roman Sionis inherited Janus Cosmetics before building a ruthless mob syndicate, and Thomas Elliot twisted his privileged upbringing into a bitter vendetta against Bruce Wayne himself. Elsewhere in Gotham’s high society, the Court of Owls manipulates the city’s economy from opulent hidden parlors, while Ferris Boyle exploits his monopoly at the expense of innocent lives.

Batman's rogues' gallery hasn't stopped growing, and that includes rival millionaires who weaponize their wealth and influence to oppose Bruce Wayne's heroic efforts.

One full year since his introduction, DC pulls back the curtain on the mysterious mastermind who has restructured Gotham’s underworld since Batman #1. Beneath the minimalist robotic bull mask and dapper three-piece suit, the Minotaur is actually a man named "Max," whose unmasked face and true name are revealed as Batman 2026 Annual #1 takes readers straight to the center of the Torus conspiracy. Max openly declares that his real superpower is cash. He weaponizes capital and banking control to bend the city's deadliest criminals to his will.

The Minotaur's unapologetically wealth-centered philosophy sets him apart from theatrical Gotham villains, who are more commonly associated with tragic accidents, scientific experiments, or gimmicky crime enterprises. Most importantly, it frames Max as a dark mirror to Bruce Wayne himself. Without superhuman abilities, Max treats organized crime like a business as he maps out plans to take a cut of every legitimate and illicit revenue stream in Gotham within twenty months. Alongside Jesse Lonergan’s companion backup, which reveals the Calculator is secretly manipulating Max's "algorithm of crime" for his own ends, Batman 2026 Annual #1 cements the Minotaur as a grounded threat with a bottomless bankroll that rivals Batman's own.

Very few Batman villains have achieved lasting household-name status alongside icons like the Joker, Two-Face, or the Riddler in the past two decades. Professor Pyg earned genuine cult acclaim through Grant Morrison’s Batman and Robin and later video game and television appearances, and The Batman Who Laughs became ubiquitous largely through an aggressive push from DC Comics across multiple multiverse crossovers. Meanwhile, modern Gotham creations like the Designer, Failsafe, Ghost-Maker, and Punchline have struggled to maintain permanent relevance once their original arcs and writers moved on.

Absolute Batman has some of the most disturbing and terrifying villains in all of DC Comics, and they all come with something that makes them unique.

The Bronze Age of the 1970s delivered Ra’s al Ghul, Talia al Ghul, and Man-Bat in rapid succession, and the early 1990s explosion of Bane, Harley Quinn, and Victor Zsasz prove it's possible for Batman to get villains that last. For the Minotaur to avoid fading into obscurity after Matt Fraction's Torus saga wraps up, future writers will need to lean into what makes him genuinely different from traditional costumed criminals. Max's ruthless "cash as a superpower" philosophy and his role as a white-collar crime lord who can bankroll or bankrupt Gotham's classic underworld are his best assets, but he may also need to showcase a wider variety of attributes to stay around longer.

Batman 2026 Annual #1 is now available from DC Comics
