#3335. Hunter Schafer Breaks Down the Meaning Behind 'Blade Runner 2099's Final Scenes

Editor's Note: The following contains spoilers for the entire season of Blade Runner 2099.Blade Runner 2099 is officially out — the thrilling eight-episode series from creator/showrunner Silka Luisa drops today on Prime Video. The series takes place 50 years after Blade Runner 2049 and 90 years after the Ridley Scott film. 2099 introduces us to a version of Los Angeles we've never seen before — one run by replicants. We meet Cora (Hunter Schafer), a human working undercover as a replicant Blade Runner. Hiding in plain sight, Cora slowly learns the truth behind this replicant-run world while partnered with Olwen (Michelle Yeoh), a Blade Runner who is dying within a matter of days.

The series takes Cora and Olwen across Los Angeles, ultimately leading them to discover that what they're hunting for is the truth of the Nexus-1 replicants. Cora learns that her adoptive mother, Helena (Sheila Atim) was one of the original replicants, born alongside Julius (Tom Burke), who eventually killed her while hunting for Tyrell's memory, which hold the secret to creating more Nexus-1 replicants. The series ends ambiguously, with Cora returning to the LAPD after Julius' death and Olwen journeying off to space, uncertain whether she's set to discover new worlds or simply finish off the last remaining days of her life.

Collider spoke with both Schafer and Yeoh about that surprising Blade Runner 2099 finale. The two actors discuss their characters' changing relationships and what leads Cora to protecting Olwen in that final fight against Julius. Yeoh also breaks down that thrilling fight with Clotilde (Amy Lennox) and why that scene was so important for Olwen. Schafer contemplates Cora's final conversation with Greta (Katelyn Rose Downey), and what it might mean for the two humans caught in a world full of replicants.

COLLIDER: One of the scenes I really liked in the finale is seeing Cora protecting Olwen from Julius; I thought that was such a great scene to show the development of their relationship. Can you guys talk about developing that bond between these two characters and going from enemies to these close friends?

HUNTER SCHAFER: Yeah. I mean, it was so magical, as we were getting to know each other as we were getting to know our own respective characters better throughout the filming process; it sort of coincided with the growth of Cora and Olwen's relationship. I think it was a matter of exploring it; I think moments would reveal themselves as more human or intimate with us, depending on the nature of the scene. But I really loved... I mean, especially by Episode 6 when they're really seeing each other for who they are; from then there's a beauty to the mutual understanding.

MICHELLE YEOH: I think the most important thing is that there were no more secrets. Because at the beginning, she had her secrets. She was like a bloody human trying to pretend to be a replicant! That's horrifying for Olwen, who is the replicant who thinks she knows everything and knows what it takes to be a replicant and to be lied to by someone like that.

But, at that point, when we came to confront each other and then finally understand that we both had secrets that we kept from each other, and that secrets freed us and made our bond stronger and made us work together, because we were on the same mission, right? We needed to find what was the answer that could destroy this very fragile place that we have. So I think it was important as a human and as a replicant, we have to work together; otherwise, everything will go to hell.

Along the way, they have learned in very strange ways to care for each other, and that bond was beautiful, because, right at the end, it was like, we fought for each other, not just with each other, but at the end it was how to defend ourselves. So I don't think Cora at any point would not jump in front if she felt Olwen was in trouble.

SCHAFER: Yeah, there's a real kinship by the end.

Michelle, you have this great scene where Olwen's fighting Clotilde, and she has the chance to let her fall to her death. Why do you think that she takes that moment and saves her? Because, obviously, that comes in to benefit her later on, but, at that moment, she could just let her die.

YEOH: I know, I think this is almost like a flashback to Roy Batty and Deckard at that point, where it's like, what is humanity? Does it mean that if you were born as a replicant, you can't find the humanity, you don't understand it? And, at that point, you're right, Olwen could have let her go, because she was getting so badly beaten up by Clotilde. I mean, she could have just [been] like, "Die, you bitch," you know? [Laughs] And then I can just move on to do other things. But then that's what it takes to be human. To save another, whether it's someone who doesn't have a soul or has a soul or whatever it is, but not to just let someone die. And I think that was the humanity that suddenly struck Olwen, and she didn't let go, which then also transferred to Clotilde, because otherwise she would not have had clarity in her head.

SCHAFER: Yeah, they both had desires to live.

YEOH: Yes, and also desires to know the truth. Like, what is this guy Julius selling us? Because he's the one that's like, "I gave you this. This is what you could have. You would come back, and you'd be stronger, and you wouldn't have to die." It was a very special moment in that scene which just turned things around.

Hunter, for you, Cora has that final scene with Greta, and I think it's just such an intriguing moment, especially since I really love Greta in the show. What's your read on what's happening there between these two people?

SCHAFER: I think Blade Runner is famous for its open-ended conclusions in that they are open to interpretation, but I think Cora sees herself in Greta. And Greta is such an intriguing character, in another way, I think, as a human who has infiltrated the LAPD in that world of Blade Runners. Greta is a human as well. So, I think there's a kinship that she feels there, even though they've barely spoken. They've only really done a few empathy tests together and had a few interactions, but human-to-human, there still is that connection together.

YEOH: Yeah, that poor human was actually quite a sad figure because she's forced to be there because she has a gift of being able to detect. And I think she detected that in Cora at the beginning because she sort of reached out to call for help, like help me get away from this.

SCHAFER: Well, yeah, I love that because you're not just part of the test, or if it's really her.

YEOH: Yeah, exactly! And that was like, whoa! Is Cora going to "fall for it"? Is it real? That was so cool.

SCHAFER: And then she drops her face, and Cora passes the test; it's awesome.

#3333. How Often You Need to Order From Amazon to Make Prime Worth It

Black Friday isn't until Nov. 27, but Amazon's early Black Friday sales have been ramping up for several days. For frequent Amazon shoppers, Prime can quickly pay for itself—mostly thanks to the free shipping perk. But how does the math shake out if you aren't regularly ordering from Amazon? Is it worth signing up if you only shop during major sales?

Millions of Amazon Prime users currently pay $14.99 per month or $139 per year for their memberships—though other plans cost less if you qualify. For example, the Amazon Prime Student program allows young adults between the ages of 18 and 24 to get all of the Prime perks for half the cost—$7.49 per month or $69 annually.

If you’re on the fence about signing up for (or renewing) your Prime membership, here’s how to judge whether or not the benefits outweigh the $139 cost.

Here are the main perks of Amazon Prime that make it worth the cost for so many users.

Free two-day shipping on millions of items: This is the main draw of Prime. If you shop frequently on Amazon and want quick free delivery, the shipping perks alone may make Prime worthwhile. Prime members also get free same-day delivery on over 3 million items in eligible areas. The ultra-fast (and morally suspect) shipping usually costs $9.99 per order for non-members, though you can choose lower-cost or free shipping options if you're willing to place larger orders and wait longer to receive them.

Access to Prime Video: Prime includes unlimited streaming of movies, TV shows, and Amazon Originals. If you ask me, the content library isn’t as robust as Netflix or Hulu, but this is still an added value.

Other Prime benefits: You also get Amazon Music for streaming songs, Prime Reading for ebooks, magazines, and audiobooks; Prime gaming, free photo storage, and occasional exclusive discounts/deals.

Amazon Prime Rewards Visa card: Cardholders get 5% back on Amazon/Whole Foods purchases. Prime members who use this card extensively can earn rewards that offset the annual fee.

Number of users: Prime benefits can be shared with other members of your household. The more users, the more value per person.

Let's say you don't care about Prime Video, Amazon Music, or free e-books, and just want to know if you'll save money you would otherwise be spending on shipping.

For non-Prime members, Amazon requires a minimum order of $35 to qualify for free shipping on eligible items. The average shipping costs for non-members aren't publicly listed, and can vary by item and shipping speed, typically ranging from $5 to $10.

For our purposes, I messed around on my non-shared, non-Prime Amazon account to find an average shipping cost of around $6 per order (assuming the order total fell below the $35 threshold, of course). Of course, shipping costs will vary depending on the item and how quickly you want it, but let’s compare the cost to the appeal of Prime’s two-day shipping option. So, we have the cost of individual online orders (around six bucks) compared to the free delivery that comes with an $139 annual fee. This means the costs you’d save on shipping alone make Prime worth the cost as long as you place more than two dozen orders in a year.

In other words: The $139 annual fee pays for itself as long as you order from Amazon Prime at least twice a month.

Of course, this conclusion is strictly in terms of shipping costs. How it stacks up ethically is between you and the person in the mirror.

And then there's this important caveat: You can still get free shipping from Amazon without a Prime membership, provided your order has $35 or more of eligible items. However, this won't grant you Prime shipping speed—your order will typically take five to eight days to be delivered. But you can place fewer, larger orders and wait a little longer, and still never pay for shipping.

Also worth considering is how much of that membership cost you'll be able to recoup via exclusive Prime Day offers. During the sale, some items will be heavily discounted only for Prime members—but whether the Prime Day price is really a "deal" will vary greatly based on the item you're buying. Some of those "big discounts" aren't any greater than what the item typically sells for. The Prime Day price can even be higher than other sale prices throughout the year. That's why it's important to make sure what you're ordering is something you planned to buy anyway—and that the sale price is actually a true bargain—before you order.

The cost of a Prime membership is a solid value for anyone using Amazon 23 times per year or more—especially if you're also watching shows on Prime Video or purchasing something that is deeply discounted for Prime Day. But if you only shop on Amazon a few times a year and don't take advantage of Prime Day offers or the other benefits, then that $139 annual fee isn't necessarily paying for itself.

Of course, if you are interested in Prime Day bargains, you can always sign up right before the start of the sale and then cancel your membership after Prime Day is over—but Amazon doesn't always make it easy on you.

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

Yes. Walmart, Best Buy, Target, and Home Depot will all have in-store deals, some of which you might not find online, so if you're able to take a trip to your local retailer, keep your eyes open for different deals.

#3332. DC Confirms Major Snyderverse Villain's Official Return

Warning: contains spoilers for Justice League Unlimited #25!

DC has confirmed the return of a major Snyderverse Justice League villain, nine years after their last appearance. The DCEU, or “the Snyderverse” as some called it, was DC’s first serious attempt at a cohesive cinematic universe, similar to the MCU. Snyderverse DC films were released consistently for nearly a decade, before the powers that be placed James Gunn in charge.

The Snyderverse launched in 2013 with the arrival of The Man of Steel in theaters. Starring Henry Cavill as Superman, Amy Adams as Lois Lane and Jesse Eisenberg as Lex Luthor, the film was a hit with audiences, but not critics or devoted fans. A follow-up, Batman vs Superman: Dawn of Justice, hit the screens in 2016. Starring Ben Affleck as The Dark Knight, the film seeded the Justice League, introducing Wonder Woman, the Flash, Aquaman and Cyborg to the mix. Like its predecessor, Dawn of Justice received mixed reviews.

During the filming of Justice League, Snyder stepped down from directorial duties due to a family tragedy. Snyder’s involvement with the DCEU faded, leading to films that, while good and entertaining, failed to connect with audiences in the same fashion that Marvel’s movies did. The Snyderverse ended with The Flash, which reset the timeline. Vocal segments of the fandom have demanded Snyder’s vision be reinstated, but the possibility of that happening fades over time. Now, those yearning for a return to the Snyderverse are in luck, as one of its biggest villains returns.

Steppenwolf was created by Jack Kirby, and first appeared in 1972's New Gods #7.

In Justice League Unlimited #25, written by Mark Waid and drawn by Dan Mora, Plastic Man and Detective Chimp are horrified to discover that Steppenwolf, Darkseid’s uncle and a major threat in his own right, has set up a weapons forge underneath the Galaxy Communications Building in Metropolis. They look on as swarms of Parademons put together fantastic weapons for Steppenwolf to use in the service of Darkseid.

The gravity of the League’s situation begins to set in, and Plastic Man starts to panic. The two heroes then learn that Maxwell Lord, wearing the sign of Darkseid on his forehead, is offering support to Steppenwolf and his hordes. Before the two can escape to warn the Justice League, they are taken out by Kanto the Assassin.

Darkseid has many zealots and henchmen waiting to do his bidding, such as Desaad, Mantis and Granny Goodness. Nearly all of Darkseid’s family is at his beck and call too, such as his children Kalibak and Grail, as well as Steppenwolf. One of the most feared warriors in the galaxy, Steppenwolf is powerful enough to take Doomsday down to the wire. On top of being a formidable combatant, Steppenwolfe also has his legions of Parademons, whose only desire is to obey and kill for Darkseid.

DC just announced its new Shazam, as the iconic Justice League hero undergoes a major identity change. Also: a new role for Black Adam.

Movie goers will remember Steppenwolf from 2017’s Justice League movie, where he served as one of the film’s antagonists. Played by Ciaran Hinds, Steppenwolfe attacked Atlantis and Themyscira and took their Mother Boxes. Steppenwolfe planned to enslave Earth’s population, but the combined efforts of the Justice League were able to stop him. Steppenwolf is one of DC’s most underrated villains, but Justice League failed him. When Snyder finally released his cut in 2021, Steppenwolf’s role was larger, allowing audiences to get to know him better, and fear him appropriately.

Steppenwolf is one of DC’s most underrated villains, but Justice League failed him.

And now, nine years after Justice League came and went into theaters, Steppenwolf is getting a shot at redemption. DC is building towards a major, Darkseid-themed event. Steppenwolf’s presence in Justice League Unlimited #25 seems to indicate he will be a part of the crossover as well. While DC’s heroes should fear Darkseid more than any other, Steppenwolfe is not to be underestimated either.

Justice League Unlimited #25 is on sale now from DC Comics!

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

As long as it's an "official" return, as opposed to an unofficial one. "Officially" is always better.

#3327. I Tried Building My Own Interactive World in Google Genie, but Real-Time AI Engines Aren't There Yet

David Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years.

He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.

Beyond the Gemini assistant, Gemini Notebook, and various other AI offerings, Google also develops Genie, a world-building engine intended to help you create immersive visual experiences and games using only text prompts. Think of them like AI videos you can interact with and move through.

With the recently launched Genie 4 update, this tool is purportedly even more powerful. It now allows you to request live edits (like "make it snow") and incorporate sound and dialog into your prompts. Google is also promising more realistic physics and natural movements in its renderings.

These promises point to the future of AI in all kinds of ways—from robotics to world sims—but the tool requires a lot of computing power, and access is limited for the time being. You can dive in now if you're on one of the Google AI Ultra plans ($99.99 or $199.99 a month), or join the waitlist if you're a Google AI Pro user ($19.99 a month). But if you've got access, is it worth the effort (and money)? I put it to the test.

It's no exaggeration to say you can build an entire virtual world in Google Genie. It's going to be a more basic, less developed, and more chaotic world than the one in, say, GTA 6, but you can do it. Think of it like generating an AI video from a prompt, but you can then walk through the video and go as deep as you like, taking turns along the way.

Everything is rendered in real time, at a resolution of 720p and at 24 frames per second. That's not to say the engine is storing a massive 3D map in memory, however—after a minute or so, it's going to start to forget the places you've already seen. And while the basic layout will stay fixed, you might notice disappearing trees or changing colors.

Google's official line is "visual details and object permanence can still shift or drift over time" in Genie 4, so it's a known limitation. The tool is presented as-is, with the intention to develop it further over time as models improve, and it's aimed at filmmakers, historians, designers, scientists, robotics engineers, and game developers. Or indeed, anyone who just wants to get lost in a world that isn't real.

Some of the demos you'll find as you step through the Genie 4 portal give you a great idea of the possibilities. There's a "Dino Field Guide" that, you guessed it, lets you wander safari-style through a prehistoric habitat. All the flora and fauna are neatly rendered, and you even get dinosaur quiz questions along the way—a nod to Genie's potential as an educational tool.

There's a "Villa Giallo" mini-game, which involves searching a haunted 1970s Italian villa and clicking on objects as you go; these objects act as clues to help you progress to the next room. I was also intrigued by a "White House: Code Red" experience that takes you into the West Wing during a "high-stakes national crisis." I couldn't quite figure out what the crisis was, but I definitely felt the highness of the stakes.

Someone's even built a "GTA 7" engine that drops you into a bright and vibrant cityscape. The slow speed and warped physics of the experience suggest Rockstar Games has nothing to worry about just yet—check out the disappearing cars and backwards-driving cops in the video above—but it's impressively detailed all the same, considering it all comes from a few text prompts.

Having checked out a few demos, I felt ready to put Genie 4 to the test myself. Eager not to infringe on any IP, I decided to generate a world where I wouldn't mind getting lost for a few minutes—somewhere I could get away from the stress of my day and enjoy some warmer weather.

I started with the prompt "Create a fully immersive, photorealistic 3D environment showing a pub in an English village in the middle of a hot and sunny day. The pub is surrounded by country lanes, old buildings, and woods, and a handful of villagers are walking around and drinking outside the pub. Use a first-person view and use a quiet background of birdsong and wind rustling in the trees."

It took a couple of minutes for my peaceful, idyllic world to be ready, and then I was immediately able to navigate through it using my keyboard and mouse. Once you're in your world, you are suggested certain prompts you can make use of, like strolling into the pub or getting the villagers to make a toast, and these worked well—evidence that your virtual world really is interactive (to a point).

Unsurprisingly, the usual AI video tells are in abundance: Everyone looks generic, the physics often go sideways, the text on signs is gibberish, and details don't remain fixed. Do a full 360-degree spin around, and you might find that not only have all the customers in the pub changed their appearance, but you're also at an entirely different pub.

The best feature is the ability to make real-time edits: I summoned both a storm and a cricket pitch with a few text prompts, though Genie decided to put a hut in the middle of the cricket pitch for some reason. I think I was most impressed by the moment when a cricketer walked past me and commented on the rain, providing hints of how this kind of tech could expand or augment games and virtual experiences in the future.

That said, even at v4 of Genie, this tech is still very much in the experimental stage, and while I can see the potential, it also shows just how difficult a task world-building is for an AI engine. Without 3D maps and proper physics engines as a foundation, you'll encounter a great deal of hastily rendered slop as you explore your environment. Even if you're a prompting pro, for the time being this is something to mess around with, rather than use in a practical way.

#3323. Tidal Is the First Streaming Platform to Ban AI Music

You have a few options when it comes to choosing a music streaming service. If you own an iPhone and a Mac, you might be tempted by Apple Music; if you have more friends on Spotify, you may feel that's the best platform for you. But if your goal is avoiding AI music as much as humanly possible, there appears to be a new uncontested winner: Tidal.

On Tuesday, Tidal announced plans to ban AI music from its platform entirely. Starting Dec. 9, the company will begin taking steps to remove music it believes is entirely made with AI. Tidal says it thinks the move “will resonate with both artists and listeners alike.”

This isn't the first stand Tidal has taken against AI-generated music. Back in July, the company announced that it would start labeling songs completely made with AI, as well as remove tracks it found to be "fraudulent and deceptive." Other platforms have similar policies, or are rolling out similar features. Apple Music, for example, is working on AI labels for its app, too, and Spotify has pushed back on AI to some degree. However, this most recent move makes Tidal the first music streaming service to outright ban AI-generated music from its catalog.

Robert Anderson, Tidal's Music Lead, posted on X about the change. According to Anderson, Tidal identified 43% of the tracks it received in the last 90 days were AI-generated. Per the company's plan, Tidal will remove 29 million songs by the beginning of 2027, roughly 80,000 to 85,000 removals per day. Some 96% of Tidal's AI-generated songs have zero plays whatsoever.

I wouldn't be surprised to see other music streaming services follow suit, particularly Apple Music. Despite rolling out AI-powered features over the past couple of years, including Apple Music's AI-generated playlists, Apple has taken some stands against AI-generated material in general. The latest Apple TV intro was shot in-camera with practical effects, in an era where the company could have easily generated something with AI. If other companies plan to follow Tidal's lead here, my money's on Apple being first in line.

However, as it stands, Tidal is the only streaming service that supports this initiative. Soon enough, it'll be the sole music app you can use with near-zero ambiguity that the music you're listening to was at least mostly created by humans. (What a sentence.) Avoiding AI-generated music can be tricky, frustrating, and, frankly, exhausting. If that's important to you, Tidal might just be your new pick.

#3321. Every Book in Brandon Sanderson's 'The Stormlight Archive' Series, Ranked

The Stormlight Archive is an ongoing series by Brandon Sanderson, which exists in his shared literary universe known as the Cosmere. The premise of the Cosmere is that each series or stand-alone story takes place on its own planet within the same galaxy. Each planet has a complex magic system, though some stories take place on worlds that are completely non-magical. Over the years, The Stormlight Archive has proven to be one of the flagship entries in the universe, as well as the absolute longest in terms of word count.

Currently, the saga consists of five mainline novels, two novellas, and one stand-alone double feature that consists of two short stories, though the plan is to have 10 mainline novels. Each book is over 1,000 pages long, so it can be quite time-consuming to read, but it's totally worth it. Set on the barren, windswept world of Roshar, each book features flashback sequences from particular characters, which build on their history and establish why and how they first got to use their magic. While every entry is brilliant on its own, they definitely have a hierarchy when compared against each other.

Rhythm of War is the fourth mainline novel of the series, and it's also arguably the worst. It gets off to a strong start, with a huge, climactic evacuation in an emotionally significant location, but it all kind of winds down from there. The flashbacks are a bit awkward and disjointed, split between Listener sisters Eshonai and Venli rather than just one character. Almost all of the main story is set in the city of Urithiru, with little opportunity for exploring the vastness of Roshar. The interludes don't allow for this either, as they generally focus on already-existing characters rather than following the pattern of featuring brief viewpoints of one-offs in distant lands.

By far the worst part of the story is how it just feels like one prolonged science lesson. So much of it is about how light works, how it is used in fabrials, how it can be manipulated, and the various properties of gemstones. It goes on and on and is incredibly overwhelming. Having a complex magic system isn't a problem, but the book tends to overload it a bit too much. Rhythm of War is not a bad book — in fact, it's a very good book — but it doesn't really hold up compared to the others.

Dawnshard is the second novella, which takes place between books three and four. Released alongside Rhythm of War, it is a thrilling tale across the sea to the lost island of Aimia. The main character is Rysn Ftori, a Thaylen merchant who, until then, was strictly an interlude character. Now in the leading role, Rysn desperately seeks Aimia in order to heal her pet larkin, Chiri-Chiri, who originated from the island.

However, Aimia is obstructed by a permanent storm, so this will be no easy feat. Aided by comic relief characters Lopen and his cousin, Huio, this is a simple, linear adventure to the farthest reaches of Roshar, where the mysteries of Aimia are finally unravelled after three full novels of buildup. It's not a perfect book, especially since it's only a side story, but it's a fantastic adventure with a thrilling climax that only thickens the overarching narrative.

Edgedancer is the first novella in the series, set between books two and three. The book opens with a prologue sequence that is a direct copy-and-paste of Lift's interlude from book two. This novella then continues the story, providing an exclusive look into the events that occurred afterwards. Lift takes the lead as she travels to the city of Yeddaw in Tashikk, where she hopes to try all 10 types of ceremonial pancakes made in the city. That might sound silly, but you must understand that Lift is kind of a chaos gremlin, so it's best to just go along with it.

Accompanied by Wyndle, her exhausted spren, Lift finds herself pursued by a vengeful Herald, the very same one she encountered in her interlude. The young rapscallion raises Hell in Yeddaw, ruining grain carts, befuddling guards, befriending orphans, and, as always, stealing food. It's a great, straightforward adventure into a fascinating location, with a hilarious buddy dynamic between Lift and her spren.

Four worlds and four completely different ideas of what a good life looks like. This is where you belong, what it would ask of you, and what you would get back in return.

You belong somewhere old enough that the mountains have names and somebody can still tell you who gave them. Middle-earth is for people who think the right thing is worth doing even when it will not be finished in their lifetime.

You want the sea, a crew, and absolutely nobody telling you where you are allowed to go. The Grand Line is the world for people whose main ambition in life is finding out what is over there.

You would rather be feared and useful than liked and useless. The Continent is a world where the monsters are the straightforward part of the job and the people are where it all gets complicated.

You want the myths to be real and loose in the actual world, and you want to find out at about thirteen that you were never anywhere near as ordinary as everybody kept telling you.

Wind and Truth is the fifth book in the series, and the concluding novel of the first arc. Since it marks the halfway point of the series overall, it's best not to expect a happy ending with this one. This book wasn't received quite so well by fans, mainly because it took a lot of departures from the Stormlight formula. Namely, it doesn't feature five distinct parts — instead, it features ten shorter parts, which correspond to one day. This means part one is day one, part two is day two, and so forth.

Wind and Truth is also the longest novel in the series, coming in at a whopping 1,300+ pages. The ending is tragic but fitting, and presents a beacon of hope while also spreading a blanket of darkness over the world. The flashbacks focus on the Assassin in White, Szeth-son-son-Vallano, and his time in Shinovar, which is an utterly fascinating backstory. Though many fans felt this book had a lot of shortcomings, it is absolutely action-packed, full of great character moments, and serves as a satisfying ending and new beginning all at once.

King Lopen the First of Alethkar / Elsecaller is a specially released double feature consisting of two short stories occurring concurrently, around the end of the second novel. They don't really add anything important to the overall narrative, but they do answer some burning questions that fans had. King Lopen the First of Alethkar occurs when Lopen is temporarily made king by the real king, Elhokar, as a means of creating a decoy so Elhokar can stay in hiding. Lopen is a comic relief character who, armed with a sock puppet, goes on numerous ridiculous misadventures. It's honestly the best story of the two, because it's genuinely hilarious.

Elsecaller follows what happens to Jasnah Kholin, who is missing in action for most of the book. This story isn't particularly funny; it's just Jasnah's adventure across the parallel dimension of Shadesmar as she seeks to find a way back to the Physical Realm. However, she does meet some interesting people who come from planets not yet revealed, which adds to the mystery of the Cosmere. This book might not add much to the story, but it is incredibly fun and quick to read.

The Way of Kings is the very first book in the series, which is nothing short of mind-blowing. It's where readers are first introduced to the world of Roshar, along with its strangeness, size, and variety. The flashbacks centre on Kaladin, a soldier-turned-slave, who is used as arrow fodder in the war between the Listeners and the Alethi. Meanwhile, Dalinar Kholin, uncle of Alethkar's king, begins experiencing strange visions and becomes convinced he needs to unite the 10 Alethi highprinces in their efforts to defeat their enemies, rather than constantly maneuvering against each other in court.

In the distant city of Kharbranth, a young student named Shallan Davar hopes to study with Jasnah Kholin, Elhokar's sister and Dalinar's niece, and one of the brightest scholars in Roshar. This might be the shortest mainline novel in the series (though it is still roughly 1,000 pages long), but it is an absolute masterpiece, not only in its worldbuilding, but in its inspirational moments and action-packed climax. The Way of Kings is one of Sanderson's finest works and is still recommended as an entry point to the Cosmere by many fans.

Words of Radiance is the second mainline novel in the series, picking up immediately where The Way of Kings leaves off. Instead of featuring Kaladin's flashbacks, the book sets its sights on Shallan Davar's past and her childhood growing up in rural Jah Keved. Words of Radiance is commonly cited as the absolute best of the series, with a lot of fans deeming it their favorite, and it's really not hard to see why.

The climax is absolutely unbelievable, genuinely filling the reader with anxiety, dread, sorrow, joy, and relief all at once. There are so many quotable moments in this book, from the fight scene in the arena to Szeth's first encounter with a Herald. A lot changes, yet a lot stays the same, all while the stakes are raised higher than ever before. This book is a solid 10 out of 10. It doesn't waste a single word, and is consistently exciting, even when little is happening.

Oathbringer takes the crown as being the absolute best of the entire saga (so far, anyway). The flashbacks are about Dalinar Kholin and his life as a terrifying combatant. Since much of Dalinar's history is marked by constant civil war and political upheavals, most of his flashbacks are chock-full of violence, with a few major and minor battles scattered in between. Outside of the flashbacks, the story is brilliant, too.

There are numerous large-scale battles that take place throughout the narrative, including the Siege of Kholinar and the climactic Battle of Thaylen Field. There are even more quotable moments in this book, and some utterly devastating death scenes, too. There's so much going on in this novel, yet it's never hard to keep track of things. Oathbringer is honestly one of the greatest fantasy novels ever written, and that's really saying something.

Yellowjackets, the time-hopping survival drama about a group of teenage girls who are stranded in the wilderness in 1996 and do terrible things to survive, is coming to an end. Whether or not it sticks the landing, it's been one helluva ride, and we'll soon have room in the streaming schedule for other other shows about young people having a pretty rough go of it while just trying to survive.

Situated between flashbacks and flash-forwards (not entirely unlike Yellowjackets), mystery/thriller The Wilds sees an airplane full of teenage girls crash on the way to an empowerment program in Hawaii. It quickly becomes clear that the accident was engineered and that the whole thing is some sort of social experiment, and the survivors are forced to compete against each other if they want to live. The show understands the ways in which young women are exploited and expected to compete against each other in the real world, not just a show about girlfights. Stream The Wilds on Prime Video.

A bit more grounded...but only at first glance, The Stranded takes place on a Thai island in the midst of a tsunami. The island was formerly home to a prestigious high school, and a bunch of students have snuck back for an ill-timed party on the last day of class. A bad idea, clearly, after the storm hits. Kraam (Papangkorn Lerkchaleampote), one of the few students who actually lives on the island, is trapped there along with a couple dozen classmates. Kraam knows the island, but Anan (Chutavuth Pattarakampol) assumes leadership while other students either take on necessary roles or fall in line. As the miniseries progresses, the new social order breaks down, even as the island's mysteries reveal themselves and things get weirder and more complex. Stream The Stranded on Netflix.

A handful of influencers get invited to a remote island, which is obviously a very good thing to agree to that will not lead to dramatic complications in any way. Behind the neon-lit party vibes, there's a cult at work and some ritualistic shenanigans with deadly consequences. Eden is more concerned with the survival horror than with some of the deeper themes and mysteries of Yellowjackets, but we're still playing with shifting power dynamics in this Spanish import. Stream Welcome to Eden on Netflix.

The premise of The Leftovers is brilliantly subdued: Around two percent of the world's population disappears without explanation, and it's enough to upend just about everything. Politics have adapted to the new normal, religions have collapsed and reformed, and families have had to make peace with the inexplicable loss of loved ones. The first season revolves around the Garvey family, led by Kevin (Justin Theroux), a sheriff whose wife (Amy Brenneman) left him to join a cult, while subsequent seasons broaden the scope to bring in other characters in other locations. It's more philosophical than Yellowjackets, and quieter, but the shows share an interest in the lingering effects of trauma, and in the stuff we get up to under threat and in the dark. Stream The Leftovers on HBO Max.

The 100 tells the story of the descendants of refugees of nuclear devastation who return to Earth from their habitat in space to encounter the remnants of humanity who have survived on Earth. Naturally, the first people sent to scope things out are the juvenile delinquents (better them than me), and they discover that three civilizations have risen up in the aftermath of the apocalypse, and they are all pretty scary (including one populated by cannibals, naturally). More sci-fi than horror, but the survivalist themes and mysteries here make it more than a decent match. The show builds an impressive mythology over the course of its run, leading to a conclusion that’s borderline metaphysical. Stream The 100 on Pluto TV or buy it from Prime Video.

When pretty, popular girl Kate Wallis (Olivia Holt) goes missing without a trace in 1993, awkward Jeanette Turner (Chiara Aurelia) steps in to fill the gap, modeling herself after Kate by working her way into the missing girl's social circle and getting close with her boyfriend. That's all going great until Kate reappears two years later, accusing Jeanette of having witnessed the events around her disappearance and keeping quiet. Whoops. There's even more going on, as the show shifts back and forth between 1993, 1994, and 1995 to slowly reveal the missing pieces. Season two takes on a different story set in 1999 and 2000, and the forthcoming (surprise) third season will shake things up again. The emphasis here is on mystery, but it's a show about the aftereffects of trauma and of the dark secrets that can tear families and communities apart. Stream Cruel Summer on Hulu.

A massive apocalyptic tidal wave strikes during the 10-year reunion of the graduating class of an all-girls high school. The event leaves them all trapped together (a nightmare in any event), and forced to survive while reliving old struggles and dramas. It's Yellowjackets-esque, absolutely, but also Australian and a comedy, which doesn't feel like as much of a stretch as you'd think given the over-the-top nature of that show. Stream Class of '07 on Prime Video.

A remote, charming town with some deep, dark secrets (the biggest of which, and one that it shares with Yellowjackets, is rather strongly hinted in the title), Gannibal stars Yuya Yagira as Daigo Agawa, a police officer from the big city who takes a job in the super cute (and, of course, remote) village of Kuge following some personal trouble. The perfectly charming Goto family runs the town, more or less, and welcomes Daigo and his family. It's all looking pretty great—until a mysterious man gives Daigo's daughter a severed finger as a gift, and his wife Yuki finds the words "Run Away" scrawled over a door in their new home. Just a couple of reasons why I'm more of a city person. Stream Gannibal on Disney+ and Hulu.

This latter-day plane crash narrative goes all-in on mystery and philosophy, virtually pioneering the timey-wimey reveal format that makes Yellowjackets so juicy. We kick off with flashbacks that peel back the layers of the various crash survivors before diving headfirst into warm-weather polar bears and mysterious underground bunkers and monsters made of smoke. Whether it's an uncommonly smart network show that rewards careful viewing or a load of nonsense is in the eye of the beholder—but it remains one of the most discussed and debated shows in TV history. Stream Lost on Disney+ and Hulu.

Kathryn Newton heads this surprisingly smart Lord of the Flies riff about a group of teenagers forced to create their own community after all the adults disappear and a dense new forest crops up around their small enclave, cutting them off from everything and everyone else. This one's about coming of age in a world where the usual rules are no longer in effect, and about how we're quick to reestablish an oppressive social order even when outside forces are no longer at work. Stream The Society on Netflix.

#3319. Darius Rucker Says Racism From Black Fans Hurts More Than From White Fans

Darius Rucker is fed up with getting hate for making country music ... and he's especially frustrated that some of the criticism is coming from his own community.

The former Hootie & the Blowfish frontman opened up on Bobby Bones' "The Bobbycast" podcast, saying he expected racism from white people when he crossed over into country music ... but never imagined he'd get the same treatment from Black folks.

Darius recalled recently going off on a woman who reminded him he was Black ... firing back that he's been Black for 60 years and doesn't need anyone pointing it out.

The "Wagon Wheel" singer says Black folks should be celebrating his success in a genre where he was told he'd never make it ... instead of criticizing him for breaking barriers.

Darius also recalled a conversation with late country legend Charley Pride, who told him he'd won Entertainer of the Year in 1971 but had never appeared on the cover of Ebony or Jet magazines.

He says both men accomplished what people told them was impossible ... yet felt their achievements were overlooked by their own community.

And while he's learned to deal with racism throughout his career, Darius says rejection from folks who look like him cuts especially deep ... because it "crushes your soul."

#3314. Apple’s ‘just works’ approach is great, but goes a little too far

“It just works” is one of the phrases most commonly associated with Apple. Interestingly, it appears to have been coined by the company’s customers and then used by reviewers before it was later picked up by Steve Jobs.

Of course, it’s now commonly used ironically when Apple products don’t do what they are supposed to (Apple Home, I’m looking at you), but I do think that it’s absolutely the right philosophy and goal – most of the time …

Macworld referenced an Apple brochure from 1996 entitled “Why do people prefer Macintosh?” This is a collection of testimonials from customers, a number of whom use the “it just works” phrasing. It was subsequently used by a number of reviewers. The earliest example I can find of Steve Jobs adopting it was in 1999, when discussing the rollout of FireWire to the Mac in the PowerMac G3.

It’s hot-pluggable. You don’t have to turn your computer off to connect and disconnect peripherals, you can just plug them right in. Again, the drivers are dynamically loaded. There are no terminators and there are no switches. It just works.

(If you have a link to any earlier example, please do let me know in the comments.)

I’m a big fan of the philosophy. Most of the time, users should just be able to get on with the tasks they want to execute without having to worry about the technology. The tech that makes it all possible should sit there quietly in the background.

However, there are cases where I think Apple takes this approach a little too far, and where tech-savvy users at least would like a little more transparency and control.

AirPods firmware updates are a good example. Back in September, there was quite a significant update in the form of custom EQ. It’s a rather basic version, but still a feature many had wanted for a long time. Instead of being able to manually trigger the update, users had to wait until it “just worked.”

Apple’s support document has a how-to guide that is essentially an outline of the conditions required to permit an update, and an instruction to simply wait until it happens. Which you will only know by repeatedly checking.

Make sure your AirPods are connected via Bluetooth to your iPhone, iPad or Mac. Connect your charging case to a power source. Put your AirPods in their charging case and close the lid. Keep the lid of the charging case closed, and keep your AirPods in Bluetooth range of your iPhone, iPad or Mac. Wait at least 30 minutes for the firmware to be updated. Check the firmware version again.

Another example, and one I’ve complained about before, is that there is no way to manually trigger an iCloud document sync, nor any progress indicator when it does finally happen. In the best of cases, it takes seconds; in the worst, many hours. And again, the only way to find out is to repeatedly check.

It’s the same story when shooting a video on your iPhone. Will it still be there an hour later, available to instantly edit and view? Maybe, or maybe it will have been offloaded to the cloud, requiring it to be downloaded before you can do anything with it – while a video you shot months earlier is still stored locally on the device! You can, of course, switch off optimization altogether, but if you choose to use it, you get no control over it. I want a setting that allows me to do things like specify local retention of all photos and videos taken within the past fortnight.

Will that video be available in the Mac Photos app when you check half an hour later? Maybe, maybe not. You can click the Sync Now button as many times as you like, and it will apparently have no effect, claiming it’s up to date despite the video being entirely absent. It will be there when it’s there.

Once it is in the Photos app on your Mac, it’s a similar story when exporting it to a folder. You can drag and drop the video into the folder, and this time you are manually triggering the transfer (yay!), but there will be absolutely no visual indication that it is in progress. No grayed-out icon, no progress bar, nothing. So far as the user interface is concerned, it appears that your drag and drop had no effect – until the video file finally appears.

I think with all of these things and more, Apple needs to offer options. Yes, most non-tech users may be perfectly happy to just wait until things happen, but there ought to be a standard way to trigger things that currently happen in their own sweet time, as well as progress indicators and confirmation that a process is complete.

Is this an ecosystem-wide improvement you’d like to see? Please share your thoughts in the comments and add any frustrating examples of your own.

#3312. Netflix Officially Loses All 100 Episodes of ‘Teen Wolf’ Next Week

The young adult genre has remained a staple of television for decades. However, the genre has shifted toward romance and cultural issues, while earlier YA was dominated by supernatural stories, giving rise to hits like Buffy the Vampire Slayer, The Vampire Diaries, Supernatural, and more. Back then, monsters and magic served as heavy-handed metaphors for the anxieties of growing up. Vampires symbolized forbidden desire, while apocalypses mirrored the overwhelming pressure of high school. No show captured all these themes as perfectly as MTV's hit series Teen Wolf.

Airing from 2011 to 2017, the series transformed a campy 1980s comedy into a dark, high-stakes teen drama. For Scott McCall (Tyler Posey), becoming a werewolf was the ultimate allegory for puberty — sudden physical changes, uncontrollable emotions, and the desperate need to fit in while hiding a terrifying secret. Teen Wolf balanced lacrosse practice and chemistry homework with bloody hunts, existential threats, and ancient lore, proving that surviving adolescence felt just as dangerous as fighting a literal monster. Its massive success marked the peak of the supernatural YA era, uniting a loyal fanbase around found family and mythical lore.

Although it ended close to a decade ago, Teen Wolf remains one of the world's most beloved shows, and fan demand has not waned. That relentless enthusiasm eventually prompted Paramount+ to release Teen Wolf: The Movie in 2023, bringing Scott McCall and the pack back to Beacon Hills. Despite mixed reviews, the reunion shattered the streamer's debut-day records, proving the fandom's undeniable staying power. While Paramount+ had planned a three-picture installment, the failure of the first led to the cancellation of the trilogy, but star Posey revealed that he had been working behind the scenes to bring the pack back together.

The series' enduring appeal sparked another resurgence when all six seasons returned to Netflix in late 2025 after a decade-long absence, racking up over 20 million views and introducing a whole new generation to its supernatural drama. However, licensing deals have expiry dates, and after a year-long stint on Netflix, Teen Wolf is set to be removed from the streaming service next week, on December 1. For viewers who aren't fully caught up with the story, all episodes will be available on Prime Video and MGM+, but they require a subscription to watch. Like other shows, Teen Wolf is also available for purchase on digital stores like Apple TV, Amazon, and Fandango.

Catch up with the series on Netflix before it leaves on December 1, and stay tuned to Collider for more updates.

#3310. If You Loved 'Cupertino,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Cupertino is one of those TV shows that arrived just when we all needed it. In this economy, a story about two lawyers who get shafted by the “move fast and break things” culture of Silicon Valley and decide to use their legal chops to fight back was almost destined to be a hit, and the great performances by Mike Colter and Rachel Keller sealed the deal. If you love the sharp legal wrangling and tech-focused storylines and want a movie that perfectly complements the show, it’s time to watch (or re-watch) Aaron Sorkin and David Fincher’s 2010 masterpiece, The Social Network.

Just like Cupertino, The Social Network arrived at precisely the right moment in history—just when everyone was beginning to wonder if the social media revolution kicked off by Facebook and Mark Zuckerberg was actually a good idea or not. While it might seem hard to imagine, there was a time when Facebook was the social media platform—everyone was on it, and it dominated the conversation like nothing else. And the outsized wealth and influence Zuckerberg accrued as a result were just starting to make people a little uneasy.

At its core, The Social Network is a legal drama—the framing narrative involves dual lawsuits brought against Zuckerberg and the depositions he is giving, which prompt flashbacks to the formation and success of Facebook in the early 2000s. Like Cupertino, the story is soaked in the “apologize later” culture of tech startups, and traces the ruthlessness and cold genius of Zuckerberg as he cements his control over the platform, ices out former partners, and generally behaves like a sociopathic genius (Jesse Eisenberg’s performance as Zuckerberg is coldly compelling).

The film doesn’t have any kind of clear-cut ending where the good guys win, but there’s a certain satisfaction in the way Sorkin’s script and Eisenberg’s performance strip away the glamour of Zuckerberg’s money and success, reducing him in many ways to an aggrieved loner who translated his rage into a brilliant idea, and then has to isolate himself from everyone in order to maintain his control over it. The Zuckerberg depicted in the film is a lonely, bitter dude, and it’s as much of a happy ending as you’ll get. It’s a fascinating story of legal maneuvering and bickering lawyers against a backdrop of one of the foundational social media moments that shaped modern culture, and fans of the show will dig it. Stream The Social Network on Pluto or rent it on Prime Video.

Still craving legal drama, tech-sector skulduggery, or more David-versus-Goliath courtroom fireworks? Here are a few more movies that fans of Cupertino will love.

It’s set nowhere near Silicon Valley, but Michael Clayton is a real barn-burner of a paranoid legal thriller. George Clooney plays the title role, a “fixer” for a big-money law firm. When his mentor and friend, Arthur Edens (Tom Wilkinson), suffers a mental breakdown while working on a case involving a toxic weedkiller produced by one of the firm’s clients and becomes a security threat, he’s assassinated, and Clayton is forced to reckon with his role in the world and how much injustice he’s willing to tolerate in exchange for money. It’s tense, smart, and has a wonderfully satisfying conclusion that fans of legal dramas where the good guys are willing to sacrifice (and win) will cheer. Rent Michael Clayton on Prime Video.

Based on real events, Dark Waters will appeal to anyone who likes to see smart lawyers take on enormous corporations in a search for the truth. A successful corporate lawyer, Robert Bilott (Mark Ruffalo), looks into a series of bizarre cattle deaths in rural West Virginia and stumbles onto evidence that the DuPont corporation has been dumping illegal, unregulated chemicals into the groundwater. Bilott’s years-long effort to hold DuPont responsible for the health impact on the community nearly costs him everything, but his determination to make the system work is ultimately the kind of inspiring legal story fans of Cupertino will appreciate. Rent Dark Waters on Prime Video.

If you just want the simple pleasures of a thrilling legal procedural, you can’t do much better than A Civil Action. John Travolta (at the height of his comeback) plays attorney Jan Schlichtmann, who takes on a class action lawsuit against two huge corporations because he thinks the case will be lucrative and relatively straightforward. As the case saps his resources and brings his firm to the brink of collapse, however, Schlichtmann slowly realizes that he’s fighting for more than just a big payday. Fair warning: This isn’t a feel-good movie in many ways, but it definitely brings those David-versus-Goliath vibes that Cupertino trades in. Rent A Civil Action on Prime Video.

The true story behind the effort to license the video game Tetris from the Soviet-era Russian government doesn’t have the same stakes as many of the stories in Cupertino, and it’s certainly no longer timely. But the globe-trotting legal maze that Henk Rogers (Taron Egerton) must navigate to secure the rights, which seem to keep twisting and slipping from his grasp as various political and corporate interests weigh in, is just as fun and fascinating as the legal battles on the show. Tetris may no longer be a novel sensation in the gaming world, but it’s fascinating to see how something so baked into modern pop culture achieved that status. Stream Tetris on Apple TV or rent it on Prime Video.

If your favorite part of Cupertino is its exploration of the way tech companies impact our lives, and the way decisions made in obscure corporate offices can have enormous consequences, BlackBerry will be a favorite. Based on true events, it tells the story of how Research in Motion (RIM) created what was, for a time, the most dominant phone in the world—and how the company lost everything when its leaders took their eye off the ball and let personal obsessions and grudges impede their work. With a cast that includes Jay Baruchel and Glenn Howerton, this story of Silicon Valley hubris is right on target for Cupertino fans. Stream Blackberry on Netflix, Kanopy, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

#3309. Hayden Panettiere's Death: Zach Hickerson Describes Her Final Moments

Zach Hickerson -- the brother of Hayden Panettiere's boyfriend who was with her when she died -- is detailing her last moments in a bombshell new interview with TMZ.

Zach sat down with our own Charlie Neff ... and he described going over to the Airbnb where Hayden and Brian Hickerson were staying on the day she died ... and the tragedy that ensued.

Zach says he initially didn't think it was odd to find Hayden sitting with her legs crossed and slumped forward ... but he began to worry when he sat down near her, and she didn't stir.

He told Brian about it, and -- when Brian lifted Hayden toward him -- Zach saw her face had turned purple ... and he knew something was wrong.

ZH says he immediately called 911 ... and began performing CPR on his close friend. Eventually, first responders took over ... and Zach said he just had to sit back, watch and pray while they tried to save her life. Zach says Brian was distraught and in disbelief during the ordeal.

Ultimately, Zach says he was kneeling at Hayden's feet and praying when the paramedics pronounced her dead ... at which point he said his goodbyes and exited the residence.

As you know ... authorities ruled Hayden's death an accidental drug overdose -- noting she had 4 drugs, including fentanyl, in her system when she died.

All of Hollywood rushed to pay tribute to the late star ... while Brian and Zach received a lot of heat, both from people who knew Hayden and fans at large.

Zach also told us about his plans to honor Hayden by starting a foundation to help people dealing with drug addiction ... and he tells a parable that perfectly describes how he views the late star.

Charlie's interview with Zach hit on numerous topics ... including Hayden's mom, Lesley Vogel, blaming Brian for her death and other backlash he and Brian have received in the last couple of months.

The full interview drops on Friday on YouTube.

Personally, I'm eyeing up the Sonos Move 2, which is $100 off — and it'll mean my current Sonos Move (Gen 1) can be relocated to the garage.

The Sonos Ace were the first over-ear headphones from Sonos and a pretty darn good attempt, too. They've since been replaced by a successor but that means the original model has dropped down to its lowest ever price. You get big, airy sound and some very good spatial tuning. The 30 hours of battery is a big bonus, and it helped them earn a 4.5-star review on launch. This is their lowest price ever and they're the same headphones I use myself most days.

The Beam Gen 2 is a step up from the Beam Gen 1 I use in my house and despite its small footprint, it can easily fill a room with sound. Check out our 4-star review to see why we rate this bar so highly. As discussed, you can build out a Sonos system so the Beam Gen 2 can connect to the sub and Era 100 elsewhere on this list for extra surround and extra bass.

The Sonos Arc Ultra is a wicked soundbar with incredible Dolby Atmos for your movies. If you want the best bass you'll want to add some form of subwoofer (the Sub 4 or Sub mini), but then you've got one of the best "out of box" home theater setups around.

This Sub Mini deal is a solid $100 off, although the starting price has been hiked since last year, so while it's a discount, it's not the biggest saving it could possibly be. This is a rich-sounding soundbar for something so small. It's the perfect audio center for a small room, giving out loads of sound without taking up much space. This compact soundbar supports Dolby Atmos for a wider soundstage when you're watching movies. You can even connect other Sonos speakers to it to act as a physical surround — a mini home cinema, just for you. As well as being reduced in the U.S., British readers can nab a discount on this bar, too.

If you want some extra bass to go with your Sonos system but don't want something as big and impressive as the Sub 4, then the Sub mini is the way to go. It provides a lovely meaty kick to your movies and enriches the sound of your TV shows.

#3307. Apple Calendar got two feature upgrades it really needed in iOS 27

Apple Calendar keeps getting better, including some design updates coming in iOS 27.3. But there are two standout feature upgrades added recently in iOS 27 that Apple’s Calendar app really needed.

I’ve used Apple’s Calendar app for years, and there’s an elegant simplicity to it. But one key area the app has long lagged behind competitors is event creation.

When you need to create a new event, the Calendar app historically has required manually filling in various fields for the title, date, time, invitees, etc. By contrast, the excellent third-party app Fantastical lets you type in natural language and it automatically fills in relevant parameters based on what you type.

In iOS 27, Apple finally introduces its own natural language input for Calendar events. You can type out your event details and certain recognized parameters will be used to automatically fill in the detail fields.

While the feature still isn’t on par with what Fantastical offers, since it doesn’t support as many data points as the third-party alternative, it’s very much a step in the right direction.

Apple has always pitched Siri as being like a personal assistant. As such, calendar-related tasks should have been Siri’s strong suit. But until iOS 27, you couldn’t actually manage your calendar very well using Siri.

With Siri AI, that’s changed in a big way. Now, you can do things like:

One of my favorite personal examples is from this summer when the NFL schedule was released. I asked Siri to find the Dallas Cowboys schedule and add every game to my calendar, and it pulled this off with ease.

Siri is so much better than before at assisting with your calendar, and iOS 27.3 will bring even more capabilities soon.

What are your favorite iOS 27 Apple Calendar upgrades? Let us know in the comments.

#3302. Terrion Arnold Accuses Prosecutors Of Sitting On Evidence In Armed Robbery Case

Terrion Arnold's lawyers say prosecutors in Florida withheld evidence that was favorable to the NFL star, only turning it over after it was too late ... and now they're demanding action.

In a motion filed Monday in Hillsborough County, Arnold's attorneys say on August 21, Terrion's co-defendant, Boakai Hilton, told prosecutors the Seahawks CB never instructed anyone to go up to the apartment, wasn't aware anyone was carrying guns, and had no idea what was going down inside the apartment during the alleged crime.

Hilton also said Arnold simply wanted to talk to one of the men about the alleged stolen property.

The problem, according to Arnold's team? They claim that evidence wasn't turned over to them for more than six weeks.

Hilton eventually cut a plea deal to testify for the prosecution on October 5, and the very next day, officials finally handed over the transcript, according to Arnold's lawyers, who say the evidence was given to them "conveniently after" the crucial deposition of a key witness just days earlier.

Arnold's team says there were several inconsistencies between the witness' account and Hilton's ... but without access to the statement at the time of the deposition, they were unable to effectively challenge her testimony, and they say that's hurt their case.

Terrion's attorney, Harvey Steinberg, told us, "I'm interested in hearing the prosecution's explanation as to why they would withhold evidence that confirms Mr. Arnold's innocence."

Steinberg is now asking the judge to sanction prosecutors over an alleged Brady violation ... arguing the state failed to turn over favorable evidence in a timely manner.

And, the stakes are high. Arnold, a former first-round draft pick, was charged with eight felonies, and is potentially facing life in prison.

He's accused of orchestrating the kidnapping and robbery of three men he allegedly believed stole from his group at an Airbnb in Florida.

Arnold has adamantly denied any wrongdoing.

Prosecutors have not yet filed a response to the motion.

#3301. The Best Last-Minute Gifts That Don't Feel Last Minute

This series will help you pick the perfect presents, decor, and activities to make this Christmas the Best Christmas Ever.

We’ve all experienced gift panic—that sinking feeling when you realize you need a present in an hour and you just don’t have one to give. Whether you spent all year chasing the “perfect” gift or simply procrastinated, your time is nearly up. But don’t panic. The clock may have nearly run out, but your options haven’t. Before you resort to re-gifting something from the back of a closet, here’s how to pull off a last-minute gift that is effortless but feels elevated and worthy of the person you’re giving it to.

With the right presentation, even the most last-minute gift can read as thoughtful. Any performer will tell you that the difference between a good show and a bad one comes down to commitment and confidence. The same is true for last-minute gifts: If you act like your gift is thoughtful and intentional, they’ll think it is. The biggest mistake people make is apologizing as they hand over a present—nothing ruins a vibe faster than, “Sorry this is so last-minute.” So give with confidence.

And focus on presentation. A handwritten note that contains a shared memory or personal joke can elevate a present. Use simple but personal wrapping; craft paper and twine, or a reusable gift bag that looks like you planned ahead. Add a small flourish, like a sprig of holly or a fancy bow. Small touches can make it seem like you’ve carefully prepared. What you don’t want are obvious panic gifts that scream, “I grabbed this on the way here.” The goal is effortless, not frantic.

Digital gifts are your friends. You can order something in minutes that arrives instantly online, and with a little thought, will still read as personal and intentional. The trick is choosing a present that speaks to the recipient’s tastes, hobbies, or quirks, and pairing it with a small note to show you remember what they love. From e-books to streaming subscriptions, these gifts hit the sweet spot of thoughtful and last-minute. Here are some suggestion:

When time is running out, gift cards are your secret weapon. They arrive instantly online, don’t require shipping, and with the right presentation, they can feel surprisingly thoughtful. The key is to pick a card that fits the recipient’s interests and add a personal note. The more specific you are, the better. If your giftee is into Italian food, get them an Eataly gift card. If they're a PC gamer, get them a Steam card. If they're into education, a membership to Skillshare is perfect. There's a gift card out there for just about any interest, and all you have to do it google it and email it.

Generic gift cards can be a last-minute lifesaver that can still seem a little personal if you give them the right way.

Pick a theme or design: Many online cards, like Amazon, Etsy, or Starbucks, let you choose designs. The right visual makes the card feel more intentional.

Include a warm, personal message: Even one line can make a digital card feel thoughtful—something like, “I couldn’t pick just one thing for you. Hope this helps you treat yourself.”

Send strategically: Deliver the card by email or text, but consider printing the email or screenshotting it in a small envelope so it feels like a “real” gift.

Sign someone up for a subscription service, write a note explaining you want to keep giving them presents all year, and you're golden. Here are some suggestions:

SnackCrate: This service sends a different snack from around the world every month.

SpiceClub: For the culinary adventurer on your list. A subscription to RawSpiceBar’s Spice Club delivers a curated selection of spices every month.

Mocktail Club: Booze-free fancy drinks delivered once a month? Sign me up.

Thera Box: If you know someone in need of some self-care, this once-a-month box is packed with wellness and relaxation items.

Loot Crate: If your giftee is geeky, consider this monthly surprise box of pop culture treasures.

Cameo is a platform where celebrities, influencers, musicians, and performers create personalized video messages for fans. If someone on your list is a fan of someone on Cameo, you can set up a session, and give a card with a mysterious note like "Keep an eye out for a special message." They'll be delighted with a personal message from wrestling legend Mick Foley or terrified when Chris Hansen appears on their screen; your choice.

I have enough crap in my house, so I love getting experiences instead of things. The challenge with experience gifts is usually timing: Many require reservations or coordination, but there are plenty of options that let your giftee schedule the time, making them perfect last-minute gifts.

Museum membership cards: Many institutions sell digital gift memberships that the recipient can activate whenever they like.

Movie tickets: Your local multiplex probably has a gift certificate you can buy online.

Local attraction passes: Some city attractions offer gift cards or “anytime admission” tickets that don’t expire immediately.

Pair these with a note explaining why you chose the experience, or, if you have that kind of relationship, something like, "I want to take you to the Museum of Modern Art." Just make sure you follow through and actually go.

Sometimes, there’s literally no time to order, wrap, or even think about a gift. If you’re scrambling out the door and need something now, you might be able to fake your way through, even if you're stopping at the liquor store on the way to the Christmas party.

Flowers or a small potted plant: Give a seasonal bouquet or a small indoor plant. Add a handwritten note, even a single line, and it might come off as thoughtful.

Gourmet chocolates or candy: Specialty chocolates from a local shop or grocery store display can feel luxe with a little ribbon or bag.

Wine, craft beer, or non-alcoholic beverage: A bottle with a clean label or interesting packaging immediately elevates your gift. Ask the clerk at the liquor store to help you find something unique.

Lottery tickets: Who wouldn't appreciate a bunch of scratch-off lottery tickets?

Hard cash is the most impersonal gift of all, but the only one you know will be used. This gift really depends on the person getting it, so be aware of whether they're likely to think "Just what I wanted!" or "Wait, I'm not poor." If you give cash, make sure it's crisp bills in a nice card, with a personalized note.

#3300. Signal now blocks screenshots on iPhone to stop Siri AI from seeing chats

Popular secure messaging app Signal has rolled out a new update that automatically disables screenshots for the sake of blocking Siri AI from reading your chats. Here are the details.

Signal’s latest app update on iPhone disables a key system feature: taking screenshots.

As Signal told Reuters, that’s because Apple doesn’t currently provide better tools for iOS developers to safeguard app content from Siri AI and third-party AI agents.

By default, users who update and try to take a screenshot will see a message that says: “Screenshot prevented by ‘Block Siri AI’ setting.”

Signal now blocks in-app screenshots on iPhone to keep Siri AI from reading chatsIt’s a new toggle in settings that’s on by default, but can be turned offNo equivalent for its Mac app pic.twitter.com/ImsinqMNPq

Here’s exactly what that toggle does, per the in-app settings:

Prevent Siri AI from scanning Signal content. This will also block you from taking screenshots in the app and App Switcher.

Apple already lets you block Siri AI from accessing whichever apps you manually exclude, and that became even easier in iOS 27.2. But rather than directing users to that system option, Signal seems to believe it needed to take action itself with this update.

What do you think of Signal’s latest move? Let us know in the comments.

I expected to see big discounts on older models of the Garmin Fenix this Black Friday, and you can save big on the Fenix 8 or Fenix 8 Pro right now, but I didn’t think Garmin would reduce the new Fenix 9.

I’m delighted to be wrong on this one, because the entire Garmin Fenix 9 line-up is currently $100 off, the first notable discount the watch has got since it launched in late August.

There are a lot of models to pick between in the sale, but the model I tested and use to track my own training is the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro, which is $1,099 at Amazon right now.

All models of the Garmin Fenix 9 are reduced by $100 for Black Friday, including the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro with InReach, which is the watch I tested for our review. It packs in all of Garmin's latest and greatest features, and looks great thanks to its all-titanium case.

The Garmin Fenix 9 line-up includes four models. The standard Fenix 9 and three variants of the Fenix 9 Pro, all of which offer a full titanium case as a key upgrade on the base Fenix 9.

When picking between Pro models you have to decide if you want an AMOLED or MIP display — you’ll find the latter on the Fenix 9 Pro Solar.

If you want the longest battery life possible on your Fenix, then opting for a Fenix 9 Pro Solar model is the smart move. The MIP display has solar panels on it to boost the battery life in sunny conditions, and the Pro Solar will outlast the AMOLED models of the Fenix 9.

You also have to make the call on whether you want a Pro model with InReach, giving you extra connectivity when you’re in the great outdoors.

Another major decision is the size you go for — there are 43mm, 47mm and 51mm options, with the battery life and screen size growing with the case size.

I tested the 51mm model, which lasts me over 10 days on a charge with the screen always-on, but it is a large watch and those with slim wrists might prefer a smaller size.

All of the Fenix 9 models offers great design and outstanding sports tracking and navigation features, and they also have useful smarts like music storage with the ability to link up with streaming services.

You can still save more by opting for an older Fenix, and the Garmin Fenix 8 Pro is $849 at Amazon right now, a great deal on a watch that has Garmin’s LTE and satellite connectivity.

The Garmin Fenix 8 Pro still offers better value than the Fenix 9 in the sales thanks to this $350 saving. While the Fenix 9 Pro has a few handy updates and a more attractive all-titanium design, the older watch matches it on key features and is much cheaper.

However, if you want to get the latest model, you can now do so for $100 less, and given how new the Fenix 9 is I think any saving at all is a surprise bonus this Black Friday.
